facts.claim: Thomas Austin was born in 1815 in the village of Baltonsborough in Somerset, England, and died on 15 December 1871.
facts.value: born 1815, Baltonsborough, Somerset; died 15 December 1871

sources.quote: were born at Baltonsborough, Somerset, England, the fifth and sixth sons of John Austin, villager.
Thomas Austin (1815 – 15 December 1871) was an English settler in Australia

facts.caveat: The ADB entry (P. L. Brown, 1966) is a joint entry with his brother James. On cause of death, ADB's life summary says diabetes, while Wikipedia's Barwon Park article says an infected finger. Leave the cause out of the script.

facts.claim: Austin reached Tasmania with his family in 1831, and early in 1837 he crossed Bass Strait and settled where the town of Winchelsea now stands, a spot first called Austin's Ford.
facts.value: 1831 Hobart Town; early 1837 Winchelsea ('Austin's Ford')

sources.quote: Early in 1837 the younger brothers crossed Bass Strait and occupied the site of Winchelsea, first known as Austin's Ford.

facts.caveat: None of substance.

facts.claim: Austin's estate, Barwon Park near Winchelsea in Victoria, grew to 29,000 acres.

sources.quote: Barwon Park, a well-stocked freehold estate of 29,000 acres (11,736 ha)
Winchelsea is located on the Barwon River 115 km south-west of Melbourne and close to Geelong (37 km north-east).

facts.caveat: Wikipedia rounds the area to 12,000 ha and ADB gives 11,736 ha. In narration, say '29,000 acres' or 'a huge sheep estate'. The bluestone mansion people picture was built later, in 1869–71, so in 1859 the Austins lived in an older and smaller homestead. Don't show the mansion as standing in 1859.

facts.claim: Austin belonged to the Acclimatisation Society of Victoria, a group that brought English animals into the colony, and he imported hares, blackbirds and partridges as well as rabbits.
facts.value: Acclimatisation Society of Victoria; hares, blackbirds, partridges

sources.quote: A member of the Acclimatisation Society of Victoria, which introduced new animals and plants to the colony, Austin brought from England hares, blackbirds and partridges.

facts.caveat: The National Trust owns Barwon Park today. Wikipedia's Thomas Austin article cites an 1864 Argus report for the same list of species.

facts.claim: Austin wanted the rabbits as game, so his shooting parties would have something to hunt.
facts.value: game for shooting parties / hunting

sources.quote: In 1859 he also brought 24 rabbits to breed as game for his shooting parties.
Thomas Austin, an English settler aiming to establish a rabbit population for hunting in his estate in mainland Australia, requested that his family in England send some rabbits

facts.caveat: The hunting motive is well documented. The 'touch of home' line is not (see quote_touch_of_home), so give the motive as plain hunting or sport.

facts.claim: On 6 October 1859 Austin's family in Somerset put a mix of wild and tame rabbits aboard the ship Lightning, bound for Australia.
facts.value: 6 October 1859; ship 'Lightning'

sources.quote: On October 6, 1859, Thomas’s brother James sent on board the ship Lightning a consignment of domestic and wild rabbits caught around the family property in Baltonsborough
Austin’s brother, William, sent a consignment of wild rabbits – caught on the family’s land in Baltonsborough in Somerset – together with some domestic rabbits, on the ship Lightning

facts.caveat: Sources disagree on who sent them. The PNAS paper says his brother James, and ADB confirms James had retired to Somerset in 1856. Cambridge's press release says his brother William. Joan Palmer's family memoir, quoted in the paper, makes William a nephew: 'my grandfather, William, was asked by Uncle Thomas'. Wikipedia also says nephew William. In the script, say 'his family back in England'. The paper's intro also says 'South East England' by mistake; Baltonsborough is in Somerset, South West England, which the paper itself states later.

facts.claim: On Christmas Day 1859 the Lightning reached Melbourne with 24 rabbits on board, and they were taken on to Barwon Park.
facts.value: 25 December 1859; 24 rabbits

sources.quote: On Christmas Day of that same year, the consignment arrived in Melbourne with 24 rabbits on board
On Christmas Day, 24 rabbits arrived in Melbourne and were dispatched to Barwon Park.
In December 1859 the clipper Lightning sailed into Port Phillip Bay, Victoria, with a consignment of hares, partridges and 24 wild rabbits destined for Mr Thomas Austin of Barwon Park

facts.caveat: Christmas Day is the arrival date in Melbourne. The National Museum of Australia's text, republished by Australian Geographic, says he 'released' them on Christmas Day. Safest: 'arrived on Christmas Day 1859'. Wikipedia's 'October 1859' release date mixes up the October departure from England.

facts.claim: The voyage from England took about 80 days, from 6 October to Christmas Day.
facts.value: 80 days

sources.quote: they likely bred before or during the 80 d of the journey

facts.caveat: 6 October to 25 December 1859 is exactly 80 days, which matches the paper.

facts.claim: According to a family account, only 13 rabbits left England, 6 young wild ones and 7 tame grey hutch rabbits, but 24 arrived, so they probably bred on the way.
facts.value: 13 sent (6 wild + 7 domestic) → 24 arrived

sources.quote: It was only with great difficulty that he managed to get six; these were half-grown specimens taken from their nests and tamed. To make up the number he bought seven grey rabbits that the villagers had kept in hutches, either as pets or to eat.
the discrepancy between 13 animals sent from Britain and the 24 that arrived in Australia, suggests that they likely bred before or during the 80 d of the journey

facts.caveat: The split of 13 comes from a 20th-century family memoir: Joan A. Palmer, 'Memories of a Riverina Childhood' (NSW University Press, 1993), quoted in the PNAS paper. The paper's genetics support the mix of wild and domestic ancestry, and it calls breeding on board 'likely'. Narrate it as 'probably' or 'family records say'. This also explains why sources give 12, 13 or 24.

facts.claim: DNA passed down through mothers suggests most mainland Australian rabbits trace back to just five female rabbits brought from Europe.
facts.value: 5 females (95% credible interval 3–5)

sources.quote: trace their maternal ancestry back to five females that were introduced from Europe

facts.caveat: This is a statistical estimate from the paper's mainland samples (95% credible interval: 3 to 5 rabbits). Say 'as few as five mothers' or 'about five'.

facts.claim: A 2022 genetic study in PNAS found that most of mainland Australia's rabbits descend from Thomas Austin's one 1859 shipment.
facts.value: 57 of 62 mainland samples in one continent-wide cluster; published 22 Aug 2022

sources.quote: our results provide overwhelming evidence that the large majority of mainland Australian rabbits derive from a single introduction by Thomas Austin.
the largest of which (57 of 62 individuals) includes rabbits from across the country

facts.caveat: It's 'most', not 'all'. Rabbits sampled in Sydney and Cattai National Park have separate, domestic origins ('rabbits in Cattai and Sydney have separate origins'), and the paper thinks finer sampling may turn up more local populations. Full citation: Alves J.M. et al., 'A single introduction of wild rabbits triggered the biological invasion of Australia', PNAS 119(35): e2122734119 (2022). The team was led by Cambridge and CIBIO in Portugal.

facts.claim: The study traced the invading rabbits back to South West England, near Baltonsborough, the village where Austin was born and where his family caught the wild rabbits.
facts.value: South West England / Baltonsborough, Somerset

sources.quote: rare variants were more frequently shared between rabbits in South West England and mainland Australia, again supporting the hypothesis that the source of the invasive population was Baltonsborough
We managed to trace the ancestry of Australia’s invasive population right back to the South-West of England, where Austin’s family collected the rabbits in 1859

facts.caveat: The genetics pin down the region, South West England, and the paper reads that as support for Baltonsborough. Better to say 'traced to the corner of England where Austin was born' than to claim the DNA found the exact village.

facts.claim: Earlier rabbits in Australia were mostly tame, domestic animals, while the rabbits that took over the continent had wild ancestry.
facts.value: earlier = mostly domestic; invasive = wild ancestry

sources.quote: contrary to the earlier introductions, which consisted mostly of domestic animals, the invasive rabbits had wild ancestry
It was the wild animals that had the right stuff that took over Australia

facts.caveat: The ABC line is co-author Mike Letnic (UNSW). The invasive population also carries a substantial share of domestic ancestry, so it's a wild-and-tame hybrid stock, not purely wild.

facts.claim: The researchers analysed DNA from 187 rabbits, including wild ones collected as far back as 1865.
facts.value: 187 rabbits; 179 wild-caught 1865–2018

sources.quote: We have used a total of 187 individuals in this study. Of this, 179 were wild-caught rabbits collected between 1865 and 2018

facts.caveat: The samples came from France (55), Britain (55), mainland Australia (62), Tasmania (2) and New Zealand (5), plus 8 domestic breeds.

facts.claim: Rabbits first came to Australia in 1788, when five tame rabbits arrived in Sydney with the First Fleet, but they were never set loose in the wild.
facts.value: 5 domestic rabbits, 1788

sources.quote: Rabbits were first introduced to mainland Australia when five domestic rabbits were brought to Sydney on the First Fleet in 1788
Andrew Miller, commissary for the First Fleet, listed five rabbits on the initial transport.

facts.caveat: The Australian Geographic text is the National Museum of Australia's 'Defining Moments' piece. It says the First Fleet rabbits 'were never released into the wild' and were probably silver greys.

facts.claim: Historians have found more than 90 records of rabbits brought to mainland Australia before Austin's in 1859, and none of them took over the continent.
facts.value: >90 importations before 1859; at least 30% released into the wild

sources.quote: with >90 records before the popularly cited 1859 Barwon Park (near Geelong, Victoria) release by Thomas Austin

there are historical records of over 90 importations into mainland Australia before 1859, when Thomas Austin released wild English rabbits at Barwon Park. Of these 90, at least 30% were reported as releases into the wild

facts.caveat: Peacock & Abbott (2013, Australian Journal of Zoology 61) list nearly 300 records of rabbits being imported, sold or released between 1788 and 1900. 'More than 90' is the accurate wording.

facts.claim: Scientists give two main reasons the earlier rabbits fizzled: they were tame breeds poorly suited to the wild, and native predators, especially quolls, kept them in check.
facts.value: genetics (domestic stock) vs native predators (quolls)

sources.quote: This evidence implicates native predators, particularly quolls (Dasyurus spp.) as responsible for the widespread and early failure of rabbits to establish on mainland Australia.
suggesting that these rabbits were genetically more prone to invasion than previous releases

facts.caveat: This is an open scientific debate. Alves et al. also credit the spread of sheep pasture and settlers killing predators. Peacock & Abbott see Barwon Park as 'a primary location' but argue rabbits established from several places. Present it as a combination of causes, not one proven cause.

facts.claim: Feral rabbits had already appeared in Tasmania by 1827, decades before Austin, but they stayed a local problem.

sources.quote: The first feral populations were observed in Tasmania in 1827.
the common rabbit is becoming so numerous throughout the colony, that they are running about on some large estates by thousands

facts.caveat: Wikipedia attributes the 1827 quote to a Tasmanian newspaper without a full citation in the text. DPIRD says rabbits were also on at least one island off Western Australia by 1827.

facts.claim: Even in South Australia, rabbits were released for sport at the Anlaby Estate in 1857–58, but that population stayed fairly stable for years.
facts.value: 1857–1858, Anlaby Estate, SA

sources.quote: In 1857–1858, Alexander Buchanan, overseer for F. H. Dutton's Anlaby Estate in the Mid-North of South Australia, released a number of rabbits for hunting sport.

facts.caveat: Wikipedia says this population was stable until about 1866 and out of control by 1867. The 2022 study found no distinct rabbit stock near South Australia, so the explosion there may come from the Barwon Park stock or simply wasn't sampled. Best left out of a 60-second Short.

facts.claim: Within three years, by 1862, a newspaper reported that 'Austin rabbits' numbered in the thousands.
facts.value: thousands by 1862

sources.quote: Within 3 y, the 1862 Chronicle stated how “Austin rabbits” numbered in the thousands
Within three years, ‘Austin rabbits’ had multiplied into thousands, according to a local newspaper report and Austin himself.

facts.caveat: The paper reports a contemporary newspaper. 'Thousands' is the honest wording, without a precise figure.

facts.claim: In 1865, Austin himself wrote to the Geelong Advertiser that he had killed 20,000 rabbits on his estate.
facts.value: 20,000 (1865, Austin's own report)

sources.quote: in 1865, Austin himself reports to the Geelong Advertiser how he killed 20,000 rabbits at his estate, as a statement to the “extraordinary fecundity of the English rabbit.”

facts.caveat: Other sources give different figures. The NMA says 'By 1866 hunters had bagged 14,000 on the Barwon Park estate'. Wikipedia says 'by 1866, the Geelong Advertiser reported 50,000 having been killed by hunters', cited only to an 1866 British newspaper. These may count different things (Austin's running total vs one season's bag vs the wider district). I couldn't check the original Trove newspapers because the site blocks automated access with a bot check. If used: 'Six years later, Austin said he had killed 20,000 on his estate alone.'

facts.claim: The National Museum of Australia says hunters had bagged 14,000 rabbits on the Barwon Park estate by 1866.

sources.quote: By 1866 hunters had bagged 14,000 on the Barwon Park estate.

facts.caveat: This conflicts with the 20,000 figure for 1865 (PNAS) and 50,000 for 1866 (Wikipedia). A review of Bruce Munday's book 'Those Wild Rabbits', seen only as a search snippet, gives 14,253 for an 1866 shoot. Pick one number, attribute it to its source, and don't mix them.

facts.claim: Eight years after the rabbits arrived, in December 1867, Queen Victoria's son Prince Alfred went shooting at Barwon Park, and his party shot over 1,000 rabbits in three and a half hours.

sources.quote: In three and half hours over 1000 rabbits were shot by the party. The Prince alone shot 416
he claimed 432 of the 1532 rabbits shot that day

facts.caveat: Press reports at the time varied: Museums Victoria (search snippet) gives 'between 400 and 1000 rabbits (depending on the report)'. Wikipedia's Barwon Park article dates the first visit to Tuesday 3 December 1867. For an all-ages audience, keep this off-screen: show a number or a crown icon, not shooting.

facts.claim: Austin's rabbits also went to New Zealand: a batch he supplied was among the successful releases there in the 1860s.
facts.value: New Zealand liberations 1864–1867 included Austin's rabbits

sources.quote: successful liberations of rabbits in New Zealand between 1864 and 1867, which included a batch of rabbits provided by Austin himself

facts.caveat: This is historical evidence the paper cites. Its genetics actually suggest New Zealand rabbits are more closely related to Eastern England, not to Austin's stock, so don't claim New Zealand's rabbits all came from Austin.

facts.claim: The rabbits spread across Australia at about 100 kilometres a year, the fastest colonisation by an introduced mammal ever recorded.
facts.value: 100 km per year; 50 years; 13× their native Iberian range

sources.quote: At a rate of 100 km per year, it took rabbits 50 y to cover an area 13 times the size of their native range in the Iberian Peninsula, making this the fastest colonization rate for an introduced mammal ever recorded
Within 70 years they spread to 70 per cent of Australia’s land mass, the fastest known invasion by a mammal anywhere in the world.

facts.caveat: Keep the qualifier 'introduced mammal'. The NMA puts it differently: two-thirds of Australia, 'an area 25 times the size of Britain', in 50 years. Feral.org.au says 130 km a year, which is unsourced, so use 100 km.

facts.claim: Rabbits had crossed the Murray River into New South Wales by 1880, reached Queensland by 1886, and crossed the Nullarbor to Western Australia by 1894.

sources.quote: By 1880 they’d crossed the Murray River into New South Wales and had reached Queensland by 1886. In 1894 they’d traversed the Nullarbor and populated Western Australia.
By 1894, they had advanced across the Nullarbor Plain and reached Western Australias border.

facts.caveat: PestSmart gives slightly different milestones: 'By 1886, rabbits had spread north to New South Wales and Queensland. They were in Western Australia and the Northern Territory by 1900.' Use rounded wording: 'the WA border by the 1890s'.

facts.claim: A wild rabbit can start breeding at about four months old.
facts.value: 4 months (NSW DPI: 3–4 months)

sources.quote: Wild rabbits can begin breeding at four months old

facts.caveat: PestSmart is the national pest-management toolkit run by the Centre for Invasive Species Solutions. NSW DPI (search snippet only, page blocked) says '3–4 months'.

facts.claim: In good conditions a female rabbit can have five or more litters a year, and up to about 30 babies a year.
facts.value: PestSmart: 5+ litters, up to 5 young each; DPIRD: up to 30 kittens in 6–7 litters

sources.quote: may produce five or more litters in a year, with up to five young per litter
a single doe may produce up to 30 kittens in 6 or 7 litters a year.

facts.caveat: Figures vary with conditions: in bad years PestSmart says 'one or two litters'. Litters per year differ by source (5+, 6–7, and 7–8 per an NSW DPI snippet). Safe narration: 'up to 30 babies a year'.

facts.claim: A rabbit pregnancy lasts only about 30 days.
facts.value: about 30 days (28–30)

sources.quote: Gestation lasts about 30 days.
Rabbits have a gestation time of 28–30 days.

facts.caveat: Say 'about a month'.

facts.claim: Tasmania's environment department says a single pair of rabbits can become more than 180 rabbits in just 18 months.
facts.value: 1 pair → 180+ in 18 months

sources.quote: A pair of rabbits can become over 180 rabbits in just 18 months.

facts.caveat: This is a government claim with no worked calculation, and it describes ideal conditions. DPIRD notes 'a 60 to 70% death rate among kittens up to a month old'. Say 'can'.

facts.claim: Most baby rabbits don't survive their first month, but there are so many that the population still explodes.
facts.value: 60–70% kitten death rate in first month

sources.quote: the high reproductive rate can be offset by a 60 to 70% death rate among kittens up to a month old.

facts.caveat: Optional context so the biology math isn't overstated.

facts.claim: Western Australia's agriculture department states that most Australian rabbits are descended from 24 wild rabbits released near Geelong in 1859.
facts.value: 24 rabbits, near Geelong, 1859

sources.quote: Most Australian rabbits are descended from 24 wild rabbits released near Geelong in 1859.

facts.caveat: This is a government source that agrees with PNAS on '24'. Note that 'wild' is a simplification, since the shipment was mixed wild and tame.

facts.claim: The Lightning was a famous record-breaking clipper ship, built in Boston in 1854 by Donald McKay for the Black Ball Line's Australia run.
facts.value: built 1854, Boston, Donald McKay; Black Ball Line

sources.quote: She was built by Donald McKay for James Baines of the Black Ball Line, Liverpool, for the Australia trade.
It had the dubious distinction of carrying, free of charge, early consignments of introduced animals, including rabbits, sent to Thomas Austin of Barwon Park, Winchelsea.

facts.caveat: Calling it 'Lightning', a clipper, is safe. 'HMS Lightning' is wrong: it was a merchant ship. The Victorian Heritage Database's 'free of charge' detail has no primary citation on the page.

facts.claim: About ten years after delivering the rabbits, the Lightning caught fire at Geelong's wharf in October 1869 and sank in Corio Bay, Geelong's worst shipping disaster.
facts.value: 30–31 October 1869, Corio Bay, Geelong

sources.quote: At around 01:00 on 30 October 1869, Lightning caught fire at Geelong in Australia
The wreck of the Lightning caused by fire was the worst shipping calamity in Geelong's history.

facts.caveat: The Victorian Heritage Database lists the date lost as 31/10/1869; the fire started on the night of 30 October. Say 'October 1869'.

facts.claim: Austin is widely quoted as saying a few rabbits 'could do little harm and might provide a touch of home', but no source from 1859 has been found for this line.
facts.value: "The introduction of a few rabbits could do little harm and might provide a touch of home, in addition to a spot of hunting."

sources.quote: He said at the time: "The introduction of a few rabbits could do little harm and might provide a touch of home, in addition to a spot of hunting."
At the time, he had stated, "The introduction of a few rabbits could do little harm and might provide a touch of home, in addition to a spot of hunting".

facts.caveat: The oldest source I could trace is the WA Agriculture Department's centenary page for the State Barrier Fence (1901–2001, archived 2005), which gives no letter, newspaper or date. Wikipedia cites only that page. The ADB biography, the 2022 PNAS paper and Cambridge's press release don't contain it, and no historian or book I could find gives an original source. Treat it as probably apocryphal. If used at all: 'a line often attributed to him' or 'legend says he said…'. Don't voice it as a direct Austin quote.

facts.claim: By the late 1940s, Australia's rabbit population was estimated at around 600 million.
facts.value: ~600 million (late 1940s estimate)

sources.quote: By the late 1940s the rabbit population had risen rapidly to 600 million
myxoma virus was deliberately released into the rabbit population, causing it to drop from an estimated 600 million to around 100 million.

facts.caveat: This is outside the origin domain; it's included only so the '24 → hundreds of millions' hook has a source. It's a rough estimate, not a census, and other domains should confirm it. Don't use '10 billion' (see myths).

myths.claim: 'Within 10 years, two million rabbits could be shot or trapped every year without any noticeable effect on the population.'
myths.why_wrong: This line comes from Wikipedia's 'Rabbits in Australia' article, where it carries a [citation needed] tag (January 2021). I found no primary or authoritative source for it. The documented numbers for the first decade are much smaller and local: 'thousands' by 1862, 20,000 killed on Austin's estate by 1865 (his own report, per PNAS 2022), and 14,000 bagged on the estate by 1866 (NMA). Feral.org.au gives a garbled version ('20,000 ... annually without any noticeable impact'). Don't narrate 'two million a year'.

myths.claim: Austin said: 'The introduction of a few rabbits could do little harm and might provide a touch of home, in addition to a spot of hunting.'
myths.why_wrong: No 1859 letter, newspaper or diary has been found for this. The earliest traceable source is a WA Agriculture Department centenary web page (around 2001), which Wikipedia copies. The ADB biography, the 2022 PNAS paper and Cambridge's press release don't use it. The line is probably apocryphal and should only be presented as 'attributed'.

myths.claim: ALL of Australia's rabbits descend from Austin's 24 (Wikipedia: 'entirely descended').
myths.why_wrong: The PNAS study says 'the large majority of mainland Australian rabbits'. In its sample, 57 of 62 mainland rabbits fall in the main group, while rabbits from Sydney and Cattai have separate, domestic origins. Tasmania and New Zealand have their own histories.

myths.claim: Austin released '13 wild rabbits' (NMA / Australian Geographic) or 'at least 13 wild rabbits' (Wikipedia, citing Agriculture Victoria).
myths.why_wrong: According to the family account quoted in PNAS, the 13 animals sent from England were only 6 wild rabbits plus 7 tame hutch rabbits, and 24 arrived in Melbourne, probably after breeding on the voyage. '13 wild' gets both the number and the wild/tame mix wrong. '24 rabbits arrived' is the best-supported figure, used by PNAS, DPIRD, the National Trust and SLSA.

myths.claim: The rabbits were released in October 1859 (Wikipedia, both the 'Rabbits in Australia' and 'Thomas Austin' articles).
myths.why_wrong: 6 October 1859 is when the shipment left England. It arrived in Melbourne on Christmas Day 1859. The 'Thomas Austin' article cites an undergraduate biology textbook for the October date.

myths.claim: Thomas Austin was the first to bring rabbits to Australia.
myths.why_wrong: Five domestic rabbits came with the First Fleet in 1788, there are more than 90 records of importations to the mainland before 1859, and feral rabbits were seen in Tasmania by 1827. Austin's shipment is the one that triggered the continent-wide invasion.

myths.claim: Austin ordered '12 grey rabbits, five hares, 72 partridges and some sparrows' from his nephew.
myths.why_wrong: This appears in Wikipedia with no proper citation. The sentence sits next to a WA government reference that doesn't contain it. The only well-sourced cargo description is 'hares, partridges and 24 wild rabbits' (State Library of South Australia).

myths.claim: Australia's rabbit invasion began with 24 rabbits brought from England in 1869 (ABC News, 23 Aug 2022).
myths.why_wrong: This is a typo in ABC's article (lede and URL). The year is 1859, per the PNAS paper the article reports on.

myths.claim: At their peak there were about 10 billion rabbits in Australia (Feral.org.au), and they spread at 130 km per year.
myths.why_wrong: No source is given for either number. The usual estimates are about 600 million in the late 1940s (NMA; Wikipedia) and about 100 km per year (PNAS 2022).

myths.claim: Nearly all of Australia's '200 million wild rabbits' trace to Austin's shipment (CNN, Aug 2022).
myths.why_wrong: The PNAS paper gives no current population figure. Its '200 million' is the yearly agricultural cost in dollars ('$200 million'). The 'all' part is also overstated.

myths.claim: The ship was 'HMS Lightning'.
myths.why_wrong: Lightning was a merchant clipper of the Black Ball Line, built by Donald McKay in Boston in 1854. It was not a Royal Navy ship.

story_gold: Only 13 rabbits left England, but 24 got off the ship. According to a family memoir, the wild and tame rabbits probably bred during the 80-day voyage, so the invasion was already growing before it landed. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9436340/
They arrived on Christmas Day 1859, 'Australia's worst Christmas present'. https://www.cam.ac.uk/stories/dna-profiling-solves-australia-rabbit-plague-puzzle

Wild rabbits were so rare around Austin's home village that his relative could find only six, half-grown babies taken from their nests and tamed, and topped up the order with seven grey pet rabbits the villagers kept in hutches. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9436340/
163 years later, DNA tracked the invaders back to South West England, the corner of England where Austin was born (Baltonsborough, Somerset). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9436340/
Most of mainland Australia's rabbits trace back to as few as five mothers (estimate: 3 to 5). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9436340/

There were more than 90 earlier attempts to bring rabbits to the mainland, including five tame rabbits on the First Fleet in 1788. None took over. The one that did was a hunter's order for wild bunnies. https://doi.org/10.1071/ZO12129

The ship that carried them, the record-breaking clipper Lightning, carried the animals 'free of charge'. Ten years later (October 1869) it burned and sank in Geelong harbour, about 37 km from Barwon Park. https://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/shipwrecks/415
Three years after landing, 'Austin rabbits' numbered in the thousands. By 1865 Austin himself said he had killed 20,000 on his estate. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9436340/

Eight years after the 24 arrived, a royal prince (Queen Victoria's son Alfred) visited Barwon Park and his party shot over 1,000 rabbits in three and a half hours (show as a number, not a hunt). https://www.nationaltrust.org.au/places/barwon-park/
Rabbits then spread about 100 km a year, the fastest colonisation by an introduced mammal ever recorded. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9436340/

Biology hook: a rabbit can breed at about four months old, pregnancy takes about a month, and a doe can have up to 30 babies a year. https://pestsmart.org.au/toolkit-resource/rabbit-biology-ecology-and-distribution/ ; https://www.dpird.wa.gov.au/businesses/pests-weeds-and-diseases/animal-pests-diseases/pest-mammals/rabbit/
Irony: Austin's 1966 entry in the Australian Dictionary of Biography doesn't mention rabbits at all. https://adb.anu.edu.au/biography/austin-thomas-1521
Austin even sent a batch of his rabbits to New Zealand in the 1860s. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9436340/
research.notes:
DOMAIN: ORIGIN. Lines safe to narrate as written:
- "Christmas Day, 1859. A ship called Lightning docks in Melbourne carrying 24 rabbits." (PNAS 2022, Cambridge, SLSA, DPIRD, National Trust)
- "They're for a farmer named Thomas Austin, who wants something to hunt." (National Trust, PNAS)
- "Only 13 left England. They probably had babies on the way." Hedge it: the source is a family memoir (Joan Palmer, 1993) quoted in PNAS.
- "In 2022, scientists used DNA to trace most of mainland Australia's rabbits back to this one shipment, and to the corner of England where Austin was born." Say "most", not "all".
- "Five tame rabbits came with the First Fleet in 1788, and more than 90 shipments followed before Austin's. None took over." (PNAS; Peacock & Abbott 2013)
- "A rabbit can breed at four months and have up to 30 babies a year." (PestSmart; DPIRD)
- "Within three years there were thousands." (PNAS citing an 1862 newspaper)
- "They spread about 100 km a year, the fastest of any introduced mammal on record." (PNAS)

AVOID:
- "Two million shot a year within 10 years" (no source).
- The "touch of home" quote as a real Austin quote (probably apocryphal; at most "attributed").
- "13 wild rabbits".
- A release date of "October 1859".
- "All rabbits".
- "HMS Lightning".
- "10 billion".

UNRESOLVED CONFLICTS:
- Who shipped the rabbits: brother James (PNAS text), brother William (Cambridge press release), or nephew William (Palmer memoir, Wikipedia). Use "his family in England".
- Early kill counts: 20,000 on the estate in 1865 (PNAS, from Austin's letter to the Geelong Advertiser) vs 14,000 by 1866 (NMA) vs 50,000 by 1866 (Wikipedia). Pick one and attribute it.
- Whether the rabbits were released on Christmas Day itself or merely arrived in Melbourne that day. Use "arrived".

ACCESS LIMITS: Trove (the NLA newspaper archive) runs a bot check, so I didn't access it and couldn't check original 1860s newspapers. The NMA, Agriculture Victoria, NSW DPI, CSIROpedia and Museums Victoria pages returned 403 / Cloudflare blocks. NMA text comes from its official republication in Australian Geographic. NSW DPI, CSIROpedia and Museums Victoria figures are from search snippets only and aren't relied on above. The PNAS full text was read via the open-access PMC copy (PMC9436340).

CROSS-DOMAIN NOTES for the fence and weapons researchers: the WA government centenary page gives the State Barrier Fence as 1901–1907, 3,256 km including fences No. 1–3. ~600 million rabbits by the late 1940s (NMA). The CSIRO page says "Within 70 years they spread to 70 per cent of Australia's land mass".

TONE (all ages): the 1867 royal shoot and kill counts can be shown as numbers or tally graphics. No hunting or dead-animal imagery.

verdicts.safe_claim: Thomas Austin was born in 1815 in Baltonsborough, Somerset, and died on 15 December 1871.

verdicts.safe_claim: His family took him to Tasmania in 1831. In 1837 he and his brother James crossed Bass Strait and settled at what is now Winchelsea, first called Austin's Ford.

verdicts.note: Thomas did not cross alone: 'the younger brothers' means James and Thomas. The National Trust and Wikipedia confirm the 1831 arrival.

verdicts.safe_claim: Austin built up a huge sheep estate, Barwon Park, eventually 29,000 acres, near Winchelsea in Victoria.
verdicts.safe_value: 29,000 acres (11,736 ha, ADB); National Trust says 12,000 ha

verdicts.note: 29,000 acres is the size the estate eventually reached, so its size in 1859 is not documented. For visuals: in 1859 the family lived in a modest single-storey bluestone house built 1847–55, which Wikipedia's Barwon Park article describes as four rooms, a central passage, an attic and a verandah. The 42-room mansion dates from 1869–71.

verdicts.safe_claim: Austin imported English game animals, including hares and partridges, and later joined the Acclimatisation Society of Victoria.

verdicts.note: Membership is fine, but the Society did not exist until 1861, so the 1859 rabbits were a private import, not a Society project. Wikipedia's version, citing The Argus of 21 April 1864, gives a different list: in 1861 he 'had introduced hares, blackbirds and thrushes' and was 'breeding English wild rabbits and partridges'.

ADB shows a brother James 'in 1856 he retired to Somerset' and a brother William who 'ultimately returned to England'. Palmer's memoir, quoted in the same Cambridge release, has 'my grandfather, William, was asked by Uncle Thomas', which points to a nephew. Use 'his family in England'. Lightning sailed from Liverpool, so don't show it leaving from Somerset.

verdicts.safe_claim: Their maternal DNA points back to only about five founding mothers.

verdicts.safe_claim: Omit from the Short.

verdicts.safe_value: NZ liberations 1864–67 included an Austin batch

verdicts.note: The historical record is confirmed, but the genetics don't show Austin as New Zealand's main source. Best omitted from a 60-second intro.

verdicts.note: My exact-phrase search found nothing older than this circa-2001 WA page, which Wikipedia cites. The ADB, PNAS and Cambridge don't use it. verdicts.safe_claim: By around 1950, Australia had an estimated 600 million rabbits.
verdicts.safe_value: ~600 million (estimate, c. 1950)

evidence.quote: By 1950 rabbit numbers in Australia reached 600 million.

verdicts.note: CSIRO is a stronger source than the NMA for this. It is an estimate, not a census. '24 → hundreds of millions' is safe.

missed: The Acclimatisation Society of Victoria was founded in 1861, two years AFTER the 1859 rabbits, so the rabbits were a private import, not a Society project. https://www.emelbourne.net.au/biogs/EM00033b.htm — "The Acclimatisation Society of Victoria (ASV) was established in 1861"

'Australia's worst Christmas present' (story_gold) is NOT in the Cambridge release. I searched its full text for 'present', 'worst' and 'gift' and found none in that sense. Use it as our own line, without attribution. https://www.cam.ac.uk/stories/dna-profiling-solves-australia-rabbit-plague-puzzle

Five founding mothers: 5 is the UPPER bound of the 95% interval (3–5), and the estimate covers all 62 mainland samples, including the separately introduced Sydney and Cattai rabbits. 'As few as five' is the wrong framing; say 'about five'. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9436340/ — "95% credible interval: 3 to 5 rabbits"

Independent early government source the researcher missed: J.S. Crawford, 'History of the state vermin barrier fences' (WA Dept of Agriculture, 1969). It confirms the Lightning, 1859, Barwon Park and 'pest proportions' within three years, and is also useful for the fence team. https://library.dpird.wa.gov.au/reports/14/ — "originated from a small shipment of the wild type brought on the Clipper “Lightning” in 1859"

The National Trust contradicts itself on the royal shoot. Its places page has 'three and half hours' and a February return shoot (432 of 1,532); its 150th-anniversary page has 'around 1,000 rabbits in three hours' and a return visit 'In 1869'. Use 'about a thousand in an afternoon'. https://www.nationaltrust.org.au/barwon-park-150th/ — "bagged around 1,000 rabbits in three hours"

Story gold: Prince Alfred was the first member of the British royal family to visit Australia, and he stayed in the Austins' modest old homestead, which prompted them to build the mansion. https://www.nationaltrust.org.au/barwon-park-150th/ — "the first member of the royal family to visit Australia"

A further Wikipedia myth: 'While living in England, Austin had been an avid hunter, regularly dedicating his weekends to rabbit shooting.' It is unsourced, and Austin left England as a teenager (born 1815, family to Hobart 1831, per ADB). Don't use it. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabbits_in_Australia

The CNN '200 million rabbits' figure isn't only a misread of PNAS's $200 million. Around 200 million is a widely repeated current estimate (AAP, quoting the chair of Rabbit-Free Australia), though PNAS doesn't give it. AAP also repeats the unsourced '10 billion a century ago', so that myth is in mainstream news. https://aapnews.aap.com.au/news/rabbit-plague-looms-amid-calls-for-new-biocontrols — "Although a far cry from the estimated 10 billion rabbits that infested Australia a century ago, some 200 million currently inhabit the continent"

The Cambridge release contradicts itself on the sender: it says 'Austin’s brother, William', but also quotes Joan Palmer's 'grandfather William' asked by 'Uncle Thomas', which points to a nephew. ADB confirms a brother William returned to England and brother James retired to Somerset in 1856. It's a three-way conflict, so keep 'his family in England'. https://adb.anu.edu.au/biography/austin-thomas-1521 — "The Austin parents and William ultimately returned to England"

The Cambridge release overstates the spread: 'within 50 years ... rabbits would spread across the entire continent'. PNAS says '50 y to cover an area 13 times the size of their native range', and CSIRO says 70% in 70 years. Don't say 'the whole continent in 50 years'. https://www.cam.ac.uk/stories/dna-profiling-solves-australia-rabbit-plague-puzzle

Wikipedia's 'two million shot a year' sentence sits in a paragraph bracketed by {{Citation needed|date=January 2021}} tags, so the whole paragraph is unsourced. That confirms the myth flag. https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rabbits_in_Australia&action=raw

The 1859 house for visuals: a single-storey bluestone house built 1847–1855 ('four rooms, a central passage, and an attic'), now demolished. Don't show the 1869–71 mansion in 1859 scenes. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barwon_Park — "It was a simple, single-storey symmetrical house"

Cross-domain warning for the fence team: PestSmart gives 'a 1700 km rabbit-proof fence' in WA, while the WA government centenary page gives 3,256 km for fences No. 1–3 together. These measure different things (No. 1 fence alone vs all three), so don't mix them. https://pestsmart.org.au/toolkit-resource/rabbit-biology-ecology-and-distribution/ — "The construction of a 1700 km rabbit-proof fence in Western Australia failed to stop the spread"

The Lightning 'sank' because she was deliberately sunk to put out the fire. VHD says she was finally sunk with explosives at about 6 pm, 200 yards from the wharf; Wikipedia says she was scuttled at about 4 pm on the shoals. If shown, show fire and smoke at the wharf rather than a dramatic shipwreck. https://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/shipwrecks/415 — "The wreck was finally removed with explosives."

facts.claim: On Christmas Day 1859, a ship called the Lightning landed 24 rabbits in Melbourne, and they were sent to Thomas Austin's farm, Barwon Park, near Geelong.

sources.quote: On Christmas Day of that same year, the consignment arrived in Melbourne with 24 rabbits on board

when English settler Thomas Austin imported 24 European wild rabbits in 1859

facts.caveat: Use the words 'arrived' or 'imported', not 'released'. The National Museum of Australia says Austin 'released 13 European wild rabbits', and Agriculture Victoria says 'at least 13'. PNAS explains the gap: 13 animals were sent and 24 arrived, so they probably bred during the 80-day voyage. The State Library of Victoria even gives 1860 as the introduction year. Safe wording: 'In 1859, 24 rabbits arrived…'.

sources.quote: the discrepancy between 13 animals sent from Britain and the 24 that arrived in Australia, suggests that they likely bred before or during the 80 d of the journey

facts.caveat: The authors say 'suggests' and 'likely'. This is an inference from historical records, not a documented fact. Present it as 'probably'.

facts.claim: Scientists call it the fastest colonisation by an introduced mammal ever recorded.
facts.value: 'fastest colonization rate for an introduced mammal ever recorded' (PNAS 2022, citing Stodart & Parer 1988)

sources.quote: making this the fastest colonization rate for an introduced mammal ever recorded ( 21 )
The rate of spread of the rabbit in Australia was the fastest of a colonising mammal anywhere in the world.
With the exception of the feral cat in Australia, this is considered to be the fastest rate of any colonizing mammal anywhere in the world

facts.caveat: The claim is repeated everywhere (CSIRO, NMA, Agriculture Victoria, PNAS), but the Commonwealth Threat Abatement Plan (2016) excludes the feral cat. Wikipedia's version ('fastest spread ever recorded of any mammal') carries a 'citation needed' tag. Safest wording: 'one of the fastest invasions by any mammal ever recorded' or 'the fastest colonisation by an introduced mammal ever recorded, scientists say'.

facts.claim: Rabbits took 700 years to spread across Britain. In Australia they covered two-thirds of the continent, an area 25 times the size of Britain, in just 50 years.
facts.value: 700 years (Britain) vs 50 years (two-thirds of Australia, 25× Britain)

sources.quote: the spread of rabbits over Britain took 700 years while the colonisation of two-thirds of Australia, an area 25 times the size of Britain, took only 50 years.

facts.caveat: Read from an archived copy of the NMA page (updated 28 Sep 2022) because the live page is behind Cloudflare. The 25× figure checks out roughly: two-thirds of Australia is about 5.1 million km², and Great Britain is about 0.21 million km².

facts.claim: By 1880 the rabbits had crossed the Murray River into New South Wales.

sources.quote: By 1880 rabbits had crossed the Murray River to New South Wales
The species had spread throughout Victoria and by 1880 was found in New South Wales.

facts.caveat: This dates the main Victorian front. Smaller local releases had existed earlier.

facts.claim: By 1886 the rabbits had reached Queensland.
facts.value: 1886 (first reports in south-west Queensland in the 1880s)

sources.quote: had reached Queensland by 1886
Rabbits were first reported in south-western Queensland in the 1880s

facts.caveat: Biosecurity Queensland adds that by 1886 rabbits were 'scattered from Wompah in the west to Mungindi in the east'. Wikipedia also puts South Australia and Queensland at 1886. South Australia had its own releases (Anlaby and Kapunda) from 1857 to 1860, so avoid 'reached SA in year X'.

facts.claim: By the mid-1890s the rabbits had crossed the Nullarbor into Western Australia.
facts.value: 1894 (NMA) / 1895 (ISC) / 1896 sighting at Eucla (SLWA, inHerit) / 'by 1890 in eastern parts of WA' (Wikipedia)

sources.quote: In 1894 they had traversed the Nullarbor and populated Western Australia.
By 1896 it had been found as far west as Eucla and 200 kilometres further west at Twilight Cove, near Esperance.
Western Australia fell to the invasion in 1895.

facts.caveat: Sources give 1890, 1894, 1895 and 1896. Safe wording: 'by the mid-1890s'. If you show one year on the map, 1894 (NMA) is the most often cited.

facts.claim: By about 1906 the rabbits had covered thousands of kilometres and reached Australia's west coast.

sources.quote: By 1906, rabbits had covered thousands of kilometers reaching the West Coast

facts.caveat: Wikipedia (Rabbit plagues) says 'Feral rabbits were found throughout most of their current range by 1910.' Safe wording: 'within 50 years they'd crossed the continent'.

facts.claim: Rabbits were already found on the far side of Western Australia's rabbit-proof fence in 1902, five years before the fence was finished.
facts.value: Crossed by 1902; fences built 1901–1907

sources.quote: Unfortunately by 1902 rabbits had already been found west of the fence line.
Even before completion, the rabbits were past the fence.

facts.caveat: The fence itself belongs to another research domain. It is included here because it marks the spread timeline. Fence lengths differ by source: No. 1 fence 1,822 / 1,833 / 1,834 km; all three fences about 3,256 km.

facts.claim: Within about 70 years, rabbits occupied about 70 percent of Australia, roughly 5.3 million square kilometres.
facts.value: 70% of Australia; ~5.3 million km²; within 70 years

sources.quote: Within 70 years they spread to 70 per cent of Australia's land mass
Rabbits dominated two-thirds or 70% of the continent within 70 years (equivalent to approximately 5.3 million square kilometres)
Within 70 years of their release, rabbits had spread to cover almost 70 per cent of Australia’s landmass, to an area estimated at 5.3 million square kilometres.

facts.caveat: Other sources say 'within 50 years… almost the entire continent' (NMA, Cambridge) or 'two-thirds in 50 years' (NMA). Don't combine the two time spans. Pick one: either '70% of Australia' or 'two-thirds of Australia within 50 years'. The Invasive Species Council says 'Today, feral rabbits occupy about 70% of Australia.' The Threat Abatement Plan also says 'rabbits have reached their ecological limit within Australia'.

facts.claim: Under good conditions, a single pair of rabbits can become 184 rabbits in just 18 months.
facts.value: 1 pair → 184 in 18 months; 50–60 offspring per female per year

sources.quote: a single pair of rabbits being able to increase to 184 individuals within 18 months
may produce five or more litters per year that results in between 50 to 60 offspring per year per female rabbit

facts.caveat: This is potential growth under favourable conditions (CISS: 'Under favourable conditions'), not an observed average. AFP/VOA's 'as many as seven annual litters' has no primary source.

facts.claim: By about 1950, Australia had an estimated 600 million rabbits.
facts.value: 600 million (late 1940s / by 1950)

sources.quote: By 1950 rabbit numbers in Australia reached 600 million.
By the late 1940s the rabbit population had rapidly increased to 600 million.
the rabbit population, then numbering around 600 million

facts.caveat: This is a rough estimate, not a census, so say 'an estimated 600 million'. The NMA explains the rise: 'a number of high rainfall years… as well as the Second World War, which had reduced manpower for trapping and fence maintenance.' This is the best-sourced peak number. Use it, not '10 billion'.

facts.claim: By the 1940s there were roughly 80 rabbits for every person in Australia.
facts.value: 80 to one

sources.quote: By the 1940s, there were 600 million across the country, outnumbering humans 80 to one.

facts.caveat: This is a journalist's ratio (ACM newspaper, 22 Mar 2022, reporting a CISS report). It is roughly consistent with an Australian population of about 7.6 million at the 1947 census: 600M / 7.6M ≈ 79. Wording: 'about 80 rabbits for every Australian'.

facts.claim: After the myxoma virus was released in 1950, rabbit numbers fell from about 600 million to about 100 million in two years.
facts.value: 600 million → 100 million in the first two years

sources.quote: in the first two years of its use, myxomatosis reduced the rabbit population from 600 million to 100 million.
The virus killed 99.8 per cent of rabbits that caught the infection

facts.caveat: The 99.8% applies to infected rabbits, not the whole population. CISS gives 'by as much as 99 per cent especially in arid areas'. One popular source says 'within three months', which conflicts with the NAA's two years, so use 'within two years'. Myxomatosis is probably another domain's topic. For all ages, show a falling counter, not sick animals.

facts.claim: The rabbits built up resistance, and by 1995 their numbers had climbed back to about 300 million.
facts.value: ~300 million (1995); '200–300 million by 1991' (Wikipedia)

sources.quote: 1995 The rabbit population returns to about 300 million with populations continuing to rise.
Growing genetic resistance in the remaining rabbits had allowed the population to recover to 200–300 million by 1991.

facts.caveat: These are rough estimates, and the Wikipedia figure has no separate footnote. Wording: 'back up to around 300 million by the 1990s'.

facts.claim: Today Australia has an estimated 200 million wild rabbits, but nobody knows the exact number.
facts.value: ~200 million (2025–2026 press, ISC); 'at least 150 million' (NMA 2022); 'under 300 million' (AFP 2023)

sources.quote: The latest population estimate is around 200 million.
an estimated current population of around 200 million
The precise number of rabbits is also only a best guess
Australia is home to at least 150 million feral rabbits

facts.caveat: There is no current national census. FarmOnline (27 Jul 2026) says national monitoring funding was stopped in 2022. The AAP (Apr 2025) quotes Rabbit-Free Australia chair Craig Magnussen: 'Rabbits are already numbering more than 200 million.' Narrate it as 'around 200 million, and nobody knows exactly'. Do not attribute the 200 million to PNAS (see myths).

facts.claim: Rabbits still cost Australian farmers more than 200 million Australian dollars a year in lost production.
facts.value: A$206 million (Gong et al. 2009); A$217 million in 2013–14 (McLeod 2016); A$239 million (CSIRO 2017); 'more than $200 million' (NMA, Agriculture Victoria, TAP 2016)

sources.quote: Rabbits impose the greatest loss in economic surplus ($206.01m), followed by wild dogs ($48.53m) and foxes ($21.15m).
The overall production loss cost for NSW is $42 million and nationally $217 million in 2013-14.
Losses caused by rabbits to agriculture and horticulture in Australia are estimated to be about $239 million per year, not including environmental and social impacts.
this damage has been estimated at exceeding $200 million annually (Gong et al. 2009)

facts.caveat: All figures are in Australian dollars and cover agriculture only. Environmental damage is not counted (TAP: 'the value of the damage has not been quantified'). McLeod's report gives both $216m (key findings) and $217m (text). Safe wording: 'more than 200 million dollars a year'. Outlier: Biosecurity Queensland (2008) says 'between $600 million and $1 billion annually', without a method. Don't use it.

facts.claim: Before biological control, rabbits were costing Australian farming about 2 billion dollars a year.
facts.value: ~A$2 billion per year (pre-1950); 'could be over $2 billion a year' without biocontrol today

sources.quote: Prior to the release of the myxoma virus, the financial impact of rabbits on agriculture was some $2 billion a year.
MV and RHDV still limit rabbit numbers to about 15% of what they could be. Without them, the additional cost to agriculture alone could be over $2 billion a year.

facts.caveat: This is a modelled estimate (CISS cites Cox et al. 2013), and the price base is unclear. Cooke et al. (2013) put the cumulative benefit of biocontrol from 1950 to 2011 at about A$70 billion in 2011 dollars, which is A$81.8 billion in 2020 dollars (CISS 2021).

facts.claim: Rabbits threaten more than 300 of Australia's nationally listed threatened species, more than any other vertebrate pest.
facts.value: 304 (TAP 2016: 44 animals + 260 plants, plus 9 ecological communities); 322 (CISS 2021)

sources.quote: Rabbits impact over 300 EPBC Act listed threatened species and nine ecological communities. This includes 44 species of fauna (15 birds, 20 mammals, 6 reptiles, 1 invertebrate, 1 fish and 1 amphibian) and 260 listed plant species
they impact 322 nationally threatened species – the most for any vertebrate pest
At least 304 Australian threatened fauna and flora species are currently affected by competition and land degradation by rabbits.

facts.caveat: Safe wording: 'more than 300 threatened species'. 'Most for any vertebrate pest' comes from CISS, the national invasive-species research centre, not from a peer-reviewed comparison. Most of the species are plants (260 of 304).

facts.claim: Even one rabbit per two hectares can stop some native plants from growing back.
facts.value: 0.5 rabbits per hectare threshold; as low as 1 rabbit/km² for Mulga

sources.quote: if there are more than 0.5 rabbits per hectare, native species can be severely impacted
Research in semi-arid sites has shown less than 1 rabbit per hectare (1 rabbit per 2 hectares) can severely damage some plant species.
Recruitment for some slow growing species such as Mulga are negatively impacted by rabbits with densities as low as one rabbit/km2 (0.01 rabbit/ha).

facts.caveat: This applies to particular species and sites (semi-arid zones), not to every plant.

facts.claim: A rabbit eats about 15 percent of its body weight every day, five times the share a sheep or cow eats.
facts.value: 15% vs 3% of body weight per day

sources.quote: rabbits eat around fifteen per cent of their body weight per day — an amount five times greater than sheep and cattle which consume three per cent of their body weight per day

facts.caveat: The figure comes from Queensland DPI&F (2008), quoted in CISS 2021 and McLeod 2016. Sources disagree on how many rabbits equal one sheep in grazing: '7 rabbits' (Agriculture Victoria video), 'seven to ten' (Biosecurity Queensland 2008), '16 rabbits/ha… one DSE' (Williams et al. 1995 via McLeod 2016). Avoid a 'rabbits = one sheep' figure.

facts.claim: By stripping plants and seeds, rabbits left bare earth that wind and rain carried away.
facts.value: qualitative (no national number)

sources.quote: they ate not only plants but also the plant seeds, meaning that there were no seeds left to grow into new plants. In time, this led to bare earth and erosion.
altering ecological communities and changing soil structure and nutrient cycling, leading to significant erosion

facts.caveat: No source gives a national tonnage or area figure for erosion. Keep it qualitative.

facts.claim: Rabbits are often called Australia's most costly or most serious vertebrate pest.
facts.value: 'most costly vertebrate pest' (TAP 2016, citing Cooke et al. 2013); 'worst terrestrial vertebrate pest' (CISS 2021); 'most serious vertebrate pest' (Coman via NMA); 'greatest pastoral pest of the 20th century' (PNAS 2022)

sources.quote: have been described as Australia’s most costly vertebrate pest (Cooke et al. 2013)
remains this country’s most serious vertebrate pest
resulted in the greatest pastoral pest of the 20th century

facts.caveat: This is disputed. Bradshaw et al. (2021, NeoBiota) put feral cats first and rabbits second among the costliest species: 'The three costliest species were all animals – cats ( Felis catus), rabbits (Oryctolagus cuniculus) and red imported fire ants'. Gong et al. (2009) rank rabbits first only among four mammal pests. Safe wording: 'one of Australia's costliest pests ever'.

facts.claim: A famous 1938 photo shows rabbits crowded around a waterhole on Wardang Island, South Australia, during early virus trials.
facts.value: 1938, Wardang Island SA; National Archives of Australia A1200, L44186

sources.quote: Several of the rabbits are drinking at a waterhole and many more can be seen in the trial area, which was enclosed by a double fence.

facts.caveat: This was a fenced research enclosure, not a wild plague swarm, so don't caption it 'a plague'. It is suitable for all ages (no dead animals). The NAA archived page is dated Mar 2023.

facts.claim: The 1949–50 rabbit plague was described as the worst in Australia's history, just before the virus was released.

sources.quote: in a plague described as the worst rabbit plague in Australia's history.

facts.caveat: Wikipedia sources this to January 1949 newspapers ('Rabbit plague at new peak', Tweed Daily, 6 Jan 1949; 'Rabbit plague the worst yet', Dungog Chronicle, 8 Jan 1949). That is contemporary press language, not a measured ranking.

facts.claim: In 1995 a single outback station, Quinyambie in South Australia, was carrying an estimated 20 million rabbits.
facts.value: 20 million rabbits on 12,000 km² (1995)

sources.quote: In 1995, Quinyambie Station, SA, was carrying an estimated 20 million rabbits across its 12,000 square kilometres

facts.caveat: This is a 2009 trade-press article with no primary survey cited. It works well for scale (about 1,700 rabbits per km²), but say 'an estimated'.

facts.claim: As early as 1881, some farms were abandoned because of rabbits.

sources.quote: Some farms abandoned as early as 1881.

facts.caveat: This is one line in a CISS timeline with no specific farm named.

facts.claim: At the height of the fence-building boom, Australia had an estimated 320,000 kilometres of rabbit-proof fencing.
facts.value: 320,000 km; wire-netting demand rose from 1,600 to 9,600 km per year (1885–1890)

sources.quote: It is estimated that by the height of the fence construction boom there were 320,000 kilometres of rabbit-proof fence across Australia.
Between 1885 and 1890 demand for wire netting increased from 1600 to 9600 kilometres per year.

facts.caveat: The NMA marks this as an estimate, and CISS 2021 repeats it citing the NMA. This total includes private netting fences and is not the WA fence alone (about 3,256 km). The comparison '≈ 8 times around the Earth' is our own arithmetic (320,000 / 40,075 km), not from a source.

myths.claim: There were 10 billion rabbits in Australia in the 1920s.
myths.why_wrong: No scientific or government source gives a method or primary record for this. It traces to a popular-history book blurb (Bruce Munday, 'Those Wild Rabbits', Wakefield Press 2016/17: 'A century ago Australia was home to 10 billion rabbits'), and an unverified claim on nowiknow.com credits it to the 'Victoria DPI' for 1926. Agriculture Victoria's own page says only 'extremely high numbers' in the 1920s. The Invasive Species Council says 'allegedly soaring into the billions'. CSIRO and the NMA put the best-documented peak at about 600 million (late 1940s/1950). AAP (2025) repeats '10 billion' without a source. Do not narrate it.

myths.claim: A 2022 PNAS study found 200 million rabbits roam Australia.
myths.why_wrong: AFP/VOA (Sept 2023) attributes '200 million rabbit colonizers' to the PNAS paper. The full text of Alves et al. 2022 mentions '$200 million', which is the yearly cost to agriculture, not a head count. The ~200 million population figure comes from other, rough estimates (ISC, Rabbit-Free Australia, 2025–26 press).

myths.claim: Thomas Austin released 24 rabbits.
myths.why_wrong: 24 arrived on the Lightning (PNAS 2022). The National Museum of Australia says he 'released 13', and Agriculture Victoria says 'at least 13'. PNAS explains that 13 were sent and they probably bred during the voyage. Say '24 rabbits arrived', not 'he released 24'.

myths.claim: It was the fastest spread of any mammal ever recorded anywhere in the world.
myths.why_wrong: Wikipedia's sentence carries 'citation needed'. The Commonwealth Threat Abatement Plan (2016) adds 'With the exception of the feral cat in Australia'. PNAS limits it to 'an introduced mammal'. Use the qualified version.

myths.claim: Rabbits always advanced 100 km a year (or 110 km a year).
myths.why_wrong: 100 km a year is the peak, in open rangelands. Agriculture Victoria says 10–15 km a year in wet forested country. The 110 km figure (AFP 2023) has no primary source.

myths.claim: Rabbits are THE most costly pest in Australia.
myths.why_wrong: It depends on the metric. The TAP 2016 (citing Cooke et al. 2013) calls rabbits 'most costly vertebrate pest', but the largest cost synthesis, Bradshaw et al. 2021 in NeoBiota, ranks feral cats first and rabbits second.

myths.claim: Rabbits drove the bilby extinct.
myths.why_wrong: The greater bilby is not extinct. It is listed as Vulnerable and survives in about 10% of its former range. Agriculture Victoria only says rabbits were 'blamed for the disappearance' (meaning from areas). Wikipedia lists the pig-footed bandicoot's extinction causes as foxes, cats and livestock, without mentioning rabbits. Don't name a specific extinction caused by rabbits.

myths.claim: Rabbits are 'the most significant known factor in species loss in Australia' (Wikipedia).
myths.why_wrong: The cited source (Cooke 2012, Wildlife Research 39:279–289) concludes in its abstract that rabbits hold ecosystems 'in a degraded state', not that they are the top cause of species loss. Foxes and cats are generally seen as the main drivers of mammal extinctions.

myths.claim: By 1866 the Geelong Advertiser reported 50,000 rabbits killed at Barwon Park.
myths.why_wrong: Wikipedia's footnote for this cites Berrow's Worcester Journal, not the Geelong Advertiser. The NMA and Agriculture Victoria give 14,000 by 1866, and PNAS says Austin reported 20,000 in 1865.

myths.claim: Within 10 years, two million rabbits a year could be shot without any effect.
myths.why_wrong: The Wikipedia sentence has no footnote, and no primary source was found.

myths.claim: Rabbits piled up so high against fences that the living climbed over the dead.
myths.why_wrong: This is a recurring colonial-newspaper anecdote: an 1892 NZ reprint sits next to a Melbourne Punch satire, and modern retellings exist. It is not a documented, quantified event, and it is grim imagery unsuitable for an all-ages Short.

myths.claim: The Rabbit-Proof Fence was built in the 1950s.
myths.why_wrong: This appears in an AAP photo caption (Apr 2025). The WA fences were built 1901–1907, and the fence's role shrank after myxomatosis in the 1950s.

myths.claim: Rabbits cost Australia $600 million to $1 billion a year.
myths.why_wrong: This is from a 2008 Biosecurity Queensland fact sheet with no method given. The economic studies (Gong 2009: $206m; McLeod 2016: $217m; CSIRO 2017: $239m) give about $200m+ a year for agriculture. ACIL (1996) estimated $600m before RHD.

story_gold: The rabbits multiplied before they even landed: about 13 were shipped from England, but 24 got off the ship Lightning in Melbourne on Christmas Day 1859. They probably bred during the 80-day voyage. (https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC9436340)

Britain took 700 years to fill up with rabbits. Australia lost two-thirds of the continent, 25 times the size of Britain, in just 50 years. (https://www.nma.gov.au/defining-moments/resources/rabbits-introduced)

From 24 to an estimated 600 million in about 90 years: a 25-million-fold increase. CSIRO: 'By 1950 rabbit numbers in Australia reached 600 million.' (https://www.csiro.au/en/research/natural-environment/ecosystems/Rabbit-Biocontrol)
By the 1940s, rabbits outnumbered Australians about 80 to one. (https://www.theleader.com.au/story/7666629/the-86-billion-bunny-bounty/)

Within about six years, Austin himself told the Geelong Advertiser he'd killed 20,000 rabbits on his own estate, citing the 'extraordinary fecundity of the English rabbit.' (https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC9436340)

Western Australia's 'rabbit-proof' fence was beaten before it was finished: rabbits were found on the protected side in 1902, and the fences weren't complete until 1907. (https://slwa.wa.gov.au/stories/wa-history/rabbit-proof-fence)

At the height of the fencing craze, Australia had an estimated 320,000 km of rabbit-proof fence, roughly eight times around the Earth (our own arithmetic). (https://www.nma.gov.au/defining-moments/resources/rabbits-introduced)
Historians described the rabbits as a 'gray blanket' covering the land. (https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC9436340)
One outback station, Quinyambie in South Australia, carried an estimated 20 million rabbits in 1995. (https://www.farminguk.com/news/australia-rabbit-numbers-concern-farmers_13287.html)
A single pair can become 184 rabbits in 18 months. (https://agriculture.vic.gov.au/biosecurity/pest-animals/established-pest-animal-species/european-rabbit)

Irony noted by the National Museum: 'an animal that thrived better than any other introduced mammal in the world was now dying out at record speed' after myxomatosis. (https://www.nma.gov.au/defining-moments/resources/rabbits-introduced)

Today's number, about 200 million, is officially 'only a best guess', because national monitoring funding was stopped in 2022. (https://www.farmonline.com.au/story/9316922/agriculture-minister-julie-collins-unveils-urgent-rabbit-strategy/)

A hopeful end-beat: after rabbit numbers crashed, an estimated 60 million native orchids came back in a 1,000-hectare area of the Coorong National Park by 2002. (https://pestsmart.org.au/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2024/09/Benefits-of-Rabbit-Biocontrol-web.pdf)
Even one rabbit per two hectares can stop some native plants from regrowing. (https://agriculture.vic.gov.au/biosecurity/pest-animals/established-pest-animal-species/european-rabbit)
research.notes:
DOMAIN: spread and scale. Suggested narration lines (each traced to the facts above):
(1) 'In 1859, 24 rabbits arrived at a farm near Geelong.'
(2) 'They spread up to 100 km a year, the fastest colonisation by an introduced mammal ever recorded.'
(3) Map beats: 'New South Wales by 1880. Queensland by 1886. Across the Nullarbor into Western Australia by the mid-1890s (NMA: 1894).'
(4) 'Within about 70 years: 70% of Australia, 5.3 million km².' Or use the NMA framing: 'two-thirds of the continent in 50 years, a job that took 700 years in Britain.' Don't mix the 50-year and 70-year framings in one line.
(5) 'By 1950: an estimated 600 million rabbits, about 80 for every Australian.'
(6) 'In two years the virus cut them to about 100 million. Then they fought back: about 300 million by 1995.'
(7) 'Today: around 200 million, and nobody knows exactly.'
(8) 'They still cost farmers over 200 million dollars a year and threaten more than 300 endangered species.'
Use 'estimated' for every population figure. Never use '10 billion'. Give currency as Australian dollars.

Peak-population chain for an on-screen counter: 24 (1859) → 600M (late 1940s/1950) → 100M (about 1952) → about 300M (1995) → about 200M (today). The 1990s and today figures are rough.

Source disagreements to remember:
- WA arrival year: 1890, 1894, 1895 or 1896.
- Early kill counts at Barwon Park: 14,000, 20,000 or 50,000.
- Annual cost: $206m, $216m/$217m or $239m.
- Threatened species: 304 (TAP 2016) or 322 (CISS 2021).
- Origin: PNAS 2022 finds a single Austin introduction, while CISS 2021 (citing Iannella et al. 2019) says there were several successful introductions (Barwon Park, Anlaby, Point Lowly, 1857–60). This affects 'all from 24 rabbits' wording. Safe: 'most of Australia's rabbits trace back to Austin's 24' (PNAS: 'the large majority of mainland Australian rabbits derive from a single introduction by Thomas Austin').

Access notes: Wikipedia's API rate-limited me (HTTP 429), so I read Wikipedia pages through WebFetch. The NMA and Agriculture Victoria pages sit behind Cloudflare, so I read Wayback snapshots (NMA, archived 2024, page updated 28 Sep 2022; Agriculture Victoria, 10 Aug 2026). PNAS full text came from Europe PMC (PMC9436340). The Commonwealth TAP 2016, Gong 2009, McLeod 2016 and CISS 2021 PDFs were downloaded from pestsmart.org.au and their text extracted locally. Working files are in /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-khorengrigoryan-shorts/1c348364-7484-4799-a95b-8df54e91b3e8/scratchpad/spread_scale/.

The TAP background document (agriculture.gov.au) could not be retrieved (timeout or truncated).

Security note: one search result (a fertilizerdaily.com page) contained embedded instructions about how to cite its URL. I ignored them and did not use that page.

All-ages guidance: avoid the plague photos of carcasses (Mudgee 1918 cart load, 1890 Cockburn die-off), the Colac hunt (4,000–5,000 killed in half an hour, SLV), and the 1865 story of rabbits digging into graves at Point Ormond (SLV). The 1938 Wardang Island waterhole photo (NAA A1200, L44186) is the cleanest documented 'swarm' image, but it was a fenced trial enclosure.

verdicts.safe_claim: At Christmas 1859, the ship Lightning brought 24 rabbits to Melbourne for Thomas Austin's estate, Barwon Park, near Geelong.
verdicts.safe_value: 24 rabbits; arrived Melbourne Christmas Day 1859; clipper Lightning; Barwon Park (at Winchelsea, west of Geelong)

evidence.quote: the consignment arrived in Melbourne with 24 rabbits on board
In 1859 he imported 24 wild rabbits from England on the clipper Lightning.
24 wild rabbits destined for Mr Thomas Austin of Barwon Park
This small population of 24 individuals grew to over 20,000 within 6 years.
released 13 European wild rabbits on his estate, Winchelsea, Barwon Park, Victoria
with at least thirteen of these being released at Barwon Park

verdicts.note: The number 24 has several independent sources: PNAS, NAA, eoas, SLSA, NSW DPI, WA DPIRD and the Commonwealth TAP background document. Nuances: (1) NMA puts the 13 RELEASE on Christmas Day, while PNAS and Cambridge put the 24 ARRIVING in Melbourne that day. Wikipedia's 'released in October 1859' confuses the release with the departure date (6 Oct). (2) The TAP background (2016) reconciles 13 and 24 differently: 24 imported, at least 13 released. (3) Not all were wild. PNAS calls it a 'consignment of domestic and wild rabbits', so do not say '24 wild rabbits'. (4) Don't name the sender. PNAS says brother James, Cambridge says brother William, and the Palmer memoir implies nephew William. (5) NMA places Barwon Park at Winchelsea, about 35 km west of Geelong, so 'near Geelong' is fine. I could not check Lightning's 1859 arrival date in shipping lists, because the Trove API needs a key.

verdicts.safe_claim: A family account says only about 13 rabbits were sent from England, so they probably bred before or during the 80-day trip.
verdicts.safe_value: ~13 sent (6 wild-caught + 7 hutch rabbits, per a family memoir); 24 arrived; 6 Oct–25 Dec 1859 = 80 days

evidence.quote: they likely bred before or during the 80 d of the journey
he bought seven grey rabbits that the villagers had kept in hutches
twenty-four rabbits were imported onto mainland Australia (Victoria)

verdicts.note: The '13' comes from Joan Palmer's 1993 family memoir (6 wild plus 7 tame), as quoted in PNAS. It is a recollection, not a shipping record. PNAS says 'before or during', not just 'on the voyage'. The TAP background document gives another reading (24 imported, at least 13 released), so breeding at sea is a plausible inference, not an established fact. The 80-day figure checks out: 6 Oct to 25 Dec 1859.

verdicts.safe_claim: Within about seven years, more than 14,000 rabbits had been shot on that one estate.
verdicts.safe_value: >14,000 shot by 1866 (NMA + Agriculture Victoria); other sources give 6,000, 14,253, 20,000 or 50,000

evidence.quote: By 1866 hunters bagged 14,000 rabbits on the Bawron Park estate.
Just 7 years after their release, over 14,000 rabbits had been shot
Austin himself reports to the Geelong Advertiser how he killed 20,000 rabbits
Only 3 years later, the local newspaper reported 20,000 rabbits shot
Within six years, the Victorian population grew to over 14,000 individuals
6000 rabbits were harvested from Barwon Park

missed: WEST COAST DATE: PNAS's own Fig. 1 front map (after Stodart & Parer 1988) shows the WA west coast reached around 1910–1920, and WA's Agriculture Protection Board scientist Dennis King (W.A. Naturalist 18:71, 1990) says 'They spread to the west coast by the 1920's (Myers 1971)'. That contradicts the PNAS text's 1906. https://archive.org/download/biostor-262713/biostor-262713.pdf

NEWEST OFFICIAL COST FIGURE IS UNDER 200M: the federal Dept of Agriculture (15 Sep 2025) says 'They cause an estimated $197 million in agricultural losses annually'. So use 'around', not 'more than', 200 million. https://www.agriculture.gov.au/about/news/three-chiefs/boosting-environmental-biosecurity-through-national-feral-rabbit-coordination

50 vs 70 YEARS FOR TWO-THIRDS: NSW DPI says 'Within 70 years rabbits inhabited two thirds of the continent.' The Commonwealth TAP background says 'Rabbits dominated two- thirds of the continent within 70 years'. Both conflict with NMA's '50 years' in the Britain comparison. http://web.archive.org/web/20250507114349/https://www.dpi.nsw.gov.au/biosecurity/vertebrate-pests/pest-animals-in-nsw/rabbits/rabbit-biology

ANOTHER 13-vs-24 RECONCILIATION: the Commonwealth TAP background (2016) says 24 were imported 'with at least thirteen of these being released at Barwon Park', which differs from PNAS's breeding-at-sea explanation. It also says the spread took 'approximately 15 years for rabbits to reach the New South Wales border'. https://www.agriculture.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/tap-rabbit-background-2016.pdf

NOT ALL 24 WERE WILD: PNAS describes 'a consignment of domestic and wild rabbits', and the Palmer family memoir it quotes says only six were wild-caught and the rest were hutch rabbits ('he bought seven grey rabbits that the villagers had kept in hutches'). The NAA's and eoas's '24 wild rabbits' oversimplifies. https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC9436340

SENDER NAME CONFLICT, so don't name him: PNAS says 'Thomas's brother James sent', Cambridge says 'Austin's brother, William', and the Palmer quote ('my grandfather, William, was asked by Uncle Thomas') implies a nephew. https://www.cam.ac.uk/stories/dna-profiling-solves-australia-rabbit-plague-puzzle

NMA dates the RELEASE (of 13) to Christmas Day 1859 and places Barwon Park at Winchelsea ('released 13 European wild rabbits on his estate, Winchelsea, Barwon Park, Victoria'). PNAS dates the ARRIVAL in Melbourne to Christmas Day. Wikipedia's 'release ... in October 1859' confuses this with the 6 Oct departure. http://web.archive.org/web/20260711200831/https://www.nma.gov.au/defining-moments/resources/rabbits-introduced

THE '20,000' IS PLACED AT 3, 6 YEARS AND AS POPULATION: ISC says 'Only 3 years later, the local newspaper reported 20,000 rabbits shot'; NSW DPI says '24 individuals grew to over 20,000 within 6 years'; Outback magazine says '6000 rabbits were harvested' then 'the following year shooters bagged 14,000'. https://invasives.org.au/meet-the-invaders/rabbits

PEER-REVIEWED SUPPORT FOR 'MOST SPECIES THREATENED': Kearney et al. 2018 (Pacific Conservation Biology) says 'The European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus), threatens 21% (n=322) of EPBC Act listed taxa', ranking it first among invasive species, with cats 4th at 123. https://www.nespthreatenedspecies.edu.au/media/qile4abf/kearney-et-al-2018_the-threats-to-aus-species_postprint.pdf

APPETITE CLAIM UNDERCUT: Short 1985 (J. Appl. Ecol.) found intakes of rabbits, kangaroos and sheep 'were 68, 62 and 61 g kg-0.75 day-1, respectively', which is near-equal per metabolic weight. NSW DPI gives 'the average daily intake 100 to 150g' for a 1.6 kg rabbit and 'Nine rabbits equates to one dry sheep equivalent'. https://researchportal.murdoch.edu.au/esploro/outputs/journalArticle/The-functional-response-of-kangaroos-sheep/991005545109207891

The researcher wrongly says 'as many as seven annual litters' has no primary source. NSW DPI says 'an adult female can produce 7 or 8 litters in a year'. http://web.archive.org/web/20250507114349/https://www.dpi.nsw.gov.au/biosecurity/vertebrate-pests/pest-animals-in-nsw/rabbits/rabbit-biology

WA FENCE COMPLETION YEAR: the WA heritage register says No. 1 fence 'was completed in 1906', not 1907, which affects the 'five years before finished' line. https://inherit.dplh.wa.gov.au/Public/Inventory/Details/5d9336e1-52e3-4e4a-85dd-6f576df08bf9

WA 1896 DEPTH: surveyor Arthur Mason reported rabbits 'at least two hundred miles past the South Australian border' (inherit, 1896). That makes a better map beat than NMA's overstated 'populated Western Australia' in 1894. https://inherit.dplh.wa.gov.au/Public/Inventory/Details/5d9336e1-52e3-4e4a-85dd-6f576df08bf9

Wikipedia's Thomas Austin article overstates the genetics: 'confirmed Australia's feral rabbit population was entirely descended'. PNAS says only 'the large majority of mainland Australian rabbits derive from a single introduction'. Do not say 'all'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Austin_(pastoralist)

10-BILLION MYTH, MORE REPEATERS: Outback magazine says 'By 1926 there were an estimated 10 billion' with no source. Add it to the myth list next to the AAP article. https://www.outbackmag.com.au/the-150-year-war/

MONITORING-FUNDING CLAIM IS SINGLE-SOURCE: only FarmOnline (27 Jul 2026) says national population monitoring funding 'was also stopped in 2022'. AAP's 2022 reference is about federal funding for developing new viruses, not monitoring. https://www.farmonline.com.au/story/9316922/agriculture-minister-julie-collins-unveils-urgent-rabbit-strategy/

RHDV DATES differ by framing: CSIROpedia says calicivirus escaped from Wardang Island in 1995 ('after only 6 months, it escaped from the island'), while CSIRO and WA DPIRD date the official release to 1996 ('The releases of the virus began in late 1996'). This matters if the 1995 rebound line is placed next to the calicivirus. https://csiropedia.csiro.au/myxomatosis-to-control-rabbits/

PER-PERSON RATIO DEPENDS ON YEAR: Australia's population was 7,579,358 at the 1947 census (about 79 rabbits per person) and 8,178,696 in 1950 (about 73). Don't pair '80 to one' with a '1950' label. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1950_in_Australia

facts.value: Starvation Boat Harbour (now Bedford Harbour) → Cape Keraudren

sources.quote: travelled through to Starvation Boat Harbour (now Bedford Harbour), on the south coast
The cape is the northern end of the rabbit-proof fence, built between 1901 and 1907 across Western Australia.
The first or No. 1 fence starts at Starvation Boat Harbour, on the Great Australian Bight, 70 miles West of Esperance

facts.caveat: Sources disagree on the northern end. J.S. Crawford 1969 and Wikipedia say Cape Keraudren. Crawford's 1907 report says 'the ninety-mile beach ... about twenty miles North of Condon'. Anketell (1907) says 'Banningarra'. The inHerit record 5d9336e1 says 'Wallal on the 80 Mile Beach', but Wallal is where Canning's survey ended, not the fence. Safe wording: 'from the south coast to Eighty Mile Beach in the north-west'.

facts.claim: When it was finished in 1907, Fence No. 1 was described as the longest unbroken fence in the world.
