facts.value: "longest unbroken fence in the world" (on completion)

sources.quote: a distance of 1,139 miles then being the longest unbroken fence in the world
When it was completed in 1907, the West Australian No1 Rabbit Proof Fence was the longest line of unbroken fence in the world.
When it was completed in 1907, the 1,833-kilometre (1,139 mi) No. 1 Fence was the longest unbroken fence in the world.

facts.caveat: Who says it: J.S. Crawford (WA Dept of Agriculture history, 1969) and F.H. Broomhall, a former boundary rider, in 'The Longest Fence in the World' (Hesperian Press, 1991). The camelfarm page says it is 'Condensed from' Broomhall, and Wikipedia cites that self-published page. Neither gives a world comparison. Narrate it as attributed and past-tense ('was called the longest unbroken fence in the world'), never as a present-day record.

facts.claim: Fence No. 1 was finished in September 1907, almost six years after work began.
facts.value: 20 Sept 1907 (J.S. Crawford) / 30 Sept 1907 (Broomhall, PWD summary); 'about 5 years and 10 months'

sources.quote: The No. 1 fence was finally completed by the 20 th September, 1907
took about 5 years and 10 months to construct
on the 30th September 1907 the whole 1,139 miles of the Barrier Fence as it was then called came under his charge

facts.caveat: The exact day disagrees (20 vs 30 September 1907). J.S. Crawford's own costs chapter says 'completed between December, 1901 and 30th September, 1907'. One inHerit record says 1906 and a Dumbleyung municipal record says 1903; both are wrong. Say 'finished in 1907'.

facts.claim: Private contractors built the first 465 miles, but the work was slow and poor. In 1904 the Public Works Department took over under Richard Anketell and built the remaining 674 miles to the north coast.
facts.value: 465 miles by contractors + 674 miles by PWD; Anketell appointed April 1904; PWD gangs started 20 Aug 1904

sources.quote: The first 465 miles of the No. 1 Rabbit Proof Fence, from the south coast northwards to the 250 mile peg, was erected by contractors, under the supervision of the Rabbit Department. From here northwards to the Indian Ocean, a further 674 miles, the Public Works Department (PWD) assumed responsibility
the move away from contractors was brought about by high contract prices, inferior work, sharp practices etc

facts.caveat: Wikipedia's PWD article gives a different picture: 465 miles found 'generally substandard' and 145 miles needing strengthening. Both agree that the PWD took over in 1904.

facts.claim: Anketell's construction force is recorded as 120 men, 350 camels, 210 horses and 41 donkeys.
facts.value: 120 men, 350 camels, 210 horses, 41 donkeys

sources.quote: During this period Anketell controlled a workforce of 120 men, 350 camels, 210 horses and 41 donkeys with an average load for transport of 375 miles.
The project was overseen by Richard John Anketell who set up a workforce comprising nine construction parties, 189 camels and 128 horses.
More than 400 men were employed as part of the labour gangs.

facts.caveat: The figures conflict. Broomhall via camelfarm: 120 men / 350 camels. Wikipedia PWD: 189 camels / 128 horses. WA Dept of Agriculture 2001: 'more than 400 men'. Anketell in a 1907 interview: '40 camels on the job, in addition to 150 horses, 50 donkeys and five bullock teams' and 'as many as 80 or 100 men in the camps'. Do NOT show a precise camel count. Say 'hundreds of men and camel teams'.

facts.claim: In the north-west, camel teams hauled netting and iron about 250 miles inland at only 10 to 12 miles a day, and a five-ton load could take up to two months.
facts.value: 250 miles; 10-12 miles/day; up to two months per 5 tons

sources.quote: it takes anything up to two months for a team to carry five tons of material from the coast to the fence, the camel only travelling from 10 to 12 miles a day
All the netting and the iron is landed at Condon, and at present is being carted 250 miles to the fence.

facts.caveat: Anketell press interview, Journal of Agriculture 1907, reprinted on the WA Dept of Agriculture centenary site. Good visual: a slow camel train through spinifex.

facts.claim: About 8,000 tonnes of materials went by ship and rail to depots, then overland by horse, camel and donkey teams.
facts.value: some 8,000 tonnes

sources.quote: Some 8,000 tonnes of materials were carried by ship and then railed to depots, before being hauled overland by horse, camel and donkey teams to the remote fence construction sites.

facts.caveat: Single source (WA Dept of Agriculture 2001 centenary site), no primary document cited.

facts.claim: The fence was wire netting on posts set 12 feet apart, with the bottom of the netting buried so rabbits could not dig under. Where there was no timber, iron posts were used.
facts.value: posts 12 ft (3.6 m) apart; netting buried ~6 in (15 cm), up to 12 in in sand

sources.quote: The height of the netting above ground averages from 2 feet 10 inches to 3 feet, and the depth underground 6 to 8 inches, except where the ground is sandy, and then it is 12 inches below the surface.
Line posts to be 12 feet (3.6m) apart

facts.caveat: Details differ by source. Reynolds & Diver (1992) say netting was buried one foot and 'There was no barbed wire at all on the original fence'. Crawford's 1907 report mentions barb wire 'where there is stock'. Wikipedia lists several wires and 6 in burial. For animation, show netting about 1 m high with an underground skirt and posts. Avoid exact wire counts.

facts.claim: Rabbits had already been found west of the fence line by 1902, five years before the fence was finished.

sources.quote: Unfortunately by 1902 rabbits had already been found west of the fence line.
even while construction was underway, rabbits were hopping into regions that the fences were intended to protect

facts.caveat: SLWA does not say where. Other sources give named places: see the next three facts. Safe wording: 'rabbits had already been found on the protected side by 1902'.

facts.claim: In 1902 and up to mid-1903 there were substantiated reports of rabbits as far west as Smiths Mill in the Darling Range near Perth, hundreds of kilometres inside the planned fence line.
facts.value: 1902 to mid-1903; Nannine to Smiths Mill (Darling Ranges)

sources.quote: Then in 1902 and up to the middle of 1903, there were substantiated reports of rabbits in such places as far apart as Nannine (then the head of the railway line in the Lower Murchison) to Smiths Mill in the Darling Ranges, not far from Perth.

facts.caveat: From J.S. Crawford 1969, who calls them 'substantiated reports'. These may have been isolated or human-carried rabbits, not the main invasion front. Crawford also lists unconfirmed reports (Moora, Watheroo, Mingenew, Bibra Lake). Use 'reports of rabbits near Perth', not 'rabbits overran Perth'.

facts.claim: In December 1904 the Acting Director of Agriculture, Alex Crawford, reported that rabbits had already got to the west side of the fence, some 15 to 20 miles in. He saw tracks where rabbits were scratching to get back east through the fence.
facts.value: Dec 1904; 15-20 miles west of fence

sources.quote: A curious thing is that the rabbits, which have got to the West of the fence, and which a few months ago were found to be 15 to 20 miles to this side, are now making East again.
We saw numerous tracks on the Western Side of the fence, where the rabbits were trying to scratch through to get back to the East.

facts.caveat: Reprinted verbatim from the Journal of Agriculture WA, 20 Dec 1904. This was on the southern section near Burracoppin and the coast.

facts.claim: A local newspaper reported the first rabbit sighted near Ravensthorpe, on the protected side, in its first issue on 31 December 1904, before the fence was finished.
facts.value: 31 December 1904; Ravensthorpe / Cordingup Gap

sources.quote: The Phillips River Times in its first issue of 31 December 1904, reported the first rabbit was sighted near Ravensthorpe.
the first rabbits were sighted near Cordingup Gap, about 8 km east of Ravensthorpe in December 1904, before The Fence was even finished

facts.caveat: Local heritage and historical-society sources. Ravensthorpe lies west of the No. 1 line (the fence crosses Highway 1 about 40 km east of the town).

facts.claim: Because rabbits had got ahead of Fence No. 1, the government built a second fence further west. Fence No. 2 ran from Point Ann on the south coast to Gum Creek, where it joined Fence No. 1.
facts.value: No. 2: ~1,166 km / 724 miles (survey line; 712-713 miles actual); built 1904-1905

sources.quote: The No. 2 fence, which was next constructed when it was found that rabbits had got ahead of the No. 1 fence, starts at Point Ann, 130 miles East of Albany
Stretching 1166 kilometres from Point Ann on the south coast through Cunderdin, 150 kilometres east of Perth, the new fence joined the original fence line at Gum Creek in the Murchison area.
The total distance of the accepted survey line from the south coast to Gum Creek is given as 724 miles. (Actually the correct mileage is 712 miles

facts.caveat: Dates: J.S. Crawford says construction 'was started about the 23rd March, 1904' with eight gangs, and that Crawford's report for the year to 30 June 1905 'reported that the No. 2 fence was completed'. SLWA says 'built in 1905'. Other sources give 1906, 1907 and 1907-08 (a local Dowerin section). Safe: 'started 1904, finished by 1905'. Length: 724 mi (1,166 km) is the commonly quoted survey length. J.S. Crawford gives 712-713 mi (about 1,147 km) actual.

facts.claim: Fence No. 3 ran east to west from Fence No. 2 north of Yalgoo to the Indian Ocean coast north of Geraldton, to protect the northern farming districts. It was built in about ten months in 1906-07.
facts.value: 171 miles (≈275 km) per J.S. Crawford; often quoted 160 miles / 257 km; begun ~16 Nov 1906

sources.quote: The No. 3 fence starts from the No. 2 fence, about 20 miles North of Yalgoo, and runs due West to the Indian Ocean, which it joins at Bluff Point, a total length of 171 miles.
(This fence is often quoted as being 160 miles, which in actual fact is incorrect).
The construction of the fence commenced around 16 th November, 1906, and was completed about 30 th September 1907, a matter of about 10 months. Only one gang was employed on this fence.

facts.caveat: Length conflict: 171 mi (Crawford 1907 report and J.S. Crawford 1969) vs 257 km = 160 mi (Onfray blog and many websites). End date: J.S. Crawford says about 30 Sept 1907, the inHerit Emu Barrier Fence record says '30 December 1907'. Start date of 16 Nov 1906 agrees. The inHerit record says the surviving 'Emu Barrier Fence' section is about 114 km.

facts.claim: All three fences together came to 2,023 miles, about 3,256 km. The Public Works Department put the total cost at £337,941, about £167 per mile.

sources.quote: The total length of the fences is 2,023 miles and the total cost has be £337,941
the average cost per mile was £167.1.0
The Rabbit Proof Fence, including No.1, 2 and 3 fence lines, was completed in 1907 and stretched 3,256 kilometres (2,023 miles)

facts.caveat: The figures come from the PWD Annual Report 1907/08 as quoted by J.S. Crawford ('has be' is a typo in the source). J.S. Crawford notes the real cost was higher: the PWD figure leaves out surveys, depots and huts. Crawford's own 1907 Rabbit Branch report gives 2,050 miles (1,155 + 724 + 171). Quairading Shire's '3,237 km' is a slip. The modern '$250/km' is a later conversion, so use pounds.

facts.claim: When the fences were handed over in 1907, Chief Inspector Alex Crawford reported that he was thoroughly convinced farmers west of the fences had practically nothing to fear.
facts.value: 1907 report

sources.quote: I am thoroughly convinced that the farmers have but little to fear and those inside of or to the West of the Nos. 1 and 2 fences, practically nothing.

facts.caveat: The same report admits rabbits were already 'fairly numerous' between fences 1 and 2, and 'almost 100 miles West of the No. 1 fence in the Upper Gascoyne'. Good irony beat.

facts.claim: Crawford described a stretch north of Burracoppin with not a blade of grass on the rabbit side of the fence and long grass on the protected side.
facts.value: bare outside vs grass 3-6 inches inside

sources.quote: On the outside of the No. 1 fence there was not a blade of grass to be seen; on the inside there was any amount of grass from three to six inches high

facts.caveat: Strong all-ages visual: a split screen with bare ground on one side and green on the other. Do not use the same report's 'thousands have died of starvation' (animal suffering).

facts.claim: In 1907 the fences were patrolled by 25 boundary riders under four sub-inspectors, roughly one rider for every 100 miles, about 160 km.
facts.value: 4 sub-inspectors (~500 miles each); 25 boundary riders (~100 miles each); far north patrolled in pairs over 300 miles

sources.quote: The maintenance staff consists of a Chief Inspector, 4 Sub-inspectors, who have about 500 miles of fencing in their charge, 25 boundary riders, or about one boundary rider to each 100 miles of fencing.

Those using camels had patrol lengths of about 70 miles, which were covered every sixth day. Other boundary riders used specially sprung bicycles, fitted with 3 speed gears, and their lengths averaged around 30 miles, and were covered twice a week.

facts.caveat: Patrol lengths differ by era and source: 1907 report about 100 miles per rider; J.S. Crawford 1908 about 70 miles by camel or 30 miles by bicycle; inHerit '240km stretches'; 1940s 100-200 miles by vehicle. The 1907 report's reason for paired riders in the north is phrased in offensive period language, so do not quote it.

facts.claim: Inspecting the fence was hard. In 1904 Crawford's motorbike broke down after about 100 miles, and a car bought in 1910 kept getting punctures and had to be towed back to camp by camels. Camel-drawn buggies worked best.
facts.value: 1904 motorbike; 1910 car towed by camels

sources.quote: I got through a little over 100 miles, when my machine broke down and I had to complete the journey on horseback and in a sulky.
After many punctures and broken springs, it had to be towed slowly back to camp by camels.

facts.caveat: The motorbike detail is primary (1904 press interview). The 1910 car anecdote comes from an inHerit heritage record, and Wikipedia carries a similar line about punctures.

facts.claim: By 1918 a parliamentary select committee found rabbits established in thousands inside Fence No. 1, and someone even suggested pulling it down and giving the netting to settlers.
facts.value: Feb-Mar 1918 Select Committee

sources.quote: The report revealed that rabbits were then established in thousands inside the No. 1 fence, to such an extent that the suggestion was made that the No. 1 fence should be removed and the netting distributed amongst the settlers.

facts.caveat: J.S. Crawford 1969 summarising the Select Committee report. The committee rejected the idea. WWI enlistments and material shortages had left the fence poorly maintained.

facts.claim: In 1948 the northern 498 miles of Fence No. 1 stopped being maintained, and parts were sold to cattle stations.
facts.value: 1948; 498 miles (heading says 493)

sources.quote: In 1948, Section 4 of the No. 1 fence ceased to be maintained.

facts.caveat: J.S. Crawford's chapter heading says '493 Miles' but the text says '498 miles'. Use 'its northern part' or 'about 800 km'.

facts.claim: By the early 1950s, the WA Department of Agriculture's own historian wrote, the fences had very little bearing on rabbit movements, with millions of rabbits west of both main fences. They were renamed vermin barrier fences.
facts.value: Agriculture Protection Board from 1 March 1951

sources.quote: The fences now had very little bearing on the control of the movements of rabbits and there were millions more of the pest to the west of both Nos 1 and 2 fences.
the construction of new Vermin Barrier Fences (a change in name from Rabbit Proof Fences)

facts.caveat: The myxomatosis link (1950s) is in Wikipedia ('Following the introduction of myxomatosis to control rabbits in the 1950s, the importance of the rabbit-proof fence diminished'). Leave the details of the biological weapons to that domain.

facts.claim: Historians mostly see the fences as a failure against rabbits, a 'unique, if inadequate' response in the State Library of WA's words. Fence historian F.H. Broomhall argued they at least slowed the rabbits down.
facts.value: failure / 'unique, if inadequate' / 'slowed up the rabbits'

sources.quote: The fence represents a unique, if inadequate, response to an overwhelming environmental problem
Overall, as a long-term barrier to rabbits, the fences were a failure
it is the opinion of historian A Broomhill that the fence definitely slowed up the rabbits and then doubled its workload by also acting as a barrier to other vermin - dingoes, foxes and emus

facts.caveat: The inHerit record misspells Broomhall as 'A Broomhill'; the book is F.H. Broomhall, 1991. Another inHerit record (Dowerin, No. 2 fence) says: 'The fences failed in their purpose although much time and money was expended to make them work.' Balanced narration: 'It slowed them, but it didn't stop them.'

facts.claim: The fence still exists as Western Australia's State Barrier Fence, about 1,350 km long, from the Zuytdorp Cliffs north of Kalbarri to west of Salmon Gums. Its main job now is keeping wild dogs and migrating emus out of farmland.
facts.value: approx. 1,350 km; wild dogs + emus

sources.quote: At approximately 1,350 km in length, the fence extends from the Zuytdorp cliffs , north of Kalbarri (in the state’s north) , to west of Salmon Gums (in the state’s southe a st ).

Today, the fence plays an important role in restricting the movement of wild dogs, which present a significant threat to livestock enterprises, into the south west of Western Australia. The fence also provides protection from large migration of emus

facts.caveat: The DPIRD page renders 'southeast' with stray spaces. Older figure: '1170 km' to Jerdacuttup (WA Dept of Agriculture 2001; Countryman 2021). The ~1,350 km figure includes part of the Esperance extension built since 2019.

facts.claim: As rabbits mattered less, the fence was renamed the State Vermin Barrier Fence and then the Emu Fence, before getting its current name, the State Barrier Fence.
facts.value: Rabbit Proof Fence → State Vermin Barrier Fence → Emu Fence → State Barrier Fence

sources.quote: The fence was later known as the State Vermin Barrier Fence, and the Emu Fence, before its current name - State Barrier Fence.
The SBF has been successful in containing these emu migrations.

facts.caveat: Nice ending beat: the fence lost to rabbits but found a second job against emus and wild dogs. Do not claim it 'won' against emus without the 'SBF project' source wording ('containing' migrations).

facts.claim: Western Australia is extending the barrier fence by about 660 km around Esperance, which will take it to over 1,800 km. The extension is still unfinished.
facts.value: 660 km extension; >1,800 km (DPIRD) / 1,850 km (Farm Weekly); 176 km done by Oct 2024

sources.quote: Once the Esperance extension is complete the State Barrier Fence will extend over 1,800 km.
To date only 176km of the 660km has been completed

facts.caveat: Progress figures change over time. An ARR.news piece dated 6 Aug 2026 (seen only in a search snippet, not opened) reportedly says 516 of 660 km are built with a 136 km gap remaining. The delays involve native title agreements, which are sensitive, so avoid them in the Short.

facts.claim: Queensland has its own rabbit fence. The Darling Downs–Moreton Rabbit Board fence runs 555 km from Mt Gipps to Goombi and is still patrolled weekly.
facts.value: 555 km; begun 1893, final link 1997; protects ~28,000 km²

sources.quote: The rabbit barrier fence is 555km long and protects roughly 28,000km2 of Southern Queensland. The fence is patrolled and maintained in its entirety on a weekly basis by our dedicated team of staff.
The Darling Downs–Moreton Rabbit Board fence is a pest-exclusion fence constructed between 1893 and 1997 to keep rabbits out of farming areas in Queensland, Australia.
The intriguing history of the oldest and longest purpose-built rabbit-proof barrier fence still in use in Australia, if not the world

facts.caveat: The State Library of Queensland says Queensland government fence work against rabbits from SA and NSW 'began on the fence in 1886', and the Darling Downs Rabbit Board was formed in 1893. Wikipedia (2010) gave about 530 km along the NSW border; the current board figure is 555 km in total.

facts.claim: Earlier, in the 1880s, about 300 miles of the New South Wales–South Australia border was netted against rabbits. These attempts largely failed.
facts.value: ~300 miles, 1880s

sources.quote: These attempts at netting failed mostly due to administrative wrangling, the remoteness of the land and the scarcity and inadequacy of building materials of the day.

facts.caveat: The PIRSA (SA government ag-history) page returned 403. The quote and the '300 miles' figure come from a search-result summary and are not verified on the page. Do not narrate this without re-checking.

facts.claim: The 2002 film 'Rabbit-Proof Fence' is about Aboriginal girls of the Stolen Generations who followed the fence home, not about the rabbit war itself.
facts.value: 2002 film; Stolen Generations

sources.quote: The Rabbit-Proof Fence has in recent years become synonymous with the ‘Stolen Generation’ through the 2002 film of the same name

facts.caveat: Sensitive. Recommend no reference in an all-ages comedic Short. If titles or thumbnails show 'Rabbit-Proof Fence', be aware the phrase strongly evokes the film for Australian viewers.

facts.claim: The fence line now divides native bush from cleared farmland so sharply that scientists studied different cloud cover on either side, with rain clouds over the native vegetation and clearer skies over the farms.
facts.value: Bunny Fence Experiment (Lyons et al., BAMS 1993; BUFEX 2005-07)

sources.quote: Within the fence area, scientists have observed a strange phenomenon: above the native vegetation, the sky is rich in rain-producing clouds. But the sky on the farmland side is clear.

facts.caveat: Peer-reviewed origin: Lyons et al., 'Land–Atmosphere Interaction in a Semiarid Region: The Bunny Fence Experiment', Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society 74(7), 1993, doi:10.1175/1520-0477(1993)074<1327:LIIASR>2.0.CO;2. The cloud effect comes from land clearing, not from the fence itself. Phrase it as 'along the fence line'.

myths.claim: The Rabbit-Proof Fence is the longest fence in the world (present tense).
myths.why_wrong: The claim only ever applied to Fence No. 1 on completion in 1907 ('then being the longest unbroken fence in the world', J.S. Crawford 1969). Today the WA State Barrier Fence is about 1,350 km, while the Dingo/Dog Fence in eastern Australia is 5,614 km. Say 'was called the longest unbroken fence in the world'.
myths.source: https://www.quairading.wa.gov.au/exploring-quairading/parks-wildlife/rabbit-proof-fence/ (says 'The Rabbit Proof Fence is the longest fence in the world!'); counter: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dingo_Fence ('it stretches 5,614 kilometres (3,488 mi)') and https://www.dpird.wa.gov.au/businesses/pests-weeds-and-diseases/control-methods/state-barrier-fence/

myths.claim: The No. 1 fence 'could be seen from space'.
myths.why_wrong: No primary source supports this. It appears in a blog attributed loosely to Broomhall. A wire-netting fence is not visible from orbit with the naked eye. What satellites do show is the contrast between native bush and cleared farmland along the line, and the cloud differences studied in the Bunny Fence Experiment.
myths.source: https://robertonfray.com/?p=2347 ('...when it was completed and could be seen from space'); counter: https://www.eol.ucar.edu/content/bufex-article-nyt

myths.claim: Fence No. 3 was 160 miles (257 km) long.
myths.why_wrong: Both Crawford's 1907 Rabbit Branch report and J.S. Crawford's 1969 departmental history give 171 miles (about 275 km). J.S. Crawford explicitly says 'This fence is often quoted as being 160 miles, which in actual fact is incorrect'.

myths.claim: Fence No. 1 was completed in 1903, or in 1906.
myths.why_wrong: Contractors finished only the southern 465 miles by May 1904. The PWD completed the full 1,139 miles in September 1907 (20 or 30 Sept by different accounts). The 1903 date (Dumbleyung inventory) probably confuses the southern section reaching 315 miles in August 1903; 1906 appears in one inHerit record.

myths.claim: The fence ran to Wallal on Eighty Mile Beach.
myths.why_wrong: Wallal is where Canning's survey ended. J.S. Crawford 1969 and Wikipedia put the fence's northern end at Cape Keraudren, the western end of Eighty Mile Beach. Crawford's 1907 report says 'about twenty miles North of Condon'.

myths.claim: It cost '$250 per kilometre'.
myths.why_wrong: The contemporary figure is £167 1s per mile (PWD Annual Report 1907/08, total £337,941). The '$250/km' is a later decimal-era conversion repeated online. It is not a period figure, and it does not match a simple conversion (£167/mile is about £104/km). Use pounds.

myths.claim: Exact construction force: '120 men, 350 camels, 210 horses and 41 donkeys' stated as settled fact.
myths.why_wrong: This comes from Broomhall's 1991 book via a self-published camel-farm page. Other sources say 'more than 400 men' (WA Dept of Agriculture 2001) and '189 camels and 128 horses' (Wikipedia PWD). Anketell himself in 1907 said '40 camels ... 150 horses, 50 donkeys' with 80-100 men in camp. No single reliable count exists.

myths.claim: Total length 3,237 km.
myths.why_wrong: Slip for 3,256 km (2,023 miles). The PWD 1907/08 total is 2,023 miles. Crawford's 1907 report gives 2,050 miles.

myths.claim: Fence No. 2 was built between March and July 1904.
myths.why_wrong: Construction started about 23 March 1904. Crawford's annual report for the year to 30 June 1905 is what reports it complete to Gum Creek. A 724-mile fence in four months is implausible, and the 'four months' line in J.S. Crawford's text lacks a year. SLWA says 'built in 1905'.

myths.claim: Rabbits reached Twilight Cove 'near Esperance'.
myths.why_wrong: Twilight Cove is on the Great Australian Bight coast, hundreds of km east of Esperance. The SLWA wording is geographically misleading, so do not use it on a map.

story_gold: THE IRONY: the State Library of WA says 'by 1902 rabbits had already been found west of the fence line', five years before Fence No. 1 was finished in 1907. https://slwa.wa.gov.au/stories/wa-history/rabbit-proof-fence

Reports reached Perth's doorstep: in 1902 to mid-1903 there were 'substantiated reports' of rabbits at Smiths Mill in the Darling Range, 'not far from Perth', while the fence was still hundreds of km from done. https://web.archive.org/web/2005/http://agspsrv34.agric.wa.gov.au/programs/app/barrier/history/Crawford_construction2.htm

Comedy beat: in December 1904 inspector Crawford found rabbit tracks on the protected west side 'where the rabbits were trying to scratch through to get back to the East'. The rabbits were already on the wrong side and wanted to go back. https://web.archive.org/web/2005/http://agspsrv34.agric.wa.gov.au/programs/app/barrier/pests/rabbits_retreat.htm

They didn't give up, they built more: Fence No. 2 because 'rabbits had got ahead of the No. 1 fence', then Fence No. 3. Total 2,023 miles (3,256 km) for £337,941. https://web.archive.org/web/2005/http://agspsrv34.agric.wa.gov.au/programs/app/barrier/history/Crawford_construction14.htm

Famous last words, 1907: Crawford was 'thoroughly convinced' farmers west of the fences had 'practically nothing' to fear. By 1918 rabbits were 'established in thousands inside the No. 1 fence' and someone suggested tearing it down and handing the netting to settlers. https://web.archive.org/web/2010/http://pandora.nla.gov.au/pan/43156/20040709/agspsrv34.agric.wa.gov.au/programs/app/barrier/history/REPORT1907.htm and https://web.archive.org/web/2005/http://agspsrv34.agric.wa.gov.au/programs/app/barrier/history/Crawford_maintenance3.htm

Perfect split-screen visual (1907): 'On the outside of the No. 1 fence there was not a blade of grass to be seen; on the inside there was any amount of grass from three to six inches high'. https://web.archive.org/web/2010/http://pandora.nla.gov.au/pan/43156/20040709/agspsrv34.agric.wa.gov.au/programs/app/barrier/history/REPORT1907.htm
Canning's survey was 'said at the time to be the longest single survey in the world', and when a camel died he walked 210 miles (338 km). https://adb.anu.edu.au/biography/canning-alfred-wernam-5499

Camel trains crawled 10 to 12 miles a day, and a five-ton load could take 'up to two months' to reach the fence in the north-west. https://web.archive.org/web/2005/http://agspsrv34.agric.wa.gov.au/programs/app/barrier/pests/rabbit_invasion.htm

Tech fail: Crawford's 1904 motorbike broke down after about 100 miles. The 1910 inspection car, after 'many punctures and broken springs, it had to be towed slowly back to camp by camels'. https://inherit.dplh.wa.gov.au/Public/Inventory/PrintSingleRecord/5d9336e1-52e3-4e4a-85dd-6f576df08bf9

Boundary riders on 'specially sprung bicycles, fitted with 3 speed gears' patrolled about 30 miles twice a week. In 1907 there were just 25 riders for about 2,000 miles of fence. https://web.archive.org/web/2005/http://agspsrv34.agric.wa.gov.au/programs/app/barrier/history/Crawford_construction16.htm

Plot twist ending: the 'Rabbit-Proof Fence' lost the rabbit war but got a second career. It was renamed the State Vermin Barrier Fence, then the 'Emu Fence', and today about 1,350 km of it keeps out wild dogs and migrating emus. https://www.dpird.wa.gov.au/businesses/pests-weeds-and-diseases/control-methods/state-barrier-fence/

Visible effect along the line: scientists found rain clouds over the native bush and clear skies over the farmland side (Bunny Fence Experiment, BAMS 1993; NCAR BUFEX). https://www.eol.ucar.edu/content/bufex-article-nyt
Queensland's own 555 km rabbit fence (Darling Downs–Moreton Rabbit Board) is still patrolled weekly, more than 130 years on. https://www.ddmrb.org.au/about-ddmrb/
research.notes:
BEST SOURCE FOUND: J.S. Crawford, 'History of the State Vermin Barrier Fences, formerly known as Rabbit Proof Fences' (WA Dept of Agriculture, 1969). The DPIRD Digital Library PDF (https://library.dpird.wa.gov.au/reports/14/) is behind a Cloudflare check, which I did not bypass. The full text, chapter by chapter, is preserved on the Department's 2001 centenary website in the Internet Archive (…/barrier/history/Crawford_*.htm). Alex Crawford's own 1907/08 'Report on Rabbit Branch' is preserved at the NLA Pandora copy via the Wayback Machine. Also blocked by bot checks, so not read: NMA blog 'Rabbit-proofing the West', Trove newspapers, NLA web archive, and the PIRSA page.

RECOMMENDED NUMBERS FOR NARRATION:
(1) Fence No. 1 = 1,833 km / 1,139 miles, south coast to Eighty Mile Beach. Begun Dec 1901 at Burracoppin, finished Sept 1907, 'about 5 years and 10 months'.
(2) Fence No. 1 'was called the longest unbroken fence in the world' when finished. This is attributed to J.S. Crawford 1969 and F.H. Broomhall 1991, not a modern record.
(3) Rabbits found west of the line 'by 1902' (SLWA). Named early breaches: Dec 1904, 15-20 miles west (Crawford); 31 Dec 1904, near Ravensthorpe; 1902-03 reports as far as Smiths Mill near Perth.
(4) All three fences = 2,023 miles / 3,256 km, cost £337,941 (PWD 1907/08).
(5) Today: State Barrier Fence about 1,350 km, against wild dogs and emus. The Esperance extension will take it to over 1,800 km.

KNOWN CONFLICTS TO AVOID ON SCREEN:
- No. 2 length: 724 mi (1,166 km) survey figure vs 712-713 mi actual.
- No. 3 length: 171 mi vs the popular 160 mi / 257 km.
- No. 1 northern end: Cape Keraudren vs Wallal or Banningarra.
- Workforce and camel counts conflict (120 vs 400+ men; 350 vs 189 vs 40 camels). Use 'hundreds of men and camel teams'.
- Construction details (barbed wire, burial depth) differ by source.
- Total length: 2,023 mi (PWD) vs 2,050 mi (Crawford 1907).
Arithmetic check: J.S. Crawford's 1,139 + 713 + 171 = 2,023 mi. The popular 1,139 + 724 + 160 also sums to 2,023 by coincidence. Conversions: 1,139 mi = 1,833 km; 2,023 mi = 3,256 km; 171 mi = 275 km; 713 mi = 1,147 km.

ALL-AGES / SENSITIVITY:
- Avoid Crawford's 'thousands have died of starvation', the trap counts (1,500-1,800 a month), the 1929-30 'Murchison Murders' (Upfield / Snowy Rowles), Canning's chaining controversy, the period language about Aboriginal people in the 1907 report, the Stolen Generations film, and the native-title delays on the Esperance extension.
- The Silver Chain nursing-charity origin story (boundary rider Arthur Grundy, 1904) appears only on the WA Dept of Agriculture centenary site and the Golden Pipeline site. Silverchain's own sources say the idea came from Muriel Chase in 1905. Low confidence; I left it out of facts.

SUGGESTED SAFE LINES:
- 'Western Australia built a fence 1,833 km long, coast to coast, to stop the rabbits.'
- 'When it was finished in 1907 it was called the longest unbroken fence in the world.'
- 'Problem: rabbits had already been found on the safe side by 1902.'
- 'So they built a second fence. And a third. 3,256 km in total.'
- 'It slowed the rabbits, but it didn't stop them.'
- 'Today, about 1,350 km of it still stands, now guarding against emus and wild dogs.'

verdicts.safe_claim: In 1901 Western Australia held a Royal Commission on the 'rabbit question'. It recommended building a barrier fence across the state, starting at once.
verdicts.safe_value: Royal Commission, 1901 (appointed Feb 1901 per J.S. Crawford)

evidence.quote: a Royal Commission to "Enquire into the Rabbit Question" was appointed in February, 1901
recommended that construction of '400 miles of fence … be at once undertaken'

verdicts.note: The National Museum of Australia blog independently confirms the 1901 Commission and its 400-mile 'at once' recommendation. The Commission's proposed line ran from Fitzgerald Inlet to Cape Bossut on the Ninety Mile (now Eighty Mile) Beach, so 'across the state' is fair. The February appointment date comes only from J.S. Crawford.

verdicts.safe_claim: The Commission warned that rabbits around Eucla were in the thousands, possibly millions. It said it had no choice but to put the fence about 500 miles inside the border, which left huge areas of pastoral land open to them.
verdicts.safe_value: 'thousands, possibly to the extent of millions'; fence '500 miles west of the State border'

evidence.quote: the rodents were in thousands, possibly to the extent of millions around Eucla
millions of acres of pastoral country would be left open to the ravages of rabbits

verdicts.note: Both phrases are J.S. Crawford's 1969 paraphrase of the findings, not the Commission's own text. Attribute them as 'a 1901 Royal Commission warned...'. Do not put 'millions' on screen as a counted figure.

verdicts.safe_claim: By the mid-1890s rabbits had crossed the Nullarbor and reached Western Australia. A government expedition found them at Eucla in 1896.
verdicts.safe_value: border c. 1894; Eucla 1896

evidence.quote: thirty five years after the initial release near Geelong, they had spread to the border of WA
From Eucla, where he found rabbits becoming noticeable
By 1896 it had been found as far west as Eucla

verdicts.note: J.S. Crawford gets 1894 by estimate (1859 + 35 years), and says only that some were 'probably' in WA about then. The first observed record is Surveyor Mason's 1896 expedition. Sources disagree on Mason's furthest-west sighting: Madura Pass (J.S. Crawford), Twilight Cove '200 km further west' (SLWA), and Eyre's Patch '200 miles beyond the border' (Broomhall via camelfarm). Do not name a furthest-west place.

verdicts.safe_claim: Surveyor Alfred Canning mapped the route. His survey, roughly 1,900 km long, was said at the time to be the longest single survey in the world, and on one stretch, after a camel died, he walked 338 km (210 miles).
verdicts.safe_value: survey 1,175 mi (1,891 km), about 3 years; walked 210 mi (338 km), per ADB

evidence.quote: Said at the time to be the longest single survey in the world, it took him three years.
when a camel died, he had to walk 210 miles (338 km)
commenced at a point on the south coast and ended at Wallal on the North west coast

verdicts.note: The survey's end point is disputed. ADB says Canning ran the line to Cape Keraudren. Broomhall (via camelfarm) says Canning's survey ended at Wallal and that Anketell surveyed 'the last seventy miles'. The NMA says Canning finished the permanent survey north in 1905, which fits ADB's 'three years'. The 210-mile walk has only one source (ADB), so keep it attributed or soft. The 'longest survey' superlative is explicitly 'said at the time'.

verdicts.safe_claim: Work on the fence began in December 1901 at Burracoppin, on the Goldfields railway. Gangs worked south towards the coast and north from there.
verdicts.safe_value: c. 21 Dec 1901 (clearing); Burracoppin

evidence.quote: About the 21 st December, 1901, the first work of erection (clearing) was begun.
Contract 1: Burracoppin south 25 miles
It was built in two stages with Burracoppin as the starting point.

verdicts.note: J.S. Crawford shows Contract 1 running south of Burracoppin and Contract 2 (begun around April 1902) running north. DPIRD and Wikipedia say 'constructed between 1902 and 1907'. 'Started in 1901' is safe.

verdicts.safe_claim: Fence No. 1 ran about 1,830 km (1,139 miles) across Western Australia, from the Southern Ocean to the Indian Ocean.
verdicts.safe_value: 1,139 mi = 1,833 km (other figures: 1,155 mi in 1907; 1,822 to 1,834 km)

evidence.quote: No. 1 Rabbit Proof Fence 1,139 miles long.
a total length of 1,155 miles
It stretched 1834 kilometres from the south coast to the northwest coast

verdicts.note: J.S. Crawford calls 1,139 mi 'as near accurate as practical'. 1,139 × 1.609 = 1,833 km. Alex Crawford's own 1907 report says 1,155 mi (about 1,859 km). Saying 'about 1,800 km' covers every version.

verdicts.safe_claim: It ran from Starvation Boat Harbour on the south coast, west of Esperance, to Cape Keraudren on Eighty Mile Beach in the north-west.
verdicts.safe_value: Starvation Boat Harbour → Cape Keraudren (most sources)

evidence.quote: to Cape Keraudren on the south end of the Eighty Mile Beach, north of Port Hedland
builders finally reached the Indian Ocean near Cape Keraudren
built on a foundation of cement that goes right into the water near Cape Keraudren

verdicts.note: The NMA independently confirms Cape Keraudren. Period variants: '20 miles North of Condon' (1907 report) and 'Banningarra' (Anketell 1907). J.S. Crawford calls it the 'south end' of Eighty Mile Beach; Wikipedia says the 'western end'. Both describe the same SW tip. 'Now Bedford Harbour' appears only in J.S. Crawford; OSM has Bedford Harbour Roads next to Starvation Boat Harbour (33.92°S, 120.56°E), which is about 120 km west of Esperance and fits the 1907 report's '70 miles West of Esperance'. Avoid the Bedford Harbour name.

verdicts.safe_claim: When it was finished in 1907, it was called the longest unbroken fence in the world.
verdicts.safe_value: 'longest unbroken fence in the world' (attributed, 1907, past tense)

evidence.quote: a distance of 1,139 miles then being the longest unbroken fence in the world
described by former boundary rider and fence historian Frank Broomhall as 'the longest unbroken line of fence in the world'

verdicts.note: No source makes a real world comparison, so keep it attributed. The NMA attaches Broomhall's phrase to the whole three-fence system, while J.S. Crawford attaches it to Fence No. 1. I found no longer continuous fence in 1907: the eastern fences were shorter (300-mile NSW–SA netting; the Queensland border fence was begun in 1886). The superlative is plausible but not proven. Never say it in the present tense; the Dingo Fence is 5,614 km.

verdicts.safe_claim: Fence No. 1 was finished in September 1907, almost six years after work began.
verdicts.safe_value: Sept 1907 (20th per J.S. Crawford; 30th per Broomhall); about 5 years 10 months

evidence.quote: The No. 1 fence was finally completed by the 20 th September, 1907
to finish Rabbit Proof Fence No.1 years later, in September 1907

verdicts.note: The NMA independently confirms September 1907. Say 'in 1907' or 'September 1907', not a specific day.

verdicts.safe_claim: Private contractors built the first stretch, but the work was expensive and shoddy. In 1904 the state's Public Works Department took over under Richard Anketell and pushed the fence north to the Indian Ocean.
verdicts.safe_value: 465 mi by contractors (finished by 2 May 1904) + 674 mi by PWD; Anketell appointed Apr 1904; PWD gangs from 20 Aug 1904

evidence.quote: high contract prices, inferior work, sharp practices etc, which were consistently encountered
a decision was made that it was generally substandard so the construction was handed over to the PWD in 1904

verdicts.note: The 2001 centenary page says the handover was in 'August 1904', which is when PWD gangs started. J.S. Crawford says the vote was handed over 'early in 1904', with Anketell appointed in April. Use '1904'.

verdicts.safe_claim: Hundreds of men and teams of camels, horses and donkeys built the northern sections.
verdicts.safe_value: no reliable count

evidence.quote: a workforce of 120 men, 350 camels, 210 horses and 41 donkeys
nine construction parties, 189 camels and 128 horses
Forty camel teams, each wagon having 14 animals, are being used

verdicts.note: Anketell's 1907 interview contradicts itself. It says 'Forty camel teams, each wagon having 14 animals' (about 560 camels) and also 'We have 40 camels on the job', so the '40 camels' line is probably a misprint for 40 teams. Counts range from 40 to about 560 camels and from 80–100 to 400+ men. Show no number.

verdicts.safe_claim: In the north-west, camel teams dragged the wire 400 km (250 miles) inland at just 15–20 km a day, and one five-ton load could take up to two months.
verdicts.safe_value: 250 mi from Condon; 10–12 mi/day; up to 2 months per 5 tons

evidence.quote: it takes anything up to two months for a team to carry five tons of material
dependant on teams of camels travelling about 10 -12 miles a day

verdicts.note: Primary source: Anketell's 1907 press interview, reprinted on the WA Dept of Agriculture centenary site. J.S. Crawford independently gives 10–12 miles a day and a longest haul of 290 miles from Nannine. Conversions: 250 mi ≈ 400 km; 10–12 mi ≈ 16–19 km. Good visual: '40 camel teams, 14 camels per wagon'.

verdicts.safe_claim: About 8,000 tonnes of material went by ship and rail, then overland by horse, camel and donkey teams.
verdicts.safe_value: some 8,000 tonnes (one source)

evidence.quote: Some 8,000 tonnes of materials were carried by ship and then railed to depots

verdicts.note: Only one source, the WA Dept of Agriculture 2001 centenary page, which cites no primary document. I found no corroboration. If the number goes on screen, attribute it; otherwise say 'thousands of tonnes'.

verdicts.safe_claim: It was wire netting about a metre high on posts set 12 feet (3.6 m) apart, with the bottom of the netting buried so rabbits couldn't dig under. Where there was no timber, iron posts were used.
verdicts.safe_value: posts 12 ft apart; netting buried about 6 in (15 cm), deeper (up to 12 in) in sand

evidence.quote: posts were closely spaced 12 feet (3.65 metres) apart and netting buried 6 inches (15.2 cm) into the earth
the depth underground 6 to 8 inches, except where the ground is sandy, and then it is 12 inches
buried one foot (300 mm) in the ground on the outside (north/east) of the posts

verdicts.note: The NMA independently confirms 12-ft posts and 6-in burial. Burial depth varies by source (6 in; 6–8 in; 1 ft) and so does mesh (1¼ in per J.S. Crawford; 'not more than one inch' per Reynolds & Diver). Height above ground was 2 ft 10 in to 3 ft in 1907, and the netting was 42–48 in wide. Animate 'about 1 m high' with an underground skirt on the east side, and avoid exact depth or wire counts.

verdicts.safe_claim: Rabbits had already been found on the 'safe' side of the planned line by 1902, five years before the fence was finished.

evidence.quote: Unfortunately by 1902 rabbits had already been found west of the fence line.
even while construction was underway, rabbits were hopping into regions the fences were intended to protect

verdicts.note: In 1902 only about 50 miles of fence had been started. So the rabbits got ahead of construction rather than 'jumping the fence'. Say 'the planned line', not 'the fence'. The NMA wording is an independent confirmation.

verdicts.safe_claim: By 1903 there were confirmed reports of rabbits near Perth, in the Darling Range, about 200 km on the protected side of the line.
verdicts.safe_value: 1902 to mid-1903; Smiths Mill (now Glen Forrest), about 225 km west of the line

evidence.quote: to Smiths Mill in the Darling Ranges, not far from Perth
The area was originally named Smith's Mill

verdicts.note: Smiths Mill is today's Glen Forrest, about 25 km east of Perth's CBD. Geocoded, that is about 225 km west of Burracoppin on the No. 1 line, so 'hundreds of km' overstates it; say 'about 200 km'. These were probably isolated incidents: Alex Crawford's 1907 report says 'No rabbits have been found to the West of the No. 2 fence in the agricultural districts'. Do not imply Perth was overrun.

verdicts.safe_claim: In 1904 the official inspecting the fence found rabbits already 15 to 20 miles on the 'safe' side, and their tracks where they were scratching to get back east through the netting.
verdicts.safe_value: 1904; 15–20 mi (about 25–30 km) west of the fence

evidence.quote: where the rabbits were trying to scratch through to get back to the East
a Press release around June, 1904 following an inspection made by the Acting Director of Agriculture

verdicts.note: The date is disputed. The centenary reprint is labelled Journal of Agriculture, 20 Dec 1904, but J.S. Crawford dates the same motorbike quote to a press release 'around June, 1904' after an inspection 'earlier in the year'. Say '1904'. In the same interview Crawford claimed the fence 'is thoroughly answering its purpose', another irony beat. Avoid the starvation and dead-rabbit lines.

verdicts.safe_claim: At the end of 1904 the local paper's very first issue reported a rabbit near Ravensthorpe, on the protected side, before the whole fence was even finished.
verdicts.safe_value: 31 Dec 1904; near Ravensthorpe (Cordingup Gap, about 8 km east of town)

evidence.quote: The Phillips River Times in its first issue of 31 December 1904, reported the first rabbit was sighted near Ravensthorpe.
By August, 1903, the 215 miles of fence was completed from the south coast to the Goldfields Railway Line

verdicts.note: The southern section near Ravensthorpe was already finished by August 1903. So this rabbit was on the protected side of a completed section, and 'before the fence was finished' only holds for the whole No. 1 line. inHerit puts the Highway 1 crossing 40 km east of Ravensthorpe, and OSM agrees (fence about 120.5°E, town 120.05°E). Sources are local heritage records.

verdicts.safe_claim: Because rabbits had got ahead of Fence No. 1, a second fence was started in 1904 further west. It ran about 1,150 km from the south coast and joined Fence No. 1 at Gum Creek.
verdicts.safe_value: No. 2: 724 mi (1,165–1,166 km) quoted / 713 mi actual; started about 23 Mar 1904; finished July 1904 (J.S. Crawford) or 1905 (SLWA, NMA)

evidence.quote: by about the 22 nd July, four months after commencement, the 724 miles of the No. 2 fence
Finished in 1905, No. 2 Fence ran for 724 miles (1165 km) from Point Ann
next constructed when it was found that rabbits had got ahead of the No. 1 fence

verdicts.note: J.S. Crawford himself says it was finished about 22 July, 'four months after' it began on 23 March 1904. That fits his note that the annual report for the year to 30 June 1905 records it as complete. SLWA and NMA say 'finished in 1905'. The 'March–July 1904' figure the researcher called a myth is therefore J.S. Crawford's own figure, so the date is disputed rather than wrong. Safe: 'started in 1904' or 'built 1904–05'. J.S. Crawford's 'as near accurate' length is 713 mi (about 1,147 km).

verdicts.safe_claim: Then came a third fence, running west from Fence No. 2 near Yalgoo to the Indian Ocean north of Geraldton, built in about ten months in 1906–07.
verdicts.safe_value: 171 mi (about 275 km) per Crawford, vs 160 mi / 257 km per NMA; about 16 Nov 1906 to about 30 Sept 1907

evidence.quote: runs due West to the Indian Ocean, which it joins at Bluff Point, a total length of 171 miles
commenced around 16 th November, 1906, and was completed about 30 th September 1907
ran the short distance of 160 miles (257 km) west

verdicts.note: The 160-mile figure is not just a low-quality-website error: the National Museum of Australia uses it. J.S. Crawford calls it 'incorrect', and 1907 primary data give 171. Do not show a No. 3 length on screen. The fence was built by one gang and was of lighter construction.

verdicts.safe_claim: All three fences together ran about 3,256 km (2,023 miles), and the official bill was £337,941.

evidence.quote: The total length of the fences is 2,023 miles and the total cost has be £337,941
in 1908 the Western Australian Public Works Department reported the cost to be an enormous – and not uncontroversial – £337 941

verdicts.note: The NMA independently confirms the figure and notes that critics estimated 'well over £400 000' because surveys and maintenance were left out. Crawford's 1907 report gives 2,050 mi. 2,023 × 1.609 = 3,256 km. Use 'about 3,250 km' and '£337,941 (official)'. Do not use '$250/km'.

verdicts.safe_claim: When the fences were handed over, the man in charge, Alex Crawford, wrote that he was 'thoroughly convinced' farmers inside the fences had 'practically nothing' to fear.
verdicts.safe_value: report on handover, about 1907–08; signed 'Acting Chief Inspector of Rabbits'

evidence.quote: I am thoroughly convinced that the farmers have but little to fear
ALEX CRAWFORD, Acting Chief Inspector of Rabbits.

verdicts.note: His title at the time was 'Acting Chief Inspector', not 'Chief Inspector'. The report carries no date. It describes all three fences as handed over, so it is late 1907 or 1908. The same report admits that rabbits between fences 1 and 2 'cannot be denied', but also says none had been found west of No. 2 in the farming districts. The irony is real, but he was partly right in the short term.

verdicts.safe_claim: Crawford described a spot where the rabbit side had 'not a blade of grass', while the protected side had grass three to six inches high.
verdicts.safe_value: bare outside vs 3–6 in grass inside, north of Burracoppin

evidence.quote: On the outside of the No. 1 fence there was not a blade of grass to be seen

verdicts.note: Verbatim from the primary 1907–08 report. Crawford offered it as proof the fence worked ('A better illustration of the value of the fence it would be difficult to find'). Good split-screen visual. Do not use the starvation lines from the same report.

verdicts.safe_claim: About 2,000 miles of fence were looked after by just 25 boundary riders, on bicycles, camels and buggies.
verdicts.safe_value: 4 sub-inspectors, 25 boundary riders (1907–08)

evidence.quote: 25 boundary riders, or about one boundary rider to each 100 miles of fencing
specially sprung bicycles, fitted with 3 speed gears

verdicts.note: The report's 'one per 100 miles' is its own rounding (2,050 ÷ 25 ≈ 82 miles each). J.S. Crawford says the 1908 numbers 'cannot be determined from the conflicting remarks'. Patrol lengths differ by source and era. The 2001 centenary page also gives 4 sub-inspectors and 25 riders. Do not quote the period wording about why northern riders rode in pairs.

verdicts.safe_claim: Inspecting the fence was hard. In 1904 the inspector's motorbike broke down after about 100 miles, and according to a heritage record a car bought in 1910 kept getting punctures until camels had to tow it back to camp.
verdicts.safe_value: 1904 motorbike (primary); 1910 car towed by camels (heritage record only)

evidence.quote: I got through a little over 100 miles, when my machine broke down
After many punctures and broken springs, it had to be towed slowly back to camp by camels.

verdicts.note: The motorbike story is primary and confirmed by J.S. Crawford, though its date is mid- or late 1904. The camel-towed car comes from a single inHerit record. Wikipedia's version mentions punctures but cites nothing. Fine as a light comic beat; narrate the car part softly ('the story goes...').

verdicts.safe_claim: By 1918 a parliamentary committee found rabbits living in the thousands inside Fence No. 1, and someone even proposed tearing it down and giving the netting to farmers.
verdicts.safe_value: Select Committee, Feb–Mar 1918

evidence.quote: rabbits were then established in thousands inside the No. 1 fence
the suggestion was made that the No. 1 fence should be removed and the netting distributed amongst the settlers

verdicts.note: This is J.S. Crawford's summary; I did not see the committee report itself. The committee rejected the idea, warning that 'A tremendous wave' of rabbits was approaching. World War I had drained men and money: Rabbit Department funding fell from £16,868 (1910/11) to £9,000 (1916/17).

verdicts.safe_claim: In 1948 the remote northern 800 km of Fence No. 1 was abandoned, and parts of it were sold to cattle stations.
verdicts.safe_value: 1948; 498 mi (about 800 km)

evidence.quote: In 1948, Section 4 of the No. 1 fence ceased to be maintained.
Section 4 extended north from 641 mile peg, to Cape Keraudren ... thus totalling 498 miles

verdicts.note: The chapter heading says '493 Miles' and the text says 498. 498 mi = 801 km. Pastoralists bought parts of it, and the rest was salvaged.

verdicts.safe_claim: By the early 1950s, the department's own history admits, the fences barely affected where rabbits went: there were millions of them west of both main fences. The fences were renamed vermin barrier fences.
verdicts.safe_value: Agriculture Protection Board from 1 March 1951

evidence.quote: The fences now had very little bearing on the control of the movements of rabbits
Following the introduction of myxomatosis to control rabbits in the 1950s, the importance of the rabbit-proof fence diminished.

verdicts.note: The 'now' in J.S. Crawford's text sits in the 1951 Agriculture Protection Board context, but he wrote in 1968–69, so 'by the 1950s' is fair. Reynolds & Diver (1992) also say that by the early-1950s refurbishment 'rabbits were by now in plague proportions west of the fence'.

verdicts.safe_claim: As a barrier against rabbits, the fences failed. They slowed the invasion, but they didn't stop it.
verdicts.safe_value: 'a failure' (NMA) / 'merely delayed' (Coman) / 'slowed up the rabbits' (Broomhall)

evidence.quote: However as a barrier to rabbits the fences were a failure
'At best, the long barrier fences merely delayed the spread of rabbits into new country'
the fence definitely slowed up the rabbits

verdicts.note: Wikipedia's 'failure' sentence is taken nearly word for word from the NMA blog (George Main, 2015), so the NMA is the stronger citation. Brian Coman, a rabbit scientist (quoted by NMA), and Broomhall (via inHerit) both support 'slowed but didn't stop'. SLWA's 'unique, if inadequate' is confirmed as well.

verdicts.safe_claim: The fence still exists as Western Australia's State Barrier Fence, more than 1,300 km long, and its main job today is keeping out wild dogs and migrating emus.
verdicts.safe_value: about 1,350 km (DPIRD page last modified Nov 2024; probably out of date)

evidence.quote: At approx imately 1,350 km in length, the fence extends from the Zuytdorp cliffs
The fence also provides protection from large migration of emus

verdicts.note: The DPIRD page metadata shows it was last modified on 22 Nov 2024. The 1,350 km figure looks like the old 1,170 km line plus about 176 km of extension built by Oct 2024. By 2026 much more of the 660 km extension is reportedly built, so the true current length is probably larger, and I found no official 2026 figure. 'More than 1,300 km' is safe at any date. Note that it is not one original fence: it combines parts of the old No. 1 and No. 2 lines with new sections.

verdicts.safe_claim: As rabbits mattered less, the fence got new names: the State Vermin Barrier Fence, then the Emu Fence, and today the State Barrier Fence.
verdicts.safe_value: Rabbit Proof Fence → State Vermin Barrier Fence → Emu Fence → State Barrier Fence

evidence.quote: The fence was later known as the State Vermin Barrier Fence, and the Emu Fence, before its current name - State Barrier Fence.
The SBF has been successful in containing these emu migrations.

verdicts.note: Official DPIRD wording. 'Containing' emu migrations is the department's own 2001 claim. Do not say 'beat the emus'.

verdicts.safe_claim: Western Australia is still extending the fence by about 660 km around Esperance, which will take it past 1,800 km. In 2026 the last section is still unfinished.
verdicts.safe_value: 660 km extension; >1,800 km on completion; 136 km gap still open in mid-2026

evidence.quote: Once the Esperance extension is complete the State Barrier Fence will extend over 1,800 km.
In 2026, a critical 136 km section is still unfinished

verdicts.note: The researcher's '176 km done' is from Farm Weekly of 22 Oct 2024 and is out of date. A June 2026 opposition (Nationals WA) release says 136 km is unfinished. An ARR.news piece of 6 Aug 2026 (Cloudflare-blocked; search snippet only) reportedly says 516 of 660 km are built. Both sources are partisan or advocacy. Say only 'still unfinished'. Keep out of the Short: the delay involves a native title agreement.

verdicts.safe_claim: Queensland has its own rabbit fence, 555 km long, which is still patrolled every week more than 130 years after it was begun.
verdicts.safe_value: 555 km; board fence begun 1893, final link 1997; about 28,000 km² protected

evidence.quote: The rabbit barrier fence is 555km long and protects roughly 28,000km2 of Southern Queensland.
constructed between 1893 and 1997

verdicts.note: Mt Gipps–Goombi comes from Wikipedia ('As of 2021'), not the board page I read. Queensland's first government rabbit fence was earlier, from 1886 near the Warrego River (NMA). 1893 to 2026 is 133 years.

verdicts.safe_claim: Western Australia wasn't first. In the 1880s about 300 miles of the New South Wales–South Australia border had already been netted against rabbits, and those attempts mostly failed.
verdicts.safe_value: about 300 miles, 1880s

evidence.quote: In the 1880s, the NSW, SA boundary was netted for a distance of 300 miles
Planners of the Western Australian fences followed the construction of similar long netting fences in New South Wales and Queensland in the 1880s.

verdicts.note: Now verified on the page itself through a Wayback snapshot (the live PIRSA page is behind Cloudflare). PIRSA cites Eric Rolls (1969). The NMA independently confirms that earlier 1880s fences existed in NSW and Queensland.

verdicts.safe_claim: (Not for narration.) The 2002 film 'Rabbit-Proof Fence' is about Aboriginal girls of the Stolen Generations who followed the fence home, not about the rabbit war.
verdicts.safe_value: 2002 film; the girls' 1931 journey followed the No. 2 fence

evidence.quote: synonymous with the 'Stolen Generation' through the 2002 film of the same name
journeyed along Western Australia's No.2 Rabbit Proof Fence in 1931

verdicts.note: Leave it out of an all-ages comedic Short. A title or thumbnail reading 'Rabbit-Proof Fence' will make Australian viewers think of the film; consider 'Australia vs Rabbits' instead.

verdicts.safe_claim: Along the fence line, cleared farmland meets native bush so sharply that scientists found it changes where clouds form.
verdicts.safe_value: Bunny Fence Experiment (Lyons et al. 1993 BAMS; Ray et al. 2003 JGR; Nair et al. 2011 JGR)

evidence.quote: over agricultural areas during the winter and over native perennial vegetation during the dry summer
preferential formation of clouds over native vegetation

verdicts.note: The researcher's phrasing ('rain clouds over native bush, clear skies over farms') oversimplifies. Ray et al. (2003, JGR, peer-reviewed) found cumulus more frequent over farmland in winter and over native vegetation in the dry summer. Nair et al. (2011) found clouds forming preferentially over native vegetation in the winter West Coast trough. The NCAR page is only a stub of a NYT article. The effect comes from land clearing, not from the wire itself; Nair et al. call it a '750 km rabbit-proof fence' (the present-day line).

missed: NATIONAL MUSEUM OF AUSTRALIA is a strong independent source the researcher could not open (Wayback works). It confirms the 1901 Commission, the Sept 1907 completion at Cape Keraudren, the £337,941 cost, 12-ft posts with 6-in burial, and the 'failure' verdict. It also says 'Some observers and newspaper columnists estimated a more likely figure to be well over £400 000'. https://web.archive.org/web/20160303152836/http://pateblog.nma.gov.au/2015/09/21/rabbit-proofing-the-west/

THE 'MARCH–JULY 1904' NO. 2 FENCE DATE IS NOT A MYTH. It is J.S. Crawford's own text: 'by about the 22 nd July, four months after commencement, the 724 miles of the No. 2 fence ... was completed'. Treat it as disputed against SLWA and NMA ('1905'). https://web.archive.org/web/20050723224313/http://agspsrv34.agric.wa.gov.au/programs/app/barrier/history/Crawford_construction9.htm

THE 160-MILE NO. 3 FIGURE IS NOT JUST A LOW-QUALITY-WEB ERROR. The National Museum of Australia uses it: 'ran the short distance of 160 miles (257 km) west'. J.S. Crawford and the 1907 report give 171 miles. Avoid on screen. https://web.archive.org/web/20160303152836/http://pateblog.nma.gov.au/2015/09/21/rabbit-proofing-the-west/

NOT THE FIRST RABBIT FENCE. The inHerit record calls WA's fence 'a world first in this method of pest control', which is false. NMA: 'Planners of the Western Australian fences followed the construction of similar long netting fences in New South Wales and Queensland in the 1880s'. PIRSA: 'In the 1880s, the NSW, SA boundary was netted for a distance of 300 miles'. https://inherit.dplh.wa.gov.au/Public/Inventory/PrintSingleRecord/15edcf36-1e9f-4be1-b478-ffb0f2158240 ; https://web.archive.org/web/20221115084302/https://pir.sa.gov.au/aghistory/natural_resources/weeds_pests_disease_management/pest_animals/rabbit_proof_fence

BALANCE: THE NO. 2 FENCE HELD FOR A WHILE. Alex Crawford's 1907–08 report: 'No rabbits have been found to the West of the No. 2 fence in the agricultural districts'. Wikipedia (citing NMA) says No. 2 'held back the rabbits for many years'. 'It slowed them, but it didn't stop them' is more accurate than 'useless from day one'. https://web.archive.org/web/2010/http://pandora.nla.gov.au/pan/43156/20040709/agspsrv34.agric.wa.gov.au/programs/app/barrier/history/REPORT1907.htm ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabbit-proof_fence

EXTRA 'FAMOUS LAST WORDS' BEAT (1908, via NMA, quoting the Chief Inspector's report as cited by A.D. Boulger in The West Australian): 'The fence as it stands to-day, is as rabbit-proof as the day it was erected.' https://web.archive.org/web/20160303152836/http://pateblog.nma.gov.au/2015/09/21/rabbit-proofing-the-west/

ANKETELL'S 1907 INTERVIEW CONTRADICTS ITSELF. It says 'Forty camel teams, each wagon having 14 animals' and also 'We have 40 camels on the job'. The '40 camels' count the researcher listed is probably a misprint for 40 teams. Teams of 14 camels make a better, safe visual. https://web.archive.org/web/2005/http://agspsrv34.agric.wa.gov.au/programs/app/barrier/pests/rabbit_invasion.htm

CANNING'S SURVEY END POINT CONFLICTS. ADB: 'from Starvation Harbour on the south coast to Cape Keraudren ... through 1175 miles'. Broomhall (via camelfarm): his survey 'ended at Wallal' and Anketell surveyed 'the last seventy miles'. https://adb.anu.edu.au/biography/canning-alfred-wernam-5499 ; https://web.archive.org/web/20110708112633/http://camelfarm.com/camels/rabbit_proof_fence.html

CRAWFORD'S TITLE AND A NICKNAME. He signed the 1907–08 report 'ALEX CRAWFORD, Acting Chief Inspector of Rabbits', and he held the job until he retired in 1922 (Broomhall). Wikipedia: 'The area inside the fence to the west became known as "Crawford's Paddock"', a usable fun beat. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabbit-proof_fence

DATE OF THE MOTORBIKE / '15–20 MILES WEST' INTERVIEW. J.S. Crawford dates the motorbike quote to 'a Press release around June, 1904'. The centenary reprint labels it Journal of Agriculture, 20 Dec 1904. Use '1904'. https://web.archive.org/web/20050723223859/http://agspsrv34.agric.wa.gov.au/programs/app/barrier/history/Crawford_construction6.htm

RAVENSTHORPE CONTEXT. The southern section was already finished: 'By August, 1903, the 215 miles of fence was completed from the south coast to the Goldfields Railway Line'. So the Dec 1904 rabbit was on the protected side of a completed section. https://web.archive.org/web/20050723224216/http://agspsrv34.agric.wa.gov.au/programs/app/barrier/history/Crawford_construction3.htm

FOR THE HOOK (outside the fence brief). J.S. Crawford: 'There is evidence of rabbits arriving in Australia as far back as 1788', and SLWA says the First Fleet brought them. The invasion is traced to the 1859 shipment on the Lightning released at Barwon Park. Say '24 wild rabbits released in 1859 started the invasion', not 'the first rabbits'. The often-quoted Austin line 'could do little harm...' appears on the 2001 WA Dept page with no primary source; do not quote it as his words. https://web.archive.org/web/20050723223701/http://agspsrv34.agric.wa.gov.au/programs/app/barrier/history/Crawford_intro.htm ; https://slwa.wa.gov.au/stories/wa-history/rabbit-proof-fence

'ACROSS THE CONTINENT' (user brief). The fence ran north–south inside Western Australia, from the Southern Ocean to the Indian Ocean, not across Australia east to west. The NMA phrasing is defensible: 'spanning the continent between north and south coastlines'. On the map, show it inside WA only. https://web.archive.org/web/20160303152836/http://pateblog.nma.gov.au/2015/09/21/rabbit-proofing-the-west/

GOLDEN PIPELINE IS UNRELIABLE FOR GEOGRAPHY. It says the No. 2 and No. 3 fences were 'constructed to the east of the No 1 fence'; they were west. Do not use it for map layout. https://www.goldenpipeline.com.au/event/no-1-rabbit-proof-fence/

1,350 KM IS PROBABLY OUT OF DATE. The DPIRD page was last modified on 22 Nov 2024, and the extension has progressed since: the opposition said in June 2026 that '136 km section is still unfinished'. Narrate 'more than 1,300 km'. https://loop.wa.gov.au/2026/06/11/nationals-demand-labor-ag-minister-finish-the-state-barrier-fence/

CLOUD EFFECT REVERSES BY SEASON (peer-reviewed Ray et al. 2003, JGR): more cumulus 'over agricultural areas during the winter and over native perennial vegetation during the dry summer'. Do not claim clouds are always over the bush. https://experts.umn.edu/en/publications/effects-of-land-use-in-southwest-australia-1-observations-of-cumu/

J.S. CRAWFORD ON GATES. NMA notes that gates proved a 'tremendous weakness', because many were left open or broken. A simple, kid-friendly reason the fence leaked, alongside floods, erosion, emus and kangaroos knocking it down, and white ants. https://web.archive.org/web/20160303152836/http://pateblog.nma.gov.au/2015/09/21/rabbit-proofing-the-west/

facts.claim: Before the viruses, Australians shot rabbits, trapped them, poisoned them and ripped up their burrows, and the rabbits kept multiplying anyway.
facts.value: shooting, trapping, poison, warren ripping: 'limited success'

sources.quote: Farmers ripped their warrens, laid poison and shot them but still they multiplied.
Conventional methods include shooting rabbits and destroying their warrens, but these had only limited success.

facts.caveat: There is no solid national number for how many rabbits were shot or trapped. Keep it qualitative. CSIROpedia was read through the Wayback Machine because the live site blocked bots.

facts.claim: In 1883 and 1884 at least 1,000 mongooses were released in New South Wales, Victoria and South Australia to hunt rabbits. The plan failed, partly because rabbit trappers killed the mongooses to protect their jobs.
facts.value: at least 1000 mongoose; 14 release sites; mainly 1883–1884

sources.quote: At least 1000 mongoose were released to control rabbits at 14 reported release locations in these states.
destruction of the mongoose by rabbit trappers, both inadvertently and in seeking to protect their employment

facts.caveat: Peer-reviewed paper (Peacock & Abbott 2010, Australian Journal of Zoology); the quotes come from its abstract. Up to 700 of the mongooses went into a single NSW trial. The paper also blames unfavourable climate.

facts.claim: In 1886 the New South Wales government sent 400 cats to a sheep station on the Paroo River to fight rabbits. A year earlier Victoria had declared cats, quolls and goannas protected 'natural enemies of the rabbit'.
facts.value: 400 cats, Tongo station, 1886; Victoria proclamation June 1885

sources.quote: In 1886 the NSW Government sent 400 cats to Tongo station, on the Paroo River NSW, to help control rabbits
In June 1885, the Victorian Government proclaimed feral cats, as well as quolls and goannas, as natural enemies of the rabbit under the Rabbit Suppression Act of 1884.

facts.caveat: Source is Abbott 2008, Conservation Science W. Aust. 7(1), a government journal. It relies on 1880s newspaper reports (The Australasian, 3 Apr 1886) and on Rolls 1969. For all-age content, avoid showing cats hunting.

facts.claim: Ferrets were used to flush rabbits out of burrows, but this was a hunting method and never a serious large-scale control.
facts.value: ferreting = hunting, not control

sources.quote: Since the number of rabbits ferrets can kill is limited, this is more a hunting activity than a serious control method.

facts.caveat: No documented Australian release of stoats or weasels for rabbit control was found. Mass releases of ferrets, stoats and weasels were a New Zealand story, so do not claim them for Australia.

facts.claim: On 31 August 1887 the New South Wales government offered a £25,000 prize for any new method of wiping out rabbits.
facts.value: £25,000; announced 31 August 1887

sources.quote: On 31 August 1887, the Colonial Government of New South Wales announced a prize of 25,000
£25,000 reward, equivalent to A$3.9 million in 2022

facts.caveat: Modern equivalents disagree: Wikipedia says A$3.9 million (2022), while the Australian Academy of Science and the Unimelb exhibit say about $10 million. On screen, say '£25,000' and skip the modern figure, or label any conversion as a rough estimate.

facts.claim: The prize commission received 1,456 suggestions and none of them was judged both safe and effective.
facts.value: 1,456 suggestions

sources.quote: The commission received 1,456 suggestions, including several schemes involving biological controls (see below), but none was found to be both safe and effective.

facts.caveat: Wikipedia's only source for this is a 1949 Queensland Country Life article ('Politics Saved the Rabbit!'). Trove could not be opened because of its bot check. No second source was found, so treat the number as unconfirmed or use 'more than a thousand ideas'.

facts.claim: Louis Pasteur entered the contest with chicken cholera, a poultry germ. He sent his nephew Adrien Loir and two colleagues to Sydney, where the commission built them a lab on tiny Rodd Island.
facts.value: Team: Adrien Loir, Germont, Frank Hinds; sailed 27 Feb 1888 on the Cuzco; lab on Rodd Island 1888

sources.quote: dispatched his nephew Adrien Loir and two colleagues, Dr François Germont and Dr Frank Hinds, to Australia to prove it and claim the reward
On 27 February 1888, the ship Cuzco set out for Australia, with three of Pasteur's representatives on board

facts.caveat: The AAS article was read through its verbatim repost at nationaltribune.com.au because the science.org.au host would not resolve. Sources name Germont as both François and Louis. Loir is called Pasteur's nephew by the AAS and Wikipedia, and Madame Pasteur's nephew by Unimelb.

facts.claim: Chicken cholera killed rabbits that ate it but did not spread well from rabbit to rabbit. In 1889 the commission rejected Pasteur's plan, and nobody ever won the prize.
facts.value: Pasteur rejected 3 April 1889; all claims rejected December 1889; no winner

sources.quote: Eventually in December 1889, a final report was issued that rejected all claims for the prize.
no evidence was found of the contagion spreading to healthy rabbits
Nobody won the £25,000 prize ‘for the effectual extermination of rabbits’.

facts.caveat: Unimelb dates the rejection of Pasteur's proposal to 3 April 1889. Some sources add that birds were also at risk; see pasteur_birds.

facts.claim: The prize rules banned any method that harmed horses, sheep, camels, goats, pigs or dogs but forgot to mention birds, the one group chicken cholera kills.
facts.value: rules omitted birds

sources.quote: ‘noxious to horses, sheep, camels, goats, swine, or dogs’ but had neglected any mention of birds
Moreover, native birds were shown to be prone to infection.

facts.caveat: This is the Academy's paraphrase of the competition terms; the primary 1887 notice was not seen. The Dictionary of Sydney's claim that native birds died after eating infected rabbits is a stronger version of this point and is not confirmed elsewhere.

facts.claim: The Pasteur team never got the rabbit prize, but on the same island they made anthrax vaccines that earned more than the prize. More than four million farm animals were vaccinated between 1890 and 1894.
facts.value: >4 million animals inoculated 1890–1894; profits exceeded the £25,000 prize

sources.quote: Loir made considerable profits manufacturing vaccines on Rodd Island over the next four years, more than the original prize for the rabbit competition.
Between 1890 and 1894 the anthrax vaccine was manufactured on the island and more than four million animals were inoculated.

facts.caveat: 'More than the prize' is the Academy's claim, and no accounting figures were seen.

facts.claim: In 1891 the rabbit-war lab island was also used to quarantine the dogs of the famous French actress Sarah Bernhardt.
facts.value: 1891; two terriers (Star and Chouette)

sources.quote: The island was briefly home to Sarah Bernhardt's dogs.
For about six months in 1891, the island also acted as a kind of makeshift quarantine station.

facts.caveat: The Dictionary of Sydney blog also mentions champagne, which suits an adult audience better than an all-ages one.

facts.claim: In 1906–07 a second Pasteur Institute scientist, Jean Danysz, tested another rabbit germ on Broughton Island in New South Wales, and it also failed.
facts.value: 1906–1907, Broughton Island NSW

sources.quote: In 1906 and 1907, Jean Danysz, of the Pasteur Institute of Paris, conducted trials on Broughton Island, New South Wales

facts.caveat: Wikipedia only. Optional detail.

facts.claim: A Brazilian scientist suggested the myxoma virus in 1919. The first field trial was on Wardang Island in South Australia on 16 November 1937, but by 1944 the researchers had concluded it would not work in most of Australia.
facts.value: 1919 suggestion; first infected rabbits released 16 Nov 1937 (Wardang Island); negative verdict 1944

sources.quote: released the first infected rabbits on the 16 November, 1937 on Wardang Island, South Australia
myxomatosis could not be used to control rabbit populations under most natural conditions in Australia with any promise of success

facts.caveat: The trials were run by Lionel Bull (CSIR). The same island later hosted the 1995 calicivirus trial.

facts.claim: In 1950 the virus was tried again in the Murray Valley and seemed to fizzle out: one site had 77 sick rabbits out of about 4,000, then none at all for weeks.
facts.value: 77 diseased of ~4000 at Gunbower; trials Mar–Nov 1950 at five sites

sources.quote: Soon after the start of the experiment 77 diseased rabbits were counted in an estimated population of 4000.
Between March and November 1950, MYXV was experimentally inoculated into wild European rabbits at five field study sites in the Murray Valley

facts.caveat: In early December 1950 the disease was thought to have died out everywhere except Rutherglen, and even there it was fading.

facts.claim: Heavy rain in 1950 bred huge numbers of mosquitoes along the Murray. They spread the virus, and nine weeks after the Balldale outbreak the disease covered an area of about 1,760 by 1,600 kilometres.
facts.value: Balldale outbreak Dec 1950; 'flood' of reports by end Jan 1951; 1,760 km x 1,600 km by mid-Feb 1951; vector Culex annulirostris

sources.quote: By mid February, nine weeks after the Balldale outbreak the disease ranged over an area 1 760 kilometres by 1 600 kilometres.
The reason for the epidemic spread of myxomatosis was to be found in the unusually heavy rains which fell during 1950.
rains in December 1950 produced more mosquitoes, the vector that spread the virus

facts.caveat: The NMA page was read through the Wayback Machine because of a 403. The mosquito species was the dusk-biting Culex annulirostris, which breeds in weedy lagoons.

facts.claim: The 1950 virus strain killed up to 99.8 percent of the rabbits it infected.
facts.value: 99.8% case fatality rate

sources.quote: case fatality rates (CFR) for laboratory and wild rabbits were estimated to be as high as 99.8%
The virus killed 99.8 per cent of rabbits that caught the infection

facts.caveat: 99.8% is the death rate among infected rabbits, not the share of all Australian rabbits killed. Field losses: 'Localized population losses of 99%–100% were observed' (Kerr et al. 2015); Fenner himself spoke of 99 percent; a 1951 Argus headline said 90%. Safe line: 'killed up to 99.8% of the rabbits it infected'.

facts.claim: By the late 1940s Australia had an estimated 600 million rabbits, and myxomatosis is said to have cut that by about half a billion in two years. Scientists caution that these totals were never actually measured.
facts.value: ~600 million (late 1940s estimate); 'dropped by half a billion in the first two years'

sources.quote: By the late 1940s the rabbit population had rapidly increased to 600 million.
The population dropped by half a billion in the first two years
The number of rabbits in Australia pre-1950 is not known but it was probably in the hundreds of millions
They estimated that tens of millions of rabbits were killed, rather than hundreds of millions, but cautioned that they had little basis for the estimation.

facts.caveat: The sources disagree. The peer-reviewed Kerr 2015 review says pre-1950 numbers are unknown, and that the 1952 field team estimated 'tens of millions' killed. Say 'an estimated 600 million'. Avoid an exact 'down to 100 million'; see myths.
