facts.claim: Once rabbits stopped eating the grass, Australia's wool and meat output rose by $68 million in 1952–53. The rabbit-skin trade collapsed at the same time.
facts.value: +$68 million (1952–53); rabbit skin exports A$14m (1950–51) to A$4.5m (1954–55)

sources.quote: In 1952-53, Australia’s wool and meat production jumped by $68 million as pastures recovered from the ravages of rabbits.
Exports of rabbit skins fell from about A$14 million in 1950-51 to A$4.5 million in 1954-55.

facts.caveat: The figures are in the currency values of the period.

facts.claim: In 1951 people blamed the rabbit virus for a deadly human brain-fever outbreak. To calm the public, Frank Fenner, Macfarlane Burnet and CSIRO chairman Ian Clunies Ross injected themselves with myxoma virus, and none of them got sick.
facts.value: 1951; dose 'strong enough to kill 100-1000 rabbits'; Murray Valley encephalitis scare

sources.quote: Burnet, Dr Ian Clunies-Ross and Dr Frank Fenner inject themselves with a dose of myxoma virus strong enough to kill 100-1000 rabbits.
Burnet agrees to a challenge issued by a councillor from Mildura – to inoculate himself with the myxoma virus to prove it is harmless to humans.
CSIRO Chairman Ian Clunies Ross and two other notable scientists, Macfarlane Burnet and Frank Fenner, injected themselves with myxoma virus.
Fenner and two colleagues inoculated themselves with the myxoma virus to successfully refute that association

facts.caveat: Confirmed as fact. Accounts differ on who injected whom: some say Burnet and Fenner injected each other and Clunies Ross insisted on joining. Say 'injected themselves'. The year 1951 comes from WEHI's timeline.

facts.claim: Within about a year the virus itself evolved into slightly milder strains. Rabbits stayed sick longer, so mosquitoes could spread those strains more easily.
facts.value: attenuation within ~1 year (1951–52); grade 3 strains dominant for ~30 years

sources.quote: Within one year mutations in the virus had led to slightly less virulence
Grade 1 viruses such as SLS quickly became relatively rare in the field and the predominant viruses were of grade 3 virulence

facts.caveat: PestSmart's timeline places the start of attenuation in 1951–52. Grade 3 strains still killed 70–95% of infected rabbits, so the virus did not become harmless.

facts.claim: The rabbits evolved too. At one study site the same virus that killed 90 percent of rabbits killed only 26 percent seven years later.
facts.value: CFR 90% to 26% over 7 years (Lake Urana, NSW)

sources.quote: CFRs dropped from 90% to 26%
when the mortality rate fell from 99 per cent, which it was originally, to 90 per cent, there were enough survivors for selection for genetic resistance to occur

facts.caveat: Measured at Lake Urana over 'seven annual epizootics' by testing each generation of rabbits with a standard strain in the laboratory. It is one site and not a national figure.

facts.claim: Then the virus fought back: most strains collected in the 1990s were more lethal to non-resistant rabbits than the 1950 original.
facts.value: 1990s field isolates more virulent than 1950 release strain

sources.quote: the majority of these viruses were more virulent than the virus used to initiate the epidemic
most virus isolates from the 1990s induced a highly lethal immune collapse syndrome

facts.caveat: The higher lethality was measured in laboratory rabbits without resistance. In wild, resistant rabbits it is an ongoing arms race, and the strategy calls it an 'arms race'. For all ages, keep the disease description abstract.

facts.claim: To help spread the virus where mosquitoes were scarce, Australia released European rabbit fleas, first on Macquarie Island in December 1968 and on the mainland from 1969. A desert-adapted Spanish flea followed in 1993.
facts.value: Dec 1968 Macquarie Island; Aug 1969 Werribee (Vic); 1969 approved; Spanish rabbit flea 1993

sources.quote: The European rabbit flea Spilopsyllus cuniculi (Dale) was first released on Macquarie Island in December 1968.
The European rabbit flea was first released in Victoria in August 1969 at Werribee.
Spanish rabbit flea ( Xenophsylla cunicularis ) adapted for arid conditions approved for release and improves transmission of MV.

facts.caveat: Mainland release dates varied by state, and early releases also ran in NSW (Sobey & Conolly 1971). CSIROpedia says both fleas had 'minimal impact', which conflicts with PestSmart's 'improves transmission'.

facts.claim: By the mid-1990s rabbits had recovered to an estimated 200 to 300 million.
facts.value: ~300 million (1995, CSIRO/PestSmart); 200–300 million by 1991 (Wikipedia)

sources.quote: by 1995 had multiplied to an estimated 300 million
Rabbit population about 300 million and climbing.

facts.caveat: These are rough estimates. Wikipedia gives '200–300 million by 1991'.

facts.claim: Next came a rabbit calicivirus. It was tested in a high-security lab from 1991 and then on Wardang Island from March 1995, ahead of a planned 1998 release.
facts.value: quarantine testing from June 1991 (AAHL Geelong); island trials March 1995; release planned 1998

sources.quote: It was due for release in 1998, but, after only 6 months, it escaped from the island, most likely carried by insects.
The virus was taken into quarantine at the CSIRO Australian Animal Health Laboratory in Geelong for comprehensive testing over three years from June 1991.

facts.caveat: The strain was Czech CAPM 351 (RHDV1). Wardang lies about 3–4 km off the coast: the EID book review says 3 km, Schwensow 2014 says 4 km.

facts.claim: In late September 1995 the virus got out of the island quarantine pens, most likely carried by flies. By 12 October it was killing rabbits on the mainland, and by 28 October it was hundreds of kilometres inland.
facts.value: experiment began 13 Sep 1995; flies positive 24 Sep; infected rabbit outside quarantine 29 Sep; mainland (Point Pearce) 12 Oct; Yunta & Gum Creek 28 Oct 1995

sources.quote: blowflies, Calliphora stygia, collected on 24th September 1995 from traps placed immediately outside the quarantine area on Wardang Island, were positive for rabbit calicivirus
were first recorded at Yunta and Gum Creek in north-eastern South Australia on 28th October
The first dead rabbit confirmed to have RHD on the mainland was discovered on 12 October 1995 on Point Pearce

facts.caveat: Exact dates vary a little between the MLA 1996 report and Schwensow 2014, which says the virus arrived on the mainland around 1 October. Use 'October 1995'. Distances to Yunta were not given in the sources, so don't state a km figure.

facts.claim: Just before the escape, the number of bushflies on the island jumped about a thousandfold.
facts.value: ~1,000-fold increase in bushflies (Musca vetustissima)

sources.quote: There was approximately a 1,000-fold increase in the number of bushflies, Musca vetustissima, shortly before the spread of the virus.

facts.caveat: Peer-reviewed (McColl et al. 2002, Epidemiology and Infection). The MLA report found the virus in blowflies, not bushflies, in its 24 Sept sample. Say 'flies'.

facts.claim: The escaped virus spread at roughly 15 to 60 kilometres a week.
facts.value: 2–9 km per day; ~15–60 km per week (minimum)

sources.quote: These records indicate a rate of spread of 2–9 km day−1 or about 15–60 km week−1

facts.caveat: The authors call this a minimum rate.

facts.claim: Calicivirus cut Australia's rabbits by about 60 percent nationally, with up to 95 percent losses in dry inland areas.
facts.value: ~60% nationwide; up to 95% (arid); arid numbers down to 10–15% of original

sources.quote: Nation-wide, rabbit numbers fell by 60%
The initial outbreak of RHD varied in its impact with up to a 95% reduction in pest rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus) populations
The numbers of rabbits are down to ten or fifteen percent of their original numbers.

facts.caveat: The figures vary by source. PestSmart says 'kills up to 98% of rabbits in arid areas' and elsewhere 'initially knocked down 90%'. The safest pair is 'about 60% nationwide, up to 95% in dry areas'. The virus worked worse in cool, wet regions.

facts.claim: The official release came only in 1996, after the virus had already spread on its own. Western Australia's ceremony was six infected rabbits on 18 October 1996, but the disease had reached the state's border by itself in May.
facts.value: approved 1996; WA controlled release began 18 Oct 1996 (6 rabbits near Cranbrook); first WA deaths May 1996

sources.quote: The controlled release of rabbit calicivirus disease (RCD) in Western Australia began today with Primary Industry Minister Monty House releasing six infected rabbits near the Great Southern town of Cranbrook.
the State's first confirmed deaths of wild rabbits from the disease were on the WA - South Australia border in May
released into the  feral rabbit population in 1996

facts.caveat: The exact national approval date in 1996 was not found.

facts.claim: Rabbits in cooler, wetter regions were partly protected by a harmless cousin virus that was discovered in 2009.
facts.value: RCV-A1 discovered 2009

sources.quote: RCV-A1 confers partial protection to lethal RHDV1 infection and therefore impedes effective RHDV based biocontrol.

facts.caveat: PestSmart also notes rabbits began developing resistance to RHDV1 in the 2000s.

facts.claim: In 2015 a new strain, RHDV2, turned up in Australia uninvited. Nobody released it.
facts.value: first isolate 13 May 2015 (ACT, Canberra region); serology shows presence ≥5 months earlier

sources.quote: The first virus isolate (BlMt-1) came from a rabbit found in Australian Capital Territory on May 13, 2015.
RHDV2: Found in Australia in May 2015, RHDV2 is a variant of RHDV that was not released
Retrospective serological analysis reveals presence of the emerging lagovirus RHDV2 in Australia in wild rabbits at least five months prior to its first detection

facts.caveat: PestSmart's timeline says it 'arrives' in 2014, which matches the retrospective serology. Say 'detected in 2015'.

facts.claim: RHDV2 cut rabbit numbers by about 60 percent on average and within 18 months became the main calicivirus strain.
facts.value: −60% average (18 sites, 2014–2018); −64% sustained at 6 sites to 2022

sources.quote: average rabbit population abundances were reduced by 60% between 2014 and 2018 based on monitoring data acquired from 18 sites across Australia
Within 18 months it had mostly replaced the existing RHDV1 strain

facts.caveat: Credit this to nature rather than humans, since it was an accidental arrival.

facts.claim: In the first week of March 2017 Australia released a Korean strain called K5 at more than 600 sites. It knocked local populations down by only about a third, and RHDV2 outcompeted it.
facts.value: first week March 2017; >600 sites (110 in WA); first new agent in 20 years; ~34% knockdown

sources.quote: More than 600 release sites were selected, including 110 sites in Western Australia (WA).
local population knockdowns of approximately 34%
Delivers a 34% national average knockdown at release sites but is outcompeted by RHDV2 at landscape scale.

facts.caveat: The DPIRD URL now redirects to library.dpird.wa.gov.au/bs_factsheets/71/. K5 is not a new virus but a Korean variant of RHDV1.

facts.claim: In 2026 Australia again has an estimated 200 million wild rabbits, and farmers report numbers not seen in decades.
facts.value: ~200 million (July 2026 estimate); NMA: 'at least 150 million'

sources.quote: with an estimated current population of around 200 million
Australia is home to at least 150 million feral rabbits
rabbit numbers had climbed to levels not seen since the mid-1990s

facts.caveat: Nobody counts rabbits nationally, so these are rough estimates and the 200 million figure comes from news reporting. Say 'an estimated 200 million'. The 'mid-1990s' line is an Invasive Species Council quote about Western Australia.

facts.claim: Rabbits still cost Australian farming about $200 million a year and threaten more than 300 native species.
facts.value: $206 million per year; 300+ native species (322 nationally listed threatened species)

sources.quote: Australia’s most costly pest animal, rabbits cause $206 million in losses each year to the agricultural industry
impacts 322 nationally listed threatened species

facts.caveat: The $206 million figure comes from a 2009 economic study (Gong et al.) that is still quoted. Use 'over $200 million a year'.

facts.claim: Today's toolkit combines everything: poison baits, fumigation, ripping or blasting warrens, padded traps, shooting, fences and virus baits. Scientists stress that no single weapon works on its own.
facts.value: national SOPs: 1080 & pindone baiting, fumigation, ripping, explosives, padded-jaw traps, shooting, K5 baits

sources.quote: K5 is not the silver bullet for rabbit eradication in Australia and  an integrated approach is required.
NATSOP-RAB005 National Standard Operating Procedure: Rabbit warren destruction by ripping

facts.caveat: Myxomatosis still circulates; PestSmart says 'Today it affects an estimated 40-50% of the rabbit population'. For all ages, show tractors, fences and lab scenes rather than dead animals.

facts.claim: Scientists say Australia needs a new rabbit virus every 10 to 15 years to stay ahead. Biocontrol research went unfunded from 2022 until a $4 million program was announced in July 2026.
facts.value: new agent every 10–15 years; unfunded since 2022; $4M program incl. $2.6M Commonwealth (July 2026); biocontrol benefit ~$70 billion 1950–2011

sources.quote: a pipeline of biocontrol agents needs to be developed, ideally to enable a new agent to be released   every  10 to 15 years
including $2.6 million in Commonwealth funding
approximately $70 billion from 1950 to 2011

facts.caveat: The program is called Future-Proofing Rabbit Biocontrol; PestSmart says Phase 1 began in 2026. The QCL article (27 July 2026) quotes the Minister and stakeholders.

facts.claim: Frank Fenner said the 1950–51 epidemic was without parallel for scale and speed in the history of infections.
facts.value: Fenner quote

sources.quote: for scale and speed [the myxomatosis epidemic] must be without parallel in the history of infections

facts.caveat: The NMA quotes Fenner. Fenner later chaired the commission that certified smallpox eradication and announced it on 8 May 1980 (Wikipedia, Frank Fenner).

myths.claim: Within 10 years two million rabbits a year could be shot or trapped with no effect on the population.
myths.why_wrong: It is repeated everywhere but has no source: the Wikipedia sentence carries a 'Citation needed' tag (Jan 2021). It may be true, but it is not verified.

myths.claim: Myxomatosis killed 99.8% of Australia's rabbits.
myths.why_wrong: 99.8% is the case-fatality rate among infected rabbits, not the share of the national population killed. Field losses were 99–100% in some places, and the 1952 field team estimated 'tens of millions' killed nationally.

myths.claim: Myxomatosis cut the rabbit population from 600 million to 100 million in two years.
myths.why_wrong: The Wikipedia 'Rabbits in Australia' article cites an archived CSIRO page that says 'from an estimated 600 million' but gives no 100 million figure, and the Wardang Island article cites only 'National Archives of Australia'. The AAS says 'dropped by half a billion', but a peer-reviewed review says pre-1950 numbers are unknown and the decline 'could not be measured'. Use 'an estimated 600 million' plus local 99% die-offs.

myths.claim: The escaped calicivirus killed 10 million rabbits within two months.
myths.why_wrong: Wikipedia cites a CSIRO 2008 factsheet for this. The archived factsheet text that could be extracted says only that the virus 'killed large numbers of rabbits' and does not show this figure. It is unverified, so don't use it.

myths.claim: The 2017 national release wiped out around 60% of rabbits.
myths.why_wrong: This mixes up two viruses. The official 2017 K5 release gave only about 34% local knockdown. The 60% average drop came from RHDV2, which arrived on its own around 2014–15 and was never released.

myths.claim: Fenner's 2010 paper abstract says wild rabbits were sent to Victoria in 1879.
myths.why_wrong: This is a typo in the abstract as indexed by ANU. Every other source, including CSIRO and the NMA, gives 1859. Don't copy dates from that abstract.

myths.claim: By 1880 rabbits were 'a plague of almost one billion'.
myths.why_wrong: This appears in the Australian Academy of Science's Loir article with no source. The peer-reviewed review says even pre-1950 numbers are unknown.

myths.claim: £25,000 equals $10 million today.
myths.why_wrong: Inflation conversions disagree. Wikipedia gives A$3.9 million (2022), while AAS, Unimelb and ABC say about $10 million. Show '£25,000' and skip the modern figure.

myths.claim: Pasteur's chicken cholera was simply too deadly to native wildlife, so it was banned.
myths.why_wrong: The commission's main reason, given on 3 April 1889, was that no evidence of sufficient contagiousness was found: the germ did not spread rabbit to rabbit. Risk to birds was a secondary concern, and the Dictionary of Sydney's 'native birds perished' line is the strongest, least-sourced version.

story_gold: The rules forgot birds: the £25,000 prize banned anything harmful to 'horses, sheep, camels, goats, swine, or dogs', and Pasteur entered chicken cholera, a bird disease. Nobody won the prize, but Pasteur's team then earned more than the prize money making anthrax vaccines on the same island. https://www.science.org.au/news-events/news-views/adrien-loir-louis-pasteur-australasian-rabbit-plague
The island lab built for the rabbit war also quarantined Sarah Bernhardt's dogs in 1891. https://dictionaryofsydney.org/blog/the_island_laboratory
Rabbits 1, Mongoose Army 0: at least 1,000 mongooses were released in 1883–84, and rabbit trappers killed them partly to protect their own jobs. https://doi.org/10.1071/ZO10043

In 1886 the NSW government shipped 400 cats to a station on the Paroo River to fight rabbits, which is ironic now that feral cats are one of Australia's worst pests. https://library.dbca.wa.gov.au/static/Journals/080559/080559-07.001.pdf

Near-miss: in December 1950 scientists thought myxomatosis had failed again. Farmhands at Balldale saw sick rabbits but fumigated the warrens before the team arrived. Nine weeks later the disease covered about 1,760 x 1,600 km, carried by mosquitoes after a record wet year. https://csiropedia.csiro.au/Myxomatosis-to-control-rabbits/

Three of Australia's top scientists, one a future Nobel laureate (Burnet, 1960) and one the man who later announced the end of smallpox (Fenner), injected themselves with enough rabbit virus to kill 100–1,000 rabbits. It started as a dare from a Mildura councillor. https://www.wehi.edu.au/about/history/myxomatosis-experiment/

Arms race: within seven years the same virus that killed 90% of rabbits at one site killed only 26%. By the 1990s the virus had evolved to be more lethal than the 1950 original. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4379559/

The great escape: calicivirus was locked in quarantine pens on an island but got out on flies within six months, three years before its planned 1998 release. Bushflies on the island had jumped about a thousandfold just before. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12558351/

Western Australia held an official release ceremony with six infected rabbits on 18 October 1996, five months after the virus had already arrived at its border on its own. https://www.wa.gov.au/government/media-statements/Court%20Coalition%20Government/Six-rabbits-infected-with-RCD-released-nr-GS-town-of-Cranbrook-19961018

The uninvited guest won: RHDV2, which nobody released, cut rabbits by about 60%, while the officially released K5 managed only about 34% and was outcompeted. https://pestsmart.org.au/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2024/05/Australias-Rabbit-Biocontrol-Pipeline-Strategy.pdf

Today there are again an estimated 200 million rabbits, and scientists say a new virus is needed every 10–15 years. The match is not over. https://www.queenslandcountrylife.com.au/story/9316922/agriculture-minister-julie-collins-unveils-urgent-rabbit-strategy/
research.notes:
CLEAN ROUND-BY-ROUND SCORE. Every line below has a sourced number:
R1 1860s–1880s guns, traps, poison, ripping: RABBITS. Qualitative only; CSIROpedia's 'still they multiplied'.
R2 1883–86 predators: RABBITS. 1,000+ mongooses at 14 sites; 400 cats.
R3 1887–89 £25,000 prize / Pasteur / Rodd Island: RABBITS. No winner; rejected 1889.
(R? 1901–07 fence: covered by another domain, also RABBITS.)
R4 1950–51 myxomatosis: HUMANS. Up to 99.8% fatality among infected rabbits; 1,760 x 1,600 km in 9 weeks.
R5 1950s–90s evolution: RABBITS. Fatality at one site fell from 90% to 26% in 7 years; numbers back to an estimated ~300M by 1995.
R6 1995–96 calicivirus: HUMANS. About -60% nationwide, up to -95% in dry areas. It was an accident, since it escaped early on flies.
R7 2017 K5: draw or partial, about -34%. RHDV2 (2015, natural arrival, -60%) counts for 'nature', not humans.
R8 2026: rabbits back to an estimated ~200M, so the match continues.
A tidy Short tally: 'Humans 2 (myxo, calici), Rabbits 4+ (guns, predators, prize, evolution), match ongoing'. A callback to the volcano episode could be 'Score: Humans two, Rabbits... still breeding.'

SAFE PHRASINGS:
- 'an estimated 600 million rabbits' (not counted).
- 'killed up to 99.8% of the rabbits it infected', not 'of all rabbits'.
- 'about 60% nationwide, up to 95% in dry areas' for calicivirus.
- 'October 1995' for the escape.
- 'detected in 2015' for RHDV2.
- 'an estimated 200 million today'.
Avoid '100 million after myxo', '10 million in two months', '2 million shot a year' and '1 billion by 1880'.

CONFLICTS TO FLAG TO OTHER DOMAINS:
- Founding release size: the AAS Loir article says '24 wild-caught rabbits'; the NMA says Austin released '13'; Wikipedia says 'at least 13'.
- Prize equivalents: A$3.9M (Wikipedia, 2022) vs ~$10M (AAS, Unimelb).
- Germont's first name: François (AAS) vs Louis (Unimelb).

ACCESS NOTES: CSIROpedia and the NMA blocked direct fetches (Cloudflare/403), so both were read through Wayback Machine copies of the same URLs. Trove (the 1949 source for '1,456') showed a bot check, which I did not bypass, so the 1,456 figure stays unconfirmed. The AAS article host would not resolve; its text was read from a verbatim repost (nationaltribune.com.au), but the URLs above are the canonical AAS ones. The MLA 1996 report quote contains OCR artefacts ('l3th', 'War dang') on the source page.

ALL-AGES: myxomatosis and RHD cause visibly distressing symptoms. Show maps, mosquitoes and flies, lab glassware, tractors and rabbits running, never sick or dead animals. Skip the 'rabbit smoothies' anecdote from the New Zealand 1997 illegal release (EID review), and skip ripping/explosives imagery.

verdicts.safe_claim: For decades Australians shot, trapped, poisoned and ripped up warrens. On some farms that kept rabbits down, but it never stopped the plague.
verdicts.safe_value: qualitative only: shooting, trapping, poison, fumigation, warren ripping

evidence.quote: Farmers ripped their warrens, laid poison and shot them but still they multiplied.
normal trapping, shooting and poisoning which kept rabbits to manageable numbers
trapping, rabbit warren ripping, fumigation and bounty systems

verdicts.note: The same CSIROpedia page says these methods kept rabbits 'to manageable numbers' in normal times. It says the late-1940s explosion happened partly because WWII took away the manpower for trapping, and NMA and PestSmart say the same. So 'kept multiplying anyway' overstates it: the methods did limit numbers, but they could not stop the plague. Read through the Wayback Machine (web.archive.org/web/2024/...).

verdicts.safe_claim: Mostly in 1883 and 1884, at least a thousand mongooses were released to hunt rabbits. They never took hold, and rabbit trappers killed many of them, some to protect their own jobs.
verdicts.safe_value: >=1,000 mongooses; 14 release sites; mainly 1883-84; up to 700 in one NSW trial

evidence.quote: At least 1000 mongoose were released to control rabbits at 14 reported release locations
primarily in 1883 and 1884
destruction of the mongoose by rabbit trappers, both inadvertently and in seeking to protect their employment
Unfavourable climate was implicated by CLIMATCH modelling in the failure of all releases

verdicts.note: The abstract was checked through the Crossref API. The trapper reason is 'the only reason stated' in historical records, and modern climate modelling adds climate as a cause. 'Partly because trappers killed them' is fair. Don't say 'at least 1,000 in 1883 and 1884' as if the years were exact: the abstract says 'primarily'.

verdicts.safe_claim: In 1886 the New South Wales government sent 400 cats to a sheep station on the Paroo River to fight rabbits. A year earlier Victoria had declared feral cats, quolls and goannas protected 'natural enemies of the rabbit'.
verdicts.safe_value: 400 cats, Tongo station, 1886; Victorian proclamation June 1885

evidence.quote: In 1886 the NSW Government sent 400 cats to Tongo station, on the Paroo River
proclaimed feral cats, as well as quolls and goannas, as natural enemies of the rabbit

verdicts.note: I read the PDF text myself and the quotes are exact. Only one modern source has it (Abbott 2008), and it cites The Australasian of 3 Apr 1886 and Rolls 1969. I found no independent second source. Fine to narrate, but treat it as a single source.

verdicts.safe_claim: Ferrets were used to chase rabbits out of burrows, but that was hunting, not a way to control a continent of rabbits.
verdicts.safe_value: qualitative

evidence.quote: this is more a hunting activity than a serious control method

verdicts.note: Only Wikipedia covers this, and it cites a 1984 UK study by Cowan. It is a qualitative point with low risk. The researcher is right to keep the stoat and weasel releases out: those happened in New Zealand.

verdicts.safe_claim: In 1887 the New South Wales government offered a £25,000 prize for any new way to wipe out rabbits.
verdicts.safe_value: £25,000; 1887 (31 August per Unimelb)

evidence.quote: On 31 August 1887, the Colonial Government of New South Wales announced a prize of 25,000
£25,000 or $10 million in today’s terms
any method of success not previously known in the Colony for the effectual extermination of rabbits

verdicts.note: The amount and year are solid. The exact date of 31 August is from the Unimelb exhibit only, and Wikipedia cites an SMH advertisement of 7 September 1887. Say '1887', not the day. Skip the modern equivalent: it is $10M per AAS, Unimelb and the Penguin blurb, and A$3.9M per Wikipedia's inflation template.

verdicts.safe_claim: Nearly 1,500 ideas poured in, and none was judged both safe and effective.
verdicts.safe_value: ~1,500 entries (1,456 per a 1949 newspaper via Wikipedia; '1500' per Dando-Collins)

evidence.quote: The commission received 1,456 suggestions
would attract 1500 entries.

verdicts.note: The exact 1,456 rests only on a 1949 Queensland Country Life article (Trove nla.news-article97120682). Trove showed a proof-of-work bot check, which I did not bypass. A separate historian (Stephen Dando-Collins, Pasteur's Gambit, 2008) gives a round '1500 entries'. 'Nearly 1,500' or 'more than a thousand' is safe; don't show '1,456' on screen.

verdicts.safe_claim: Louis Pasteur entered with chicken cholera, a poultry germ. He sent his young relative Adrien Loir and two colleagues to Sydney, and the commission built them a lab on tiny Rodd Island.
verdicts.safe_value: Loir + Germont + Hinds; sailed 27 Feb 1888 (Cuzco); Rodd Island lab

evidence.quote: dispatched his nephew Adrien Loir and two colleagues
Pasteur's assistant and Madame Pasteur's nephew
Il est le neveu par alliance de Louis Pasteur
Rodd Island, situated in Iron Cove at the western end of Sydney Harbour, was chosen

verdicts.note: The AAS article loaded directly this time. Loir was Pasteur's nephew by marriage: his mother was the sister of Marie Pasteur. 'Nephew' is acceptable, and 'nephew by marriage' or 'young assistant' is the most accurate. The sailing date of 27 Feb 1888 on the Cuzco comes from Unimelb only. Germont's first name differs between sources (François in AAS, Louis in Unimelb), so leave it out.

verdicts.safe_claim: Chicken cholera killed rabbits but didn't spread well from rabbit to rabbit. In 1889 the commission rejected the plan, and nobody ever won the prize.
verdicts.safe_value: Pasteur rejected 3 Apr 1889; all claims rejected Dec 1889; no winner

evidence.quote: The main reason for the rejection was that no evidence of sufficient contagiousness had been found.
in December 1889, a final report was issued that rejected all claims for the prize
while chicken cholera killed rabbits, it was not sufficiently transmissible

verdicts.note: Unimelb and AAS agree. Loir later claimed in his 1892 thesis that the commission was politically hostile (Unimelb page 4), so 'the commission rejected it' is the neutral way to put it.

verdicts.safe_claim: The prize rules banned anything harmful to horses, sheep, camels, goats, pigs or dogs, but forgot birds, the very animals chicken cholera is named after.
verdicts.safe_value: rules omitted birds

evidence.quote: had neglected any mention of birds
the disease appeared fatal to all birds
native birds were shown to be prone to infection.

verdicts.note: The researcher's phrase 'the one group chicken cholera kills' is false: the whole scheme depended on it killing rabbits. The list of six animals comes from the AAS paraphrase. I could not reach the 1887 notice itself: Trove and the Tasmanian parliamentary PDFs were blocked. The birds point was a secondary reason for rejection, after poor contagion.

verdicts.safe_claim: Pasteur's team never won the rabbit prize, but on the same island it made anthrax vaccine, and more than four million farm animals were vaccinated between 1890 and 1894.
verdicts.safe_value: >4 million animals inoculated 1890-1894; profits 'more than the prize' (AAS only)

evidence.quote: more than four million animals were inoculated
more than four million animals being inoculated between 1890 and 1894
more than the original prize for the rabbit competition

verdicts.note: The four million figure appears in two Dictionary of Sydney texts, which are not fully independent of each other. 'Earned more than the prize' rests on the AAS alone with no accounts shown, so hedge it ('reportedly earned more than the prize') or drop it. Wikipedia says vaccine production began in June 1890.

verdicts.safe_claim: In 1891 the rabbit-war island even served as a quarantine station for the dogs of the famous actress Sarah Bernhardt.
verdicts.safe_value: 1891; about six months; terriers Star and Chouette

evidence.quote: They were quarantined there during her 1891 world tour at the suggestion of Loir.
For about six months in 1891, the island also acted as a kind of makeshift quarantine station.
two small terriers named Star and Chouette

verdicts.note: The main Dictionary of Sydney entry does not mention Bernhardt. The blog post and Wikipedia do.

verdicts.safe_claim: In 1906 and 1907, another Pasteur Institute scientist, Jean Danysz, tested a different rabbit germ on Broughton Island in New South Wales, and it failed too.
verdicts.safe_value: 1906-1907, Broughton Island NSW; Danysz left May 1907

evidence.quote: In 1906 and 1907, Jean Danysz, of the Pasteur Institute of Paris, conducted trials on Broughton Island
not an effective method of culling the feral rabbit population

verdicts.note: The Encyclopedia of Australian Science (EOAS) independently confirms it: he arrived in 1906 and left in May 1907, and his strain was 'identical to one already isolated in Australia'. The agent was a Pasteurella bacterium, so call it a 'germ', not a virus.

verdicts.safe_claim: A Brazilian scientist suggested the rabbit virus myxoma back in 1919. The first field trial was on Wardang Island in South Australia in November 1937, and by 1944 the scientists had concluded it wouldn't work in most of Australia.
verdicts.safe_value: 1919; 16 Nov 1937 Wardang Island; 1944 negative verdict (Bull & Mules)

evidence.quote: released the first infected rabbits on the 16 November, 1937 on Wardang Island
could not be used to control rabbit populations under most natural conditions in Australia
In November 1937, the CSIRO began to use Wardang to conduct its first field trials of myxomatosis
In 1919 the potential use of myxomatosis for rabbit control was first drawn to the attention of Australian authorities

verdicts.note: Say CSIR, not CSIRO, for 1937: CSIRO was formed in 1949. The day '16 November' comes from a CSIROpedia photo caption, so 'November 1937' is the safer choice.

verdicts.safe_claim: In 1950 scientists tried again in the Murray Valley. At one farm 77 sick rabbits turned up among about 4,000, then none at all for weeks. It looked like another failure.
verdicts.safe_value: 77 of ~4,000 at Gunbower; five sites, March-November 1950

evidence.quote: 77 diseased rabbits were counted in an estimated population of 4000.
by the end of July not a single sick rabbit had been seen for weeks
MYXV spread poorly through the local rabbit populations and quickly died out, or so it appeared

verdicts.note: The CSIROpedia site list (Gunbower plus Wymah, Rutherglen, Coreen and Balldale) matches Kerr 2015's 'five field study sites'. The 4,000 is itself an estimate.

verdicts.safe_claim: Then 1950's unusually heavy rains bred clouds of mosquitoes along the rivers. They carried the virus, and within nine weeks outbreaks stretched across an area about 1,760 by 1,600 kilometres.
verdicts.safe_value: 1,760 km x 1,600 km, nine weeks after the Balldale outbreak (by mid-Feb 1951)

evidence.quote: nine weeks after the Balldale outbreak the disease ranged over an area 1 760 kilometres by 1 600 kilometres
unusually heavy rains which fell during 1950
rains in December 1950 produced more mosquitoes, the vector that spread the virus

verdicts.note: 'Ranged over' means scattered outbreaks across that span, not a uniformly infected block, so say 'outbreaks stretched across'. The km figures are probably metric conversions of mile figures. CSIROpedia's 1,760 x 1,600 km figure comes from a single page, but it is CSIRO's own history page.

verdicts.safe_claim: The 1950 virus killed up to 99.8 percent of the rabbits it infected.
verdicts.safe_value: 99.8% case fatality (infected rabbits only)

evidence.quote: case fatality rates (CFR) for laboratory and wild rabbits were estimated to be as high as 99.8%
The virus killed 99.8 per cent of rabbits that caught the infection
Localized population losses of 99%–100% were observed.

verdicts.note: Never say '99.8% of Australia's rabbits'. The same CSIRO 2011 page also says '99 per cent of infected rabbits', so if you want a round number, 99% is safe.

verdicts.safe_claim: By 1950 Australia had an estimated 600 million rabbits, though nobody ever counted them. In the worst-hit areas the virus wiped out nearly every rabbit.
verdicts.safe_value: 'an estimated 600 million' (late 1940s/1950); national drop unmeasured

evidence.quote: By the late 1940s the rabbit population had rapidly increased to 600 million.
The number of rabbits in Australia pre-1950 is not known
the reduction in population size during the first epizootic of 1950–1951 could not be measured
tens of millions of rabbits were killed, rather than hundreds of millions
The population dropped by half a billion in the first two years

verdicts.note: The 600 million figure has institutional backing (NMA; CSIRO 2011: 'By 1950 rabbit numbers in Australia reached 600 million'; PestSmart), but it is an estimate. The AAS 'half a billion' line conflicts with the peer-reviewed Kerr 2015 review, which says the drop could not be measured and that the 1952 field team estimated 'tens of millions' killed. Kerr also says pre-1950 numbers 'may have been an order of magnitude higher'. Do not narrate the half-billion drop.

verdicts.safe_claim: With the rabbits gone, pastures recovered. In 1952–53 the extra wool and meat was worth about 34 million pounds, A$68 million in today's decimal currency but not adjusted for inflation. Meanwhile the rabbit-skin export trade lost about two-thirds of its value.
verdicts.safe_value: ~£34 million (= A$68 million at the 1966 conversion rate, not inflation-adjusted); skin exports A$14m (1950-51) to A$4.5m (1954-55)

evidence.quote: In 1952-53, Australia’s wool and meat production jumped by $68 million
due to the absence of rabbits was worth some£34 million in one year.
Exports of rabbit skins fell from about A$14 million in 1950-51 to A$4.5 million in 1954-55.

verdicts.note: The researcher's caveat that these are 'currency values of the period' is wrong. Australia used pounds until 1966, so $68m is the decimal conversion (2 dollars to 1 pound) of about £34m and is not inflation-adjusted. The Unimelb Technology in Australia text credits the £34m to 'the sheep industry alone' after 1953, and says benefits to other industries were never assessed. Skin exports fell by about two-thirds, which is less dramatic than 'collapsed'.

verdicts.safe_claim: When people blamed the rabbit virus for a deadly human brain-fever outbreak, three of Australia's top scientists, Frank Fenner, Macfarlane Burnet and CSIRO chairman Ian Clunies Ross, injected themselves with it. None of them got sick.
verdicts.safe_value: 1951 (WEHI); dose 'strong enough to kill 100-1000 rabbits' (WEHI only); Murray Valley encephalitis

evidence.quote: strong enough to kill 100-1000 rabbits
a challenge issued by a councillor from Mildura
injected themselves with myxoma virus. They were unaffected
Fenner and two colleagues inoculated themselves with the myxoma virus

verdicts.note: The core event is confirmed by CSIROpedia, WEHI, MJA and Wikipedia. The '100–1,000 rabbits' dose appears only in WEHI's timeline, so phrase it as 'enough to kill hundreds of rabbits' or drop it. On the year, WEHI says 1951 and one CSIRO-published memoir reportedly says 1952 (not opened). Wikipedia wrongly puts the injection 'prior to the release'. Safest is no year, or 'in 1951' credited to WEHI.

verdicts.safe_claim: Within about a year the virus itself evolved slightly milder strains. Rabbits stayed sick longer, so mosquitoes could pass those strains on more easily.
verdicts.safe_value: slight attenuation within ~1 year; grade 3 strains (70-95% fatal) dominant ~30 years

evidence.quote: Within one year mutations in the virus had led to slightly less virulence
more readily transmitted by the mosquito vector because the infected rabbit survived longer
This situation persisted for the next 30 years

verdicts.note: In Kerr 2015's Table 5, grade 3A kills 90–95% and grade 3B 70–90%. Milder did not mean harmless.

verdicts.safe_claim: The rabbits evolved too. At one study site in New South Wales, the same test strain that killed 90 percent of the local rabbits killed only 26 percent seven generations later.
verdicts.safe_value: CFR 90% to 26% over 7 annual epizootics (Lake Urana, NSW; lab test with KM13 strain)

evidence.quote: CFRs dropped from 90% to 26%
seven annual epizootics of myxomatosis and approximately seven generations of selection
infection of non-immune rabbits from each generation with the KM13 strain

verdicts.note: This is one site, measured in the lab with a standard grade-3 strain, not the 1950 strain and not a national figure. 'Seven years later' is fine.

verdicts.safe_claim: Then the virus struck back. By the 1990s most field strains were even deadlier, in rabbits with no resistance, than the 1950 original.
verdicts.safe_value: most 1990s isolates more virulent than the 1950 strain (lab rabbits without resistance)

evidence.quote: most virus isolates from the 1990s induced a highly lethal immune collapse syndrome
the majority of these viruses were more virulent than the virus used to initiate the epidemic
far more virulent than the initially released strains in laboratory rabbits

verdicts.note: Three independent sources agree. The tests were done on laboratory rabbits without resistance, and Kerr 2017 says this explicitly. In wild, resistant rabbits it is an ongoing 'arms race', not a clean win for the virus. Keep the disease description abstract for an all-ages audience.

verdicts.safe_claim: To spread the virus where mosquitoes were scarce, Australia released European rabbit fleas: first on remote Macquarie Island in 1968, then on the mainland from 1969. A desert-adapted Spanish flea followed in 1993.
verdicts.safe_value: Dec 1968 Macquarie Is.; Aug 1969 Werribee (Vic); Spanish flea approved 1993

evidence.quote: first released on Macquarie Island in December 1968
The European rabbit flea was first released in Victoria in August 1969 at Werribee.
1993 Spanish rabbit flea ( Xenophsylla cunicularis ) adapted for arid conditions approved for release
were introduced but with minimal impact

verdicts.note: The abstracts were checked through Europe PMC. The 2024 Pipeline Strategy loosely dates the two fleas to 'the 1970s and 1990s'. How much they helped is disputed (CSIROpedia vs PestSmart), so don't claim they worked.

verdicts.safe_claim: The rabbits bounced back. By 1995 CSIRO estimated there were about 300 million again, and rising.
verdicts.safe_value: ~300 million (1995, CSIRO/PestSmart estimate)

evidence.quote: by 1995 had multiplied to an estimated 300 million
1995 Rabbit population about 300 million and climbing.
perhaps 5% of its previous level in the agricultural zone and perhaps 25% in the rangelands
rabbit numbers increased, but never to pre-1950 levels

verdicts.note: The estimates disagree. Against a pre-1950 figure of 600M, the peer-reviewed Kerr 2015 figures (5% of the former level on farmland, 25% in the rangelands in the early 1990s) imply far fewer than 300M, unless the pre-1950 total was much higher, which Kerr says is possible. Wikipedia's '200–300M by 1991' has no source in the text. Credit the number to CSIRO and use 'about'; on screen, 'hundreds of millions' is the safest wording.

verdicts.safe_claim: Next came a rabbit calicivirus. It was tested for three years in a high-security lab and then, from March 1995, in quarantine pens on Wardang Island, ahead of a release planned for 1998.
verdicts.safe_value: lab testing from June 1991 (AAHL Geelong); Wardang from March 1995; planned 1998

evidence.quote: for comprehensive testing over three years from June 1991
In March 1995, a quarantine station was set up on tiny Wardang Island
It was due for release in 1998, but, after only 6 months, it escaped

verdicts.note: The archived CSIRO 2008 factsheet independently confirms the June 1991 date and the 1995 escape. The planned 1998 release date comes from CSIROpedia only. Schwensow 2014 puts Wardang about 4 km offshore.

verdicts.safe_claim: In late September 1995 the virus got out of its pens, most likely carried by flies. By mid-October it was killing rabbits on the mainland, and within weeks it had turned up more than 300 kilometres away.
verdicts.safe_value: pen-to-pen spread 23 Sep; first infection outside quarantine ~24 Sep; mainland (Point Pearce) 12 Oct (arrived ~1 Oct); Yunta/Gum Creek 25-28 Oct 1995, >300 km

evidence.quote: began with its spread between rabbit pens on 23 September 1995
discovered on 12 October 1995 on Point Pearce
two widely separated sites over 300 km from Wardang Island
first recorded at Yunta and Gum Creek in north-eastern South Australia on 28th October

verdicts.note: The researcher missed that Schwensow 2014 does give a distance: Yunta and Gum Creek are 'over 300 km from Wardang Island'. First dead rabbits there are dated 25–26 Oct in Schwensow and 28 Oct in MLA, so say 'late October' or 'within weeks'.

verdicts.safe_claim: Just before the escape, the number of flies on the island shot up about a thousandfold.
verdicts.safe_value: ~1,000-fold increase in bushflies (Musca vetustissima)

evidence.quote: approximately a 1,000-fold increase in the number of bushflies, Musca vetustissima
No rabbit calicivirus was detected on C. nociva or bushflies

verdicts.note: The abstract was checked through Europe PMC. The bushfly surge is peer-reviewed, but in the 24 September sample MLA found the virus on blowflies, not bushflies. Say 'flies'.

verdicts.safe_claim: The escaped virus spread at roughly 15 to 60 kilometres a week, and that's the minimum.
verdicts.safe_value: 2-9 km/day = ~15-60 km/week (minimum)

evidence.quote: a rate of spread of 2–9 km day −1 or about 15–60 km week −1
This must be taken as a minimum rate

verdicts.note: Measured in South Australia. Across the Adelaide region the rate was about 20 km a week.

verdicts.safe_claim: Calicivirus cut Australia's rabbits by about 60 percent nationwide, and by up to 95 percent in the dry inland.
verdicts.safe_value: ~60% nationwide; up to 95% in arid areas

evidence.quote: Nation-wide, rabbit numbers fell by 60%
up to a 95% reduction in pest rabbit
It initially knocked down 90% of the feral rabbit population
The numbers of rabbits are down to ten or fifteen percent of their original numbers.

verdicts.note: Sources disagree on the national figure: PestSmart says 90% at first, while Schwensow 2014 says 60%, citing the 1998 studies by Bowen & Read and Mutze et al. PestSmart's timeline also says 'up to 98%' in arid areas. The peer-reviewed pair of 60% nationwide and up to 95% in dry areas is the most defensible. CSIROpedia's 10–15% figure refers only to arid zones.

verdicts.safe_claim: The official release came only in 1996. Western Australia's ceremony was six infected rabbits in October 1996, but by then the virus had already reached the state on its own and spread through more than 30 shires.
verdicts.safe_value: WA controlled release 18 Oct 1996 (6 rabbits, near Cranbrook); first WA deaths May 1996; >30 shires already affected

evidence.quote: releasing six infected rabbits near the Great Southern town of Cranbrook
first confirmed deaths of wild rabbits from the disease were on the WA - South Australia border in May
It had since spread through more than 30 agricultural and southern pastoral shires in WA.
has been used since 1996

verdicts.note: The researcher missed the stronger detail that by the time of the ceremony the virus had spread through 30+ WA shires. NMA wrongly says calicivirus was 'released in 1995', and the Pipeline Strategy says the release 'took place in 1995–96'. I found no exact national approval date.

verdicts.safe_claim: Rabbits in cooler, wetter regions had help: a harmless cousin virus, identified in 2009, partly protected them.
verdicts.safe_value: RCV-A1 identified 2009; most prevalent in temperate south-east

evidence.quote: 2009 Benign endemic rabbit calicivirus (RCV-A1) discovered and characterised.
RCV-A1 was most prevalent in the temperate zones of south-east Australia
may give rabbits some resistance to RCD, particularly in cooler and wetter areas

verdicts.note: The virus was 'identified' in 2009 but had been in Australia long before. Its protection is 'transient and partial' (Pipeline).

verdicts.safe_claim: In 2015 a new strain, RHDV2, was found in Australia. Nobody released it; it just turned up.
verdicts.safe_value: first isolate 13 May 2015 (ACT); likely arrived 2014

evidence.quote: came from a rabbit found in Australian Capital Territory on May 13, 2015
a variant of RHDV that was not released
likely arrival on the Australian continent up to 6 to 18 months earlier

verdicts.note: The full texts were read through Europe PMC. 'Detected in 2015' is the safe wording. How it got into Australia is unknown, so don't say 'from Europe'.

verdicts.safe_claim: That uninvited strain cut rabbit numbers by about 60 percent on average and within 18 months had become the main strain.
verdicts.safe_value: -60% average (18 sites, 2014-2018); -64% sustained at 6 sites to 2022; dominant within 18 months

evidence.quote: reduced by 60% between 2014 and 2018 based on monitoring data acquired from 18 sites
Within 18 months it had mostly replaced the existing RHDV1 strain
Reduces rabbit populations by 60% on average and up to 80% in some populations

verdicts.note: The 60% figure is an average from monitored sites, not a national census. Credit it to nature, since nobody released this strain.

verdicts.safe_claim: In March 2017 Australia deliberately released a Korean strain called K5 at hundreds of sites. Early volunteer counts suggested about a one-third drop, but scientists' own monitoring sites showed no clear decline, and the uninvited strain won out.
verdicts.safe_value: first week March 2017; >600 sites selected (DPIRD) / 738 citizen-science sites (Cox 2019); ~34% one-month drop at citizen-science sites only

evidence.quote: took place during the first week of March 2017
More than 600 release sites were selected, including 110 sites in Western Australia
averaging a monthly reduction of 34% at the citizen science sites one month after the release
No such declines were observed at the professionally monitored sites (n = 22).
It is likely that RHDV1-K5 was outcompeted by RHDV2

verdicts.note: This is the key nuance the researcher missed. The 34% comes from the paper behind it (Cox et al. 2019, Sci Rep): it was a one-month drop at sites run by citizen scientists, and the authors flag possible unconscious bias, while professional sites showed no decline. The site count also differs: DPIRD says 'more than 600 selected' and Cox reports 738 citizen-science release sites, so say 'hundreds of sites'. K5 is a variant of RHDV1, not a new virus.

verdicts.safe_claim: Today Australia again has an estimated 200 million wild rabbits, and in Western Australia numbers are back to levels not seen since the mid-1990s.
verdicts.safe_value: ~200 million (news estimate, July 2026); NMA 'at least 150 million'

evidence.quote: an estimated current population of around 200 million
Australia is home to at least 150 million feral rabbits
rabbit numbers had climbed to levels not seen since the mid-1990s

verdicts.note: The 'not seen in decades' line applies only to Western Australia. It is a quote from the Invasive Species Council found in secondary outlets, not a measurement. Caution: the same QCL article that gives '200 million' also wrongly says the 2017 release 'wiped out around 60pc of the rabbit population', so its figures need double-checking. Always say 'an estimated'.

verdicts.safe_claim: Rabbits still cost Australian farming over $200 million a year and threaten more than 300 native species.
verdicts.safe_value: >$200 million/yr ($206M, Gong et al. 2009); >300 native species (322 nationally listed threatened species)

evidence.quote: rabbits cause $206 million in losses each year to the agricultural industry
rabbits cost the Australian economy more than $200 million per year
more than 300 Australian native flora and fauna species
impacts 322 nationally listed threatened species

verdicts.note: The cost figure comes from a 2009 study and has not been updated. 'Over $200 million' is backed independently by NMA and Wool.com. Note that 'species' includes plants.

verdicts.safe_claim: Today's toolkit combines everything: baits, fumigation, ripping warrens, traps, shooting, fences and viruses. Scientists say no single weapon works on its own.
verdicts.safe_value: NATSOP-RAB001-009 (1080 & pindone baits, fumigation, ripping, explosives, padded-jaw traps, shooting, K5 baits)

evidence.quote: K5 is not the silver bullet for rabbit eradication in Australia
NATSOP-RAB005 National Standard Operating Procedure: Rabbit warren destruction by ripping
Today it affects an estimated 40-50% of the rabbit population

verdicts.note: The 40–50% figure refers to myxomatosis still circulating. For an all-ages audience, show tractors, fences and lab scenes, not dead animals.

verdicts.safe_claim: Scientists say Australia needs a new rabbit virus every 10 to 15 years to stay ahead. Yet national funding for that work lapsed in 2022, until a new $4 million program was announced in July 2026.
verdicts.safe_value: new agent every 10-15 years; national program unfunded 2022-2026; $4M incl. $2.6M Commonwealth (27 July 2026); ~$70 billion benefit 1950-2011

evidence.quote: ideally to enable a new agent to be released every 10 to 15 years or so
the biocontrol program has remained unfunded since 2022
$2.6 million in Commonwealth funding
Meat & Livestock Australia and CSIRO are co-funding a series of projects

verdicts.note: 'Biocontrol research went unfunded' overstates it. What lapsed was the national, federally backed program: QCL says 'the biocontrol program' and the ISC says there was no federal funding. Meanwhile MLA and CSIRO co-funded projects, per the 2024 Pipeline Strategy. The ~$70 billion benefit for 1950–2011 is confirmed in the same PDF.

verdicts.safe_claim: Frank Fenner said that for scale and speed, the epidemic must be without parallel in the history of infections.
verdicts.safe_value: Fenner quote via NMA

evidence.quote: for scale and speed [the myxomatosis epidemic] must be without parallel in the history of infections
Fenner announced the eradication of smallpox to the World Health Assembly on 8 May 1980.

verdicts.note: The quote is attributed to Fenner by the NMA, a government museum. The bracketed words are NMA's insertion. A web search found no original publication, probably Fenner & Ratcliffe's 1965 book 'Myxomatosis', so present it as a quote, not exact wording from a named publication. The smallpox announcement detail is confirmed.

missed: Conventional control did work locally before WWII. CSIROpedia says the war took away the manpower for 'normal trapping, shooting and poisoning which kept rabbits to manageable numbers', and NMA and PestSmart both blame the late-1940s 600-million peak partly on WWII manpower shortages. https://csiropedia.csiro.au/Myxomatosis-to-control-rabbits/ quote: 'Farmers and graziers had been away at the war, unable to carry out normal trapping, shooting and poisoning'

The '$68 million' is not 'currency of the period'. Australia used pounds until 1966, and a contemporary-based estimate is about £34 million for the sheep industry alone. https://austehc.unimelb.edu.au/tia/045.html quote: 'due to the absence of rabbits was worth some£34 million in one year.'

K5's 34% knockdown comes only from citizen-science spotlight counts one month after release. Professionally monitored sites showed no decline, and the authors warn of possible unconscious bias. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6811621/ quote: 'No such declines were observed at the professionally monitored sites (n = 22).'

There is a usable distance for the 1995 escape: the first inland outbreaks were more than 300 km from the island within about a month. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4231595/ quote: 'two widely separated sites over 300 km from Wardang Island'

WA's 18 Oct 1996 'official release' came after the virus had already spread through more than 30 WA shires, which is a stronger version of the story-gold point. https://www.wa.gov.au/government/media-statements/Court%20Coalition%20Government/Six-rabbits-infected-with-RCD-released-nr-GS-town-of-Cranbrook-19961018 quote: 'It had since spread through more than 30 agricultural and southern pastoral shires in WA.'

The peer-reviewed estimate for the early 1990s conflicts with 'recovered to 300 million'. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4379559/ quote: 'perhaps 5% of its previous level in the agricultural zone and perhaps 25% in the rangelands'

The QCL article used for 'around 200 million' itself repeats the myth that the 2017 release removed 60%, so its numbers need cross-checking. https://www.queenslandcountrylife.com.au/story/9316922/agriculture-minister-julie-collins-unveils-urgent-rabbit-strategy/ quote: 'wiped out around 60pc of the rabbit population'

PestSmart's own 'initially knocked down 90%' for RHDV1 conflicts with the peer-reviewed 'about 60% nationwide'. Use the latter and don't mix the two. https://pestsmart.org.au/toolkit-resource/key-facts-about-rabbit-biocontrol-in-australia/ quote: 'It initially knocked down 90% of the feral rabbit population'
Loir was Pasteur's nephew by marriage: his mother was Marie Pasteur's sister. https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrien_Loir quote: 'Il est le neveu par alliance de Louis Pasteur'

The prize-entries count has a second, independent rough figure that supports 'nearly 1,500' rather than the unverifiable '1,456'. https://www.penguin.com.au/books/pasteurs-gambit-9781742745398 quote: 'would attract 1500 entries.'

The researcher's phrase 'birds, the one group chicken cholera kills' is false, because the plan relied on it killing rabbits. The AAS says it appeared fatal to all birds. https://www.science.org.au/news-events/news-views/adrien-loir-louis-pasteur-australasian-rabbit-plague quote: 'while chicken cholera killed rabbits, it was not sufficiently transmissible'

The '10 million rabbits in two months' myth is now confirmed as unsupported: the archived CSIRO 2008 RCD factsheet that Wikipedia cites says only 'killed large numbers of rabbits'. https://web.archive.org/web/2012id_/http://www.csiro.au/resources/~/media/CSIROau/Divisions/CSIRO%20Entomology/RabbitCalicivirusDiseas_Ento_PDF%20Standard.pdf quote: 'The virus swept across the Flinders Ranges through the arid zone and killed large numbers of rabbits.'

There is a usable sourced superlative if wanted: CSIRO calls myxomatosis the world's first successful biological control of a mammal pest. It is CSIRO's own claim, so attribute it. https://web.archive.org/web/20111125204128/http://www.csiro.au/science/Myxomatosis-History quote: 'It was the world's first successful biological control program of a mammalian pest'

Founding release, for the other domain: the brief's '24 rabbits' comes from the AAS article, while the NMA says 13 rabbits were released on Christmas Day 1859. https://www.nma.gov.au/defining-moments/resources/rabbits-introduced quote: 'On Christmas day 1859 Thomas Austin ... released 13 European wild rabbits on his estate'

Mongoose: the abstract says none of the releases established a population, which is a clean 'Rabbits win' line. https://doi.org/10.1071/ZO10043 quote: 'Australia escaped the additional devastation of an established mongoose population'

Access notes: CSIROpedia, the NMA and CSIRO 2011 were read through Wayback Machine copies. The AAS article loaded directly. PMC articles were read through Europe PMC because PMC showed a reCAPTCHA. Trove and the Tasmanian parliamentary PDFs showed bot checks and were not bypassed, so the 1887 prize-condition wording and the 1,456 figure stay unverified at the primary source.

geodata.name: Dated rabbit-spread isochrones (redraw, do not copy): Stodart & Parer 1988, as drawn in Alves et al. 2022 PNAS Fig. 1
geodata.url: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC9436340/fullTextXML  (figure: https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/407f/9436340/df4117741509/pnas.2122734119fig01.jpg). Original: Stodart E., Parer I. (1988) 'Colonisation of Australia by the Rabbit Oryctolagus cuniculus (L.)', CSIRO Division of Wildlife and Ecology Project Report No. 6.
geodata.license: The article and figure are 'Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives License 4.0 (CC BY-NC-ND)', so do not use the figure itself. The dated frontier positions are facts and may be redrawn; cite 'after Stodart & Parer 1988'.
geodata.notes:
Caption (verbatim): 'Dashed lines in mainland Australia show the frontier of spread of rabbits across the continent from the Thomas Austin property in Barwon Park (based on Stodart and Parer, ref. 21)'. Lines are labelled 1859, 1870, 1880, 1890, 1900, 1910, 1920 and 1980. These approximate courses are read from a 763 px figure, so get the original report for precision:
- 1859: point at Barwon Park (-38.22, 143.99).
- 1870: small arc round western Victoria to about the SA border.
- 1880: from the head of Spencer Gulf (SA) east along about 32°S into western NSW, then south to the Victorian highlands. A separate '1880' label sits near Sydney ('earliest records of rabbits in mainland Australia', the 1788 First Fleet).
- 1890: from the Great Australian Bight coast (about 131°E) NE into SW Queensland (about 26°S, 141°E), then down along the NSW ranges to the coast.
- 1900: from the WA/SA Nullarbor coast near Eucla north-east through central Australia to about 23°S at the NT/Qld border.
- 1910 west: from the WA south coast near Esperance/Hopetoun north through the WA interior to about the Pilbara, roughly along the No.1 fence line, which is a strong visual.
- 1910 north: across central NT at about 20°S to the Gulf country, then SE to the central Queensland coast.
- 1920: WA west coast (Geraldton–Shark Bay and the SW corner), plus an inner arc in Queensland.
- 1980: across the far north at about 17°S (Kimberley to the base of Cape York).
The paper also states: 'At a rate of 100 km per year, it took rabbits 50 y to cover an area 13 times the size of their native range'. A dated point list is in the next entry.

geodata.name: Dated spread points for map pins (text sources)
geodata.url: Low & Strong 1981, 'A preliminary assessment of distribution and abundance of rabbits in land systems in the Northern Territory': https://rangelandsgateway.org/sites/default/files/2021-01/arsbc-1981-86-93.pdf | SLWA: https://slwa.wa.gov.au/stories/wa-history/rabbit-proof-fence | Rabbit Free Australia: https://rabbitfreeaustralia.org.au/?p=3162
geodata.license: Text facts with citations; no image reuse.
geodata.notes:
Low & Strong 1981 (verbatim): 'The rabbit had reached the N.T. border from NW South Australia in small numbers by 1901 (Murray, 1904a)'. They also report Lake Amadeus by 1901, 'By 1915 it was well established on the Hale River near Aritunga (Day, 1916)', 'by the mid -1920s it had reached the Tanami Desert area (Terry, 1927)', and 'had probably reached the N.T. along the Georgina River by 1920 (Myers, 1970)'.
SLWA: 'By 1896 it had been found as far west as Eucla and 200 kilometres further west at Twilight Cove'. A web-search summary gave 1894 for the first Eucla sighting with no verifiable source, so treat Eucla as 1894 vs 1896 and verify.
Rabbit Free Australia: 'By 1867, eight years after Austin's initial release, rabbits in large numbers were reported up to 60 km from Barwon Park'. Donald, 270 km north, was reached four years later, carried there by pastoralists, so human transport played a part.
Wikipedia/GeoHack coordinates: Barwon Park -38.2247, 143.9955; Wardang Island -34.50, 137.367; Cape Keraudren -19.95, 119.767; Burracoppin -31.397, 118.477; Eucla -31.675, 128.883; Jigalong -23.361, 120.784; Hopetoun -33.948, 120.126.

research.gaps:
Beats with no free real image, which need a diagram, 3D or a redraw:
(1) The 1859 release itself, the 24 rabbits and Austin's original two-room homestead. Only the 1888 Austin portrait, 2025 photos of the 1869–71 mansion and the 1869 shooting engraving exist. The clipper Lightning prints (A02/A03) can stand in for the voyage.
(2) Fence CONSTRUCTION 1901–1907. No free high-res photo was found. Wikipedia gives the crew as '120 men, 350 camels, 210 horses and 41 donkeys' under Anketell from 1904. Every free fence photo is from the 1920s–30s maintenance era. A lead is 'Camel team leaving Carnarvon for Rabbit Proof Fence', 1903, Kellerberrin Historical Society (https://collectionswa.net.au/items/7a8b6b53-dd6a-451b-8d30-5621cef8a848), but it is low-res with no rights statement. Do the build as an animated map line with camel icons.
(3) Rabbit SPREAD by year. There is no reusable image (Alves 2022 Fig. 1 is CC BY-NC-ND, and the NMA 'Spread of rabbits throughout Australia (approximate dates only)' map credited to CSIRO is behind Cloudflare with an unknown licence). Redraw the isochrones on Natural Earth from the description in geodata, ideally checked against Stodart & Parer 1988.
(4) Fence route map. Redraw from the DPIRD-046/047/048 GeoJSON (check the licence conflict) or trace by hand; Commons A23 is a fallback.
(5) The 1950–53 myxomatosis outbreak in the field and the 1995 calicivirus (RHDV) escape. There are no free, non-gory field photos. Use the CSIRO release photo (A25), the QSA 1951–52 lab and kit images (721 px only) and electron micrographs (A30) or an animated 'virus' graphic.
(6) Huge plague masses. The only strong free image is the 1938 Wardang waterhole photo (A06/A07). It is NOT a natural plague scene: CSIRO says it was taken 'under controlled conditions during myxoma virus trials'. Use it with an honest caption, or as a stylised plague moment without claiming date or place.
(7) Rabbit drives. The Commons hits are US jackrabbit drives (California, Oregon) with dead animals, so they are the wrong country and not all-ages.
AVOID for an all-ages audience (carcasses): File:Rabbit_plague_1918.jpg ('Load of over 3,800 rabbits at Mudgee', 588 px), File:Rabbits_in_Warren.jpg (1949, rows of hung carcasses), File:Port_Adelaide_Freezing_Works_Showing_Rabbits_and_Workers(GN05297).jpg (CC0, hanging carcasses), File:Preparing_to_skin_some_rabbits..., the SLNSW 'In a rabbit factory' images and all 'Rabbit with myxomatosis' photos.
Other flags:
- The SLWA 1926 set (A14–A17) is out of copyright, but the SLWA viewer says 'personal use only... contact SLWA'. Get permission or upload to Commons first; A12 and A13 are already on Commons as PD-Australia.
- The Cobar 1905 photo shows a NSW netting fence, not the WA fence, despite its Commons category.
- Barwon Park's Wikipedia lead says Austin released 'a dozen' rabbits, while Alves et al. 2022 say the consignment 'arrived in Melbourne with 24 rabbits on board'. The research/fact agent should settle this.
- The Commons date '1769' on the Lightning print is the ship's tonnage, not a year.
- The Commons API rate-limits fast requests; scripts should honour retry-after.

verdicts.note: The licence is right. Correction: RMG gives the date as 1854, not 'c.1854–1860s'. The ID is PAD6464, even though the filename says PU6464. The Commons date '1769' is the tonnage, as stated. The imprint reads 'John R. Isaac, 62 Castle St Liverpool' (Commons category: John Raphael Isaac). Alves et al. name only 'the ship Lightning'. The Black Ball clipper fits, since it was built in 1854 for the Liverpool–Australia trade and burned at Geelong in 1869. I could not check a Dec 1859 Port Phillip shipping list because Trove blocked automated access. Caption it 'the clipper Lightning', not 'the exact moment the rabbits arrived'. RMG sells image licences, but the Commons PD-Art position covers this faithful 2D scan.

Only 599 x 400, and as a 1949 Australian photo it was still in copyright on 1 Jan 1996, so its US status is doubtful (URAA). Use with caution.

Car driving through the Stanthorpe rabbit gate, 1934, a companion to A18: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:StateLibQld_1_132376_Driving_through_rabbit_gate,_Stanthorpe,_1934.jpg. Licence: '{{PD-Australia}}', 1000 x 599.

SLWA's own policy supports reusing its PD photos such as A12–A17 with acknowledgement: https://slwa.wa.gov.au/about/corporate-information/copyright-library-collections. Quote: 'Where this material is out of copyright it may be freely used provided the Library and the creator are acknowledged'. The item pages still say 'personal use only… contact', so request written OK for A14–A17.

US rule of thumb for Australian photos: a photo must have been PD in Australia on 1 Jan 1996 to be safe in the US (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Template:PD-1996: 'in the public domain in its home country on the URAA date'). Under the 50-year term, that means photos taken in 1945 or earlier. The 1949 Warren images and the c.1951–52 Queensland State Archives myxomatosis photos fail this test; the 1926 SLWA, 1934 Stanthorpe and 1938 Wardang photos pass.

Fact nuance for the script: Alves et al. 2022 quote family member Joan Palmer saying only 13 rabbits were sent (6 wild, 7 domestic), and they speak of 'the discrepancy between 13 animals sent from Britain and the 24 that arrived'. So '24 rabbits' is the number that ARRIVED. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC9436340/fullTextXML

Wikipedia's Barwon Park article contradicts itself: the lead says 'release a dozen of them', while the History section says 'two dozen wild rabbits'. Do not cite its lead for the number. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barwon_Park

Attribution detail for A05: the engraving carries the monograms 'NC' (Nicholas Chevalier, who travelled with the Duke's 1867 tour) and 'R.B.'. The National Museum of Australia lists it as 'The Prince at the Rabbit Warren, Barwon Park', engraved by Robert Bruce: https://digital-classroom.nma.gov.au/images/prince-rabbit-warren-barwon-park-engraving-robert-bruce (page behind Cloudflare; title from the URL slug and search listing).
