saturated_angles: '24 rabbits → hundreds of millions / ruined / broke / took over a continent' (Thomas Austin, 1859, hunting): Pomegranate 4.52M plus 20+ near-copies in about 10 languages. 23 such Shorts in our sample were uploaded in 2026 alone (~16.2M combined views), against 11 in 2025.

The full chronological recap: release → no predators → fence failed → myxomatosis kills 90% → survivors resistant → calicivirus 1995/96 → still ~200M. Almost every transcript checked follows exactly this order (Bilgilenme, Light in sky, Casual Discovery, Wild Heart, the Korean and Telugu channels). A 'history recap' adds nothing new.

Inflated-number titles: '600 million', '300 million in 70 years', '10 billion' ('24 rabbits → 10B', 'How 1 Man Turned 24 Rabbits into 10 BILLION', Mandarin Tech '10 Billion Rabbits'). The number escalation is overused, and the biggest numbers are badly sourced.
'They brought foxes and cats to eat the rabbits and it backfired' (gautam explain, Sahabat Hewan, Minutes Mystery, Fact Eagle). The script is literally cloned across languages.
'Why don't Australians just eat them?' Incredible Stories 3.07M long plus a 2.02M reupload; Shorts from Afortunado (391k), Wild Heart (54k) and Lucky (33k); 'each person would have to eat X kg' math.

'World's longest fence isn't US–Mexico / isn't for humans' reveal (VeeVex 3.81M, Geo All Day 1.18M, GeoNique 890k, Fluxi 776k, Johnny Harris 1.40M, Half as Interesting 1.62M). Heavily saturated, and it is about the DINGO fence (5,614 km), not the rabbit-proof fence. Competitors already mix the two up (Walter's Shorts: '5,600 km Fence to Stop... Rabbits').
Great Emu War / 'Australia lost a war to birds': More Parz Short 10.2M, OverSimplified 28.7M, dozens of Shorts. Use it at most as a one-line callback, never as the subject.

The search 'rabbit proof fence' is dominated by the 2002 film Rabbit-Proof Fence and Stolen Generations clips (trailer 1.24M, Bollywood explainers 5.49M). A title built only on 'Rabbit-Proof Fence' competes with that and is ambiguous.
fresh_angles: Pasteur and the prize: no video in any of our searches tells it. 'pasteur rabbits australia' returns only generic rabbit videos; 'pasteur prize rabbits' returns unrelated FNAF videos. Wikipedia (Rabbits in Australia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabbits_in_Australia): 'An offer by the New South Wales government of a £25,000 reward for a biological control of rabbits attracted the attention of Louis Pasteur'. A world-famous scientist enters the war and doesn't win: a strong 'Round 2' beat.

The virus that escaped from the test island: the 'wardang island virus' and 'calicivirus escaped wardang island' searches return no relevant video at all. Wikipedia: 'The virus escaped from a quarantine compound on Wardang Island, South Australia, where the field tests were being carried out'. A plot twist nobody uses (and no gore needed).

The fence finished after the rabbits were already past it (WA fence 1901–1907): only two micro Shorts exist, 'The Fence the Rabbits Had Already Crossed' (32 views) and 'Australia Built a 1,139-Mile Fence to Stop Rabbits. The Rabbits Won.' (~2.2k). Demand for 'Australian fence' curiosity is proven (VeeVex 3.81M, Isaac Butterfield 1.81M), but nobody with reach has told the irony in English. Exact dates and lengths must come from the fact agents (Wikipedia: 'From 1901 to 1907, a rabbit-proof fence was built in Western Australia in an unsuccessful attempt to contain the rabbits').

Scoreboard format 'Australia vs Rabbits' with numbered rounds (hunting → fence → Pasteur → myxoma → calicivirus) and a running score: no competitor uses a score. 'rabbits 1 australia 0' and 'australia vs rabbits score' return only NRL Rabbitohs results. Proven siblings: 'Cane Toads vs Australia' 2.74M; 'lost a war/battle to animals' (emu 10.2M, Napoleon vs 3,000 rabbits 1.87M). It continues the series line ('Humans two, Volcano zero'). Twist: this is the first episode humans don't win cleanly.

Evolutionary arms race (rabbits evolve resistance, the virus evolves milder): English Shorts barely touch it ('Australia's Rabbits Started Surviving the Virus', ~1.3k). Only the Korean 숫자로 보는 역사 (122k) and Tamil Unmaigal mention the '0.2% survivors'. Good as the 'the rabbits fought back' round.

2026 news peg / open ending: ABC News (Australia), 17 Sep 2026, 'Why are rabbits making a comeback?' says calicivirus is 'no longer effective and a new biocontrol still years away'. Lets the Short end on 'the match isn't over' instead of a closed recap. None of the big Shorts has a current ending.

Genetic 'detective' proof that one release started it: only a single line in Pomegranate's script/description ('Genetic studies have since proven...'). A hook like 'DNA traced Australia's rabbits back to one farm' is unused as a lead (fact agents must confirm the paper and wording).

Fence with an unintended side effect (climate/clouds): Isaac Butterfield's 'Australia built a fence that change the climate' (1.81M) proves the hook but is about the dingo fence. A rabbit-proof-fence version has not been done in Shorts. Use only if the fact agents find a solid primary source; otherwise skip.
title_patterns_that_win: '[Country] lost a war to [ANIMAL]' / '[Famous person] Lost a Battle Against [N] RABBITS': 'Australia lost a war to EMUS' 10.2M, 'How Napoleon Lost a Battle Against 3,000 RABBITS' 1.87M, 'How Australia Keeps Losing Wars To Animals' 1.49M (long), 'Australia Had a Full-Blown War Against Emus and Lost' 973k (long). The highest ceiling in this niche.

'[Small number] [Animal] [Ruined / Broke / Took Over] [Australia / an Entire Continent]': '24 Rabbits Ruined Australia' 4.52M, 'How Rabbits Took Over Australia' 2.74M, '24 Rabbits Broke an Entire Continent' 1.19M, 'How Rabbits TOOK OVER Australia' 784k, 'How 102 Toads Took Over an Entire Continent' 465k. Works, but crowded, so it needs a twist word.
'[X] vs [Country]', 3–4 words: 'Cane Toads vs Australia' 2.74M in ~6 weeks. Fits 'Australia vs Rabbits' and the channel's 'Humans vs Volcano' series.
Equation/arrow titles: '1 Mistake = 600 Million Rabbits' 3.23M; '24 → 200 million' (BBC Earth). Strong, but only if the number is sourced.
Myth-reversal question: 'Longest FENCE Border in the World isn't for Humans?!' 3.81M; 'Why the World's Longest Fence Exists' 1.18M; 'Why Did Australia Build the World's Longest Fence?' 776k.
Impossible-sounding consequence: 'Australia built a fence that change the climate' 1.81M; '200 Billion Teeth!' 575k.
Curiosity 'why don't they…': 'Why don't they eat wild rabbits in Australia?' 3.07M (long).

Common features of the winners: 3–6 words, a number in the title, 'Australia' named explicitly, one word in CAPS (RABBITS / EMUS / TOOK OVER), optional 🐇🇦🇺. Winning Shorts run 20–66 s (Pomegranate wins at 20 s).
research.notes:
METHOD: Innertube client from /Users/khorengrigoryan/shorts/markt-analyse/tools/yt.py (file not modified), English client hl=en, gl=US. About 45 queries, each run four ways: Shorts by views, Shorts by relevance, long videos by views, and relevance. That gave about 2,100 unique videos. All view counts in the lists are exact viewCount from the player endpoint, fetched 19 Oct 2026. Short status was checked via youtube.com/shorts/ID (200 = Short, 303 = long). Hooks come from auto-captions fetched with the iOS client.

Raw data is in /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-khorengrigoryan-shorts/1c348364-7484-4799-a95b-8df54e91b3e8/scratchpad/:
- details.json: 458 candidates with descriptions
- caps.json: transcripts
- fresh.json: the fresh-angle queries
- all.json
- scripts: rabbits.py, rabbits2.py, details.py, caps.py, fresh.py

Caveat: YouTube returns only about 20–50 results per Shorts search, so some mid-size Shorts may be missing. Pure cute-bunny or hunting clips with 10M–97M views turned up in the searches and were left out as off-topic.

KEY MARKET FINDINGS
1. The topic is hot in 2026, but crowded mainly outside English. Of the top 10 Australia-rabbit Shorts, only Pomegranate (4.52M, 20 s) has English audio. Fact Eagle Rs, gautam explain and Bilgilenme Projesi use English titles over Hindi or Turkish audio. With English audio, only six reach 50k or more: Pomegranate 4.52M, Casual Discovery 784k, Good Enough 195k, stakuyi 120k, BBC Earth 54k, Wild Heart 54k. So the English Short space has one dominant 20-second retelling and no strong storytelling version.
2. The best-performing frame across neighbour topics is 'humans/army/country LOST to animals' (emu 10.2M, Napoleon vs rabbits 1.87M), plus a bare 'X vs Australia' (cane toads 2.74M). Our 'Australia vs Rabbits' plus a scoreboard combines both, and no one has used a score.
3. The closest stylistic competitor is PolySoldier, a low-poly 3D, number-dense Short ('They Declared War On Emus And Lost', 204k, 6 Oct 2026). Mapper Maniac does what-if emu maps (538k).

TITLE IDEAS (they follow the winning patterns; every number must be cleared by the fact agents):
- 'Australia vs Rabbits'
- 'Australia Built a Fence. The Rabbits Were Already Through.'
- 'Australia vs Rabbits: Final Score?'
- 'Even Pasteur Couldn't Beat Australia's Rabbits'

MYTH AND INCONSISTENCY FLAGS FROM COMPETITOR CONTENT (for the fact-check agents):
- '10 billion rabbits' (often '…in the 1920s') appears in Casual Discovery, Good Enough, the Arabic story channel, Tamil Unmaigal, Mandarin Tech, Big vibes and Dhil. ABC News (Australia)'s reporter also says 'peak of 10 billion in the 1920s' (Sep 2026). The Wikipedia article Rabbits in Australia does not contain the word 'billion'. It gives 'an estimated 600 million' before myxomatosis, which brought the number 'to around 100 million', then '200–300 million by 1991'. Treat 10 billion as unsourced unless the fact agents find a primary source.
- 'How many rabbits?' varies by competitor: 24 (most), 13 (PBS Terra, Wild Heart, gautam explain, Илья Пригожин, MDEEZY SHORTS), '12 pairs' (Casual Discovery), 20 (Eul4). Wikipedia says 'the release of at least 13 wild rabbits by Thomas Austin for hunting purposes in October 1859, on his property, Barwon Park, near Winchelsea, Victoria'. The user's '24' therefore needs exact sourcing and possibly careful wording.
- 'Christmas Day 1859' / 'Christmas gift' (Wild Heart, the Korean channel, Narasimha FactVerse) clashes with Wikipedia's 'October 1859'. Flag it.
- Fence lengths in competitor content: '2,000 miles' (Casual Discovery), '3,000 km', '3,256 km' (most), '3,250 km', '1,139-Mile'. Walter's Shorts wrongly calls the 5,600 km dingo fence the rabbit fence. Fluxi says the dingo fence 'started in the 1880s as a rabbit fence'.
- Calicivirus is dated 1996 by Casual Discovery and Wild Heart, against Wikipedia's escape 'by late October 1995'. Myxomatosis kill rate is '90%' in some videos and '99.8%' in the Korean one; RHDV is said to have killed '90%'.
- Unsourced figures to verify or avoid: '300 million in 70 years', '70% of Australia', '$200 million damage per year', '$20 million' (bhagath tv), '800 million in the 1940s' (Korean), '14,000 shot in one season on Austin's land' (Илья Пригожин); Wikipedia instead cites the Geelong Advertiser reporting 50,000 killed by 1866.

AUDIENCE-SAFETY NOTE: competitors lean on gore-adjacent framing ('the bloodiest war in history', 'inject them with deadly diseases', myxomatosis footage with millions of views). The virus rounds can be told as an outbreak spreading on a map or a scoreboard ticking, with no sick animals shown. That fits the all-ages brief and sets us apart.
